World.title: Buried Inside Liberia’s Port Decentralization Bill: A Potential 2029 Rivalry – and the Security Gaps Nobody Wrote In
World.content:
A Vice President and a Senate Pro Tempore are quietly positioning for 2029 over who profits most from Liberia’s new port law — while the bill itself creates four independent port security forces with no shared command, no seat for the Liberia Drug Enforcement Agency or Coast Guard, and no security mandate at all. The recent Mark Kuiah/IB Atlantic IV case already showed what that gap costs under one port. The law is about to test those same gaps under four ports.

By Rodney D, Sieh, [email protected]

Monrovia – There was a ceremony, a signature, and the kind of applause that photographs well. What the cameras did not catch is the quieter dogfight that has been building in the corridors of power for months underneath President Boakai’s decision to sign away the National Port Authority’s roughly seven-decade monopoly — one some insiders describe as a strategic, if premature, political play that could yet derail the president’s broader development agenda. In one corner stands Senator Nyonblee Karnga-Lawrence, architect of the legislation and a lawmaker hoping it transforms her home county, Grand Bassa, into something it has never quite been allowed to become. In the other stands Vice President Jeremiah Koung, from vote-rich Nimba County, watching a bill he has never publicly endorsed hand a rival exactly the kind of political win he cannot easily match.

The two have circled each other since the 2023 presidential campaign, when Boakai narrowed his running-mate shortlist to the pair before settling on the man from Nimba. It was a decision that left one camp elevated and the other, by most accounts, quietly stung. Their relationship has been strained ever since, and while recent speculation about a rift stems largely from prior positioning and legislative influence rather than any open, formal feud, the pattern is hard to miss for anyone watching Monrovia’s political class closely: two ambitious officials, both plausible 2029 contenders, each watching for the moment the other overreaches.

A Port City, and a Turkish Delegation

For Karnga-Lawrence, port decentralization is an unambiguous win: a path toward economic growth and “port city” status for Grand Bassa. After the president’s signature, she publicly praised House Speaker Richard N. Koon and the House for passing the Port Authority and Port Autonomy Bills, declaring flatly, “Grand Bassa will surely be a port city.” She has since announced that a special economic zone in the county is set to be contracted to a new company, a move she says will transform the local economy and add value to agricultural products.

That is also where the story gets murkier. Karnga-Lawrence’s posture and evident personal interest in the outcome have drawn public concern that she stands to benefit directly from decentralization. In January 2025, a visiting delegation from the Albayrak Group — an Istanbul-headquartered multinational conglomerate with interests spanning port operations, fleet rental and tourism — paid a courtesy visit to the Senate Pro Tempore in Monrovia. Both Karnga-Lawrence and Montserrado Senator Abraham Darius Dillon, who chairs the Senate Foreign Affairs Committee, have already faced public criticism over concerns about improper interactions with foreign entities regarding national assets like ports and infrastructure.

Vice President Koung, for his part, has favored a strong and efficient port system generally under the ruling Unity Party government’s ARREST Agenda, but has not publicly voiced support for decentralization specifically. Government insiders describe the bill’s signing as a clear edge for Karnga-Lawrence over a man widely seen as her most likely 2029 rival — a read reinforced by reports that the Albayrak Group is already positioned to take over the Buchanan port once the bill’s transitional clause restrictions are satisfied.

And all this depends on whether President Boakai eventually decides he will seek a second term.

What the Law Actually Creates

Set the politics aside and the legislation itself is straightforward on paper. In place of the National Port Authority, four autonomous, county-based port authorities — the Freeport of Monrovia, and the ports of Buchanan, Greenville and Harper — become independent bodies corporate, each with its own board, management team, budget, and power to sue, borrow, contract and set tariffs (§51, §53, §54). A companion law creates the National Ports Regulatory Commission, a three-member, presidentially appointed body meant to license, supervise and, if necessary, dissolve these autonomous ports. The National Port Authority does not vanish overnight; it continues operating for 18 months while a seven-member presidential committee plans its dissolution and divides its assets, liabilities and contracts among the four new authorities (§57). The new structure does not go live until 2028.

That is the reform on paper. Whether it is a safe reform depends on provisions the text simply does not contain — and this summer’s cocaine investigation has already produced a live case study of exactly where those gaps sit.

The Gap Critics Are Pointing To: Four Security Forces, No Unifying Framework

Section 54(5) of the Act gives each of the four autonomous ports the power to “operate its own security force which will have adequate police powers to enforce compliance with its regulations and by-laws.” Section 54(6) gives each port its own Harbor Master to “direct and regulate the movement of vessels within said port.”

Read those two provisions together and the structural problem becomes clear: the law creates four separate port security apparatuses, each answerable to its own board and its own Managing Director (§56.1), with no provision anywhere in either act establishing a shared command structure, a joint maritime domain-awareness system, or a mandatory information-sharing protocol between them — let alone with the Liberia Drug Enforcement Agency, the Liberia Maritime Authority, the Liberia Coast Guard, the Armed Forces of Liberia, or the National Security Agency.

Nowhere in the regulatory act’s list of Commission functions (§3) does the word “security,” “trafficking,” “narcotics” or “smuggling” appear. The Commission’s mandate — licensing, tariffs, technical, economic, transportation, logistical, health and safety standards — is explicitly about commercial and operational regulation. Counter-narcotics and maritime security are not written into either bill as anyone’s job. This is not a hypothetical concern. It is close to a description of what already happened this summer under the single, centralized system the bill is dismantling.

The Case Study: How a Docking Request Became a Five-Agency Pileup

The clearest evidence that these are not abstract worries did not come from a hearing room or a think tank. It came from a single letter, sent on July 13, while the port and airport system was still fully centralized under the very structure this bill just dismantled. Mark Egon Kuiah — then a sitting Deputy Director for Operations at Roberts International Airport — wrote to the Liberia Maritime Authority that day, not in his government capacity but as “registered agent” for a company called Madris Group of Companies Incorporated, a firm business records would later show he owned outright. The letter described a vessel, later identified as the IB Atlantic IV, as being in distress with propeller damage and requested docking privileges at the Freeport of Monrovia. LiMA rejected the request — the vessel was still in Sierra Leonean waters and had not docked anywhere yet was already being described as needing emergency access.

That rejection should have been the end of it. Instead, the vessel spent the better part of a week drifting in and around Liberian waters while three different institutions — LiMA, the National Security Agency, and the Armed Forces of Liberia — each told reporters a different piece of the story and pointed to one another when asked who oversaw the response. This newspaper’s editorial board has noted that the government’s own account of its response was that officials tracked which side of the Sierra Leone–Liberia maritime line the ship was on, day by day, and waited for it to drift fully into Liberian waters before ordering it searched, rather than intercepting it while the outcome was still in doubt. By the time an interception was ordered, the vessel had moved into deep water; Liberia’s Coast Guard, under-resourced for long-distance pursuit, could not catch it, and the country had to request help from Ivory Coast and Guinea before the ship was finally detained in Abidjan. Investigators are still examining reports that a smaller boat approached the vessel at sea in the days after it first drew scrutiny and attempted to pass something aboard it.

Kuiah was dismissed by presidential order on July 30, in the same sweep that removed a police intelligence commissioner and an NSA deputy director and recalled a fourth official from an LDEA secondment — four people, three separate institutions, one signature. He has not been charged in connection with the July 13 letter, and the presumption of innocence still applies; but his case is now cited by this newspaper’s editorial board as the clearest illustration yet of a vulnerability the port bill does nothing to close: a single well-placed insider, operating through a private company rather than his official title, was able to seek preferential port access for a vessel later at the center of a trafficking investigation — and it took a public records search, not any institutional safeguard, to surface the conflict. That is what a security lapse looks like inside one centrally managed port and maritime system, with a comparatively small number of institutions to hold accountable. The port bill does not explain what happens to that same vulnerability once there are four separately governed ports, each issuing its own docking approvals, each running its own security force, with no shared vetting standard or disclosure requirement written into either act.

Other Structural Gaps in the Bill Itself

Ironically, the board composition includes no security or maritime agency.

Each port board consists of two members per relevant county, a chairperson, and the Ministers of Justice, Finance, and Development Planning and Transport as statutory members (§55.2). There is no seat, standing or advisory, for the LDEA, the Liberia Maritime Authority, the National Security Agency, or the Coast Guard. Justice sits on the board; the agencies that issue docking clearances, track vessels and interdict drugs do not — the same gap the Kuiah case exposed at a single facility, now proposed to be replicated across four independent ones.

Private ports and concessions have almost no vetting criteria

Section 58 of the Act is one sentence: “The Government of Liberia shall utilize its power to grant concession(s) for private port operations in Liberia.” No security clearance standard, no ownership-transparency requirement, no counter-narcotics compliance obligation attaches to that concession power. That gap is not abstract — Kuiah’s own company, formed in 2018 for “fishing, fisheries, cold-storage and related import-export business,” is exactly the kind of private entity such a concession structure could touch, and the Act gives regulators no explicit tool to screen for exactly that overlap between a private commercial identity and a public port official.

Territorial radius creates jurisdictional seams — the same kind that let the IB Atlantic IV run

Section 52 gives each port a 30-mile radius of territorial control from its existing base. Liberia’s four ports are not evenly spaced along its roughly 350-mile coastline; a 30-mile radius from each leaf stretches of coast that fall inside no port’s jurisdiction at all. The IB Atlantic IV chase turned in large part on exactly this kind of jurisdictional ambiguity — Liberian forces reportedly held back for days because the vessel sat on the Sierra Leonean side of a maritime boundary, and by the time it crossed into unambiguous Liberian jurisdiction, it had drifted into deep water the Coast Guard could not follow. A law that creates four new, smaller jurisdictional zones without a unifying maritime security mandate risks multiplying that same “whose water is this” problem rather than resolving it.

The offenses section is about property and unpaid dues, not contraband

Section 60 of the Act — the only enforcement and penalties section in either law — criminalizes willful damage to port property, evading tariffs, discharging firearms in port, and giving false vessel information. “Contraband” is defined in the terms section (§50), but no offense in §60 attaches to it. Enforcement against smuggling and trafficking through the ports is left entirely to laws outside this Act, with no integration or cross-reference built in.

The 18-month runway is unassigned

The transition clause (§57) is, as FrontPageAfrica has previously noted, either the most responsible feature of the law or the most convenient. It buys time to build the missing security framework — but nothing in the text obligates the administration to use it that way. The Act requires the dissolution committee to produce an asset-and-liability plan within six months (§57.2); it does not require a maritime security plan on any timeline at all.

Why the Near-Term Risk Is Not Theoretical

The backdrop against which this bill was signed is not background color; it is the closest thing Liberia currently has to a live-fire test of the system the law proposes to replicate four times over. Since June, Liberia has processed a $19.2 million cocaine seizure at Roberts International Airport, where cargo was falsely declared as food seasoning and textiles — the case that first named Mark Kuiah in a writ of arrest while he was still a sitting deputy director.

It has processed a record $317 million cocaine seizure in Duazon, Margibi County — nearly four metric tons, found in a warehouse raid that investigators say followed more than a year of surveillance into networks active since 2018. It has processed a convoy escort scandal in which, according to Liberia’s own police chief, cocaine was allegedly moved through the capital escorted by two of his own senior commanders in marked police cruisers.

It has processed a presidential purge removing or suspending ten officials across five different agencies in a single week, after the country’s own inspector general said the trafficking had been “definitively sanctioned by state actors at very, very senior level” — without saying who. And it still has not resolved the IB Atlantic IV case, in which a single vessel exposed, in this newspaper’s own words, “a government that cannot yet tell its own citizens what is moving through its waters.”

Against that record, FrontPageAfrica’s editorial board argued directly that the sequencing of the port bill was “close to indefensible”: a country that cannot yet explain who let two record shipments through a single, centrally managed port and airport system has not demonstrated it can secure four independently managed ones. The board’s proposed fix — pause final passage, or at minimum write a single, unified maritime security and counter-narcotics authority with clear jurisdiction across all four ports into the bill before signing — was not adopted. The law as signed does not contain that authority.

President Boakai vetoed earlier versions of this legislation twice, citing exactly this category of concern — risks to Liberia’s international maritime security obligations, in his own language returning the bill to the Legislature. Minister of State Samuel Stevequoah has said the president signed this week on the advice of the Minister of Justice. What specifically changed, on security grounds, between the rejected versions and the one now law has not been publicly detailed by the administration. The version signed still contains the same core architecture — four independent port security forces, a Commission with no security mandate, no interagency coordination requirement — that the earlier vetoes flagged, and that this summer’s cases have since tested in miniature.

The Bottom Line

The reform’s economic logic — ending decades of Monrovia-centered control that left Buchanan, Greenville and Harper starved of investment and local authority — is a legitimate policy goal on its own terms, and nothing in the bill’s text undermines that case. But the Act and its companion regulatory law, read on their own words, do not answer the question now being asked publicly: who is responsible for stopping traffickers from simply choosing whichever of the four newly independent ports has the weakest security posture, and what compels those four ports to coordinate before the structure goes live in 2028. This summer already produced a preview of what happens when that question goes unanswered inside a single port system. As written, the law creates the autonomy. It does not, on its face, create the safety net — and the 18 months before the new structure takes effect is, at this point, the only remaining window to write one in. Whether that window closes on a fixed vulnerability or a political victory lap for whichever camp, Karnga-Lawrence’s or Koung’s, comes out ahead by 2029, is a question this bill’s text alone cannot answer.

World.title: Liberia: A Woman Is Dead. The Man Who Operated on Her Pretended to Be a Surgeon: The Case That Shows Authorities Are Doing Nothing to Protect Liberians From Fake Doctors
World.content:
Blama Kamara comforts his two-year-old son during the funeral of his wife who died after undergoing surgery by a fake doctor at Stockton Creek Health Center in Caldwell.

Summary

A woman died in May after botched surgery at Stockton Creek Health Center in Caldwell, where a man posing as a doctor but with no medical qualifications operated on her.

The Liberia Medical and Dental Council, the government agency tasked with overseeing medical practitioners in the country, said it had asked the man to provide a medical license in 2022 but did not stop him practicing when he did not supply it.

Former solicitor general Tiawan Gongloe and Joseph Somwarbi, former chair of House committee on health, said the case shows that the government agency has been “derelict” in its duty, leaving all Liberians at risk.

By Tetee Gebro, health and gender correspondent with New Narratives

CALDWELL, Monrovia — Saybah Kollie collapsed on a Sunday morning in early April, two days after her son’s second birthday.

Her husband, Blama Kamara, and the community chairman rushed her to the closest clinic. Over the next few weeks, Saybah’s family said, she suffered at the hands of a fake doctor who claimed he was qualified to operate and heal her, but who was in fact, a fraud preying on desperate families like hers.

“The only thing I wanted was to see her survive,” says Kamara. The supposed doctor, Mohamed Ali Bah, warned him Saybah would die if he waited. “He said I should not take a risk with her life. So I trusted him.”

Forty-seven days later, Saybah was dead.

Saybah had become the latest in an unknown number of people to die in Liberia at the hands of fake medical personnel. The Liberian Medical and Dental Council, tasked with licensing health practitioners and facilities in the country, does not keep track of how many people die or suffer injuries as a result of medical treatments by unlicensed individuals, but regular posts on social media show Saybah’s case is not isolated.

With a barely functioning health care system with just one doctor for every 10,0000 people (the World Health Organization recommends one for every 1,000) and half the population living in poverty, Liberia has become an easy place for dishonest people to take advantage of their fellow citizens.

But experts say the problem is compounded by the complete failure of the Liberian Medical and Dental Council to check licenses and shut down those impersonating as doctors. That is leaving Liberians across the country vulnerable.

“This showed that the LMDC’s oversight and regulatory enforcement capacity is very weak, especially in this case where they are saying that the individual… has been practicing without a license for years while they [the Council] are being paid with taxpayers’ money,” said Joseph Somwarbi, former chair of the House of Representatives Committee on Health,

No Tests, Surgery Ordered Based Only on “Pressing the Stomach”

When Saybah first arrived at Stockton Creek, the family was introduced to “Doctor Bah”. Her sister, Janga Kollie, who came later, was worried from the start.

“They didn’t run any tests,” Janga said. “If they do a test, at least they will tell us something. But the man only used his hand to press her stomach, and he said she had a fibroid.”

A fibroid is a non-cancerous growth in the womb that is more common in African women. To identify fibroids and rule out other causes, doctors would use an ultrasound machine or test her blood in a laboratory. Pressing someone’s stomach with your hand is a guess.

Before Saybah could even be examined, Kamara was asked to pay US$20. “Doctor” Bah said Saybah had lost so much blood she needed seven pints replaced at a cost of US$50 a pint. Within a week the bill for the accommodation and treatment reached US$330.

Saybah seemed to improve so Kamara took her home. But then she collapsed again.

This time Bah said she needed surgery. He claimed he was a surgeon at JFK Hospital and a professor at a major medical school in Monrovia. Kamara asked whether the clinic had an ultrasound machine — a device doctors use to see inside the body without surgery. “He said he had everything,” Kamara recalled. “He said this place is almost like a hospital.” He convinced Kamara. “Bah really got sweet mouth,” said Janga. Saybah’s brother was called to sign a form agreeing to the surgery. The operation happened quickly — Kamara only learned it was finished when he arrived that evening and found her in recovery.

Stockton Clinic in May credit: Capital Online TV

The Bleeding That Would Not Stop

After the surgery, the bleeding got worse. Every day and night the clinic called saying she needed more blood — more than fifteen pints in total, US$750, paid straight to Bah in cash. “He said it will not stop right away. It will take time,” said Janga.

But Saybah grew weaker and afraid. She began begging to be moved to another hospital. Bah refused, telling her he could treat her. Finally Saybah’s ex-husband, calling from abroad, insisted the family take her to 14 Military Hospital. Bah refused to write a referral note. Instead, he handed the family a blank paper. “Since you people want to carry the girl, if you carry her, my hand is not inside. You people just make paper,” Janga recalled him saying. At 14 Military Hospital, doctors, clearly worried, asked where Saybah’s surgery had been done. They asked her directly — “Is he a licensed doctor?” They told the family they did not have the right kind of doctor for what had been done and referred her to JFK. At JFK, doctors called Bah and asked what tests he had run before operating. According to Janga, the call cut off. She tried calling back. Bah did not answer.

A Deadly Disease, Discovered Too Late

JFK doctors revealed a diagnosis the family had never heard: cervical cancer. Dr. Avee Kamah told the family Saybah came to them too late. “She said they tried their best,” Janga said. But it was up to God to save her.

A day later, Saybah died. The death certificate said her cancer caused her kidneys to fail and her blood to become severely depleted. Fluid built up in her lungs and toxins built up in her brain — this combination killed her.

James-Emmanuel D. Cole Jr., JFK’s communications director, confirmed in a statement that Saybah was received as a serious medical emergency following a referral from 14 Military Hospital, and that she died despite the efforts of the clinical team.

The hospital declined to say whether its doctors believed the original surgery at Stockton Creek contributed to her death or whether JFK reported concerns about Stockton Creek to the Medical and Dental Council or any other authority.

But Cole wrote that the hospital would cooperate fully with any competent regulatory, investigative, or judicial authority that requested access to Saybah’s records. He also noted that cases involving severe complications “may be reviewed by the relevant authorities, including the Liberia Medical and Dental Council.”

“There Was A Foul Play Somewhere”

After Saybah’s funeral, Bah called Kamara to give his sympathies. Kamara hung up on him. But Bah called again, after a reporter working on this story visited his clinic, to ask Kamara why he was speaking to journalists. Kamara ended the call again.

After numerous requests Bah agreed to an interview with FrontPage Africa/New Narratives. He refused to allow his comments to go on the record. But he did deny that Saybah had been treated at his clinic.

Kamara has Saybah’s patient card from Stockton Creek, dated April 5, 2026. He and Janga said they visited her there. They said more than ten people, including members of Saybah’s church, can confirm she was treated there.

“That statement alone makes me know there was a foul play,” Kamara said. “Why are you refusing that Saybah was at your hospital and you did the operation? For that I can’t keep silent. If I keep silent I will not be fair to Saybah.”

The Liberia Medical and Dental Council Repeatedly Does Nothing to Stop Fake Doctor

But experts say Bah is not the only one complicit in Saybah’s suffering. The Liberia Medical and Dental Council, tasked by government with regular medical practitioners in the country, repeatedly failed to do its job.

The Council’s credential committee first asked Bah to supply his license in 2022 according to Joseph Colmah, the LMDC’s Medical and Research Director. Bah never did and the Council did nothing to stop him practicing.

In 2024, Stockton Creek, having got away with not complying with the Council’s requests for two years, became bold. They asked the Council for permission to upgrade from a basic clinic to a full health center — a higher level of facility with stricter requirements for staff, equipment, and record-keeping. Even though Bah had never supplied a medical license, the Council began to process the application. It told the clinic to pause all patient care until inspectors could confirm it met the standard. But the inspectors never returned and the clinic kept seeing patients for another two years.

It was only this May— one week after Saybah died and the family began posting on Facebook – that the Council shut the clinic down , four years and an unknown number of deaths and injuries, after the Council was first alerted to Bah’s deception. In a press release the Council said it “remains committed to ensuring quality, safe, and professional healthcare delivery throughout the country and will continue its nationwide regulatory assessment across Liberia’s fifteen counties over the next one month.”

The Council did not report the case to the police.

But when a reporter visited the clinic three weeks later, in June, asking for medical help, the clinic was still operating. The reporter was given treatment and charged L$1000 and saw a man identified as “Dr. Bah” on the premises.

In July, after questions from this reporter, the Council published a list of 532 licensed doctors in Liberia, for the first time. The registry includes an active license for “Dr. Bah Mohammed Aliou,” license number NL/636, valid from January 17, 2026 to January 16, 2027. A source familiar with the matter told New Narratives that the person listed is the same Mohammed Ali Bah at Stockton Creek. The Council did not respond to questions asking whether the two names refer to the same person.

Liberia Medical and Dental Council denies responsibility for policing fake doctors

In a surprising revelation, Colmah said it was not the Council’s role to check whether Bah had continued to practice without accreditation. He said the Council can only pursue charges against someone for falsely calling themselves a doctor with written proof — like a prescription or medical record signed using the title “doctor.” Patient testimony that they were treated by someone using that title is not enough.

Colmah said the Council has no power to physically lock a building — only a court can do that. The Council can only post a notice and ask the facility to stop. Colmah claimed the Council had posted a notice on the facility in 2024. “But as you might be aware, maybe renovation, someone may get to it.”

But experts said that Colmah’s statement was wrong.

Joseph Somwarbi, pharmacologist, former representative for Nimba county and chair of the House of Representatives Committee on Health, said it is the Council’s duty to ensure that all medical clinics, health centers, and hospitals are licensed and demand that all licensed practitioners and facilities place their licenses in visible locations. And they must work with the Liberia National Police to shut down illegal operations and refer unlicensed practitioners for criminal prosecution.

He said those at the Council found responsible for failure to act should be replaced.

Tiawan Gongloe, former solicitor general, agreed. He demanded the Liberian National Police explore criminal charges Bah. “What he did is almost like shooting somebody with a gun, because he is not authorized to practice medicine.”

Gongloe said the Council also bears responsibility and the family could bring a lawsuit.

“The LMDC takes some responsibility by not closing [the clinic]. They were derelict in their action.” Gongloe urged the Council to act now. “LMDC should stop him. He is a menace. Every second that that man is operating, Liberians are at risk.”

Kamara is now the sole carer for their two young children who cry for their mother. He strains to understand how authorities could have left his family so unprotected.

“If a man like that is not a doctor, and his place is still operating at a time like this,” Kamara said, “My mouth is full. I don’t know.”

World.title: Liberia: Sections of Monrovia City Hall Deteriorate as MCC Blames Past Administration
World.content:
Monrovia— Concerns are mounting over the deteriorating condition of portions of Monrovia City Hall, with a FrontPage Africa investigation finding the building’s once-active theater section in a state of disrepair, while the Monrovia City Corporation (MCC) says the current administration inherited the facility in poor condition and has begun efforts to restore it.

By Emmanuel Weedee-Conway, [email protected]

An on-the-ground assessment by FrontPage Africa found significant deterioration in the theater section, including a leaking roof, damaged ceilings, cracked and weathered walls, a deteriorating stage, and broken chairs.

The section has reportedly remained largely closed to regular public use, raising questions among residents and critics about the preservation of one of Monrovia’s historic public buildings.

The condition of the theater has also renewed broader concerns about the maintenance of public infrastructure under the administration of Mayor John-Charuk S. Siafa, who assumed office with promises of making the modernization, cleanliness, and improvement of Monrovia key priorities.

More than two years into his administration, however, critics say conditions at some public facilities remain troubling and that the city government must do more to protect and rehabilitate municipal assets.

FPA Findings Raise Questions

FrontPage Africa observed that the theater section appeared significantly more deteriorated than the functioning portions of City Hall.

The area includes facilities that were once used for public events and gatherings but are now largely inaccessible.

The paper also observed deteriorating sanitary facilities near the theater, including a bathroom area that appeared abandoned, with spider webs and an unpleasant odor.

The findings prompted questions about the structural condition of the theater, the reasons for its continued deterioration and whether the MCC has a funded rehabilitation plan for the facility.

FPA also asked the MCC why major rehabilitation work had not been undertaken despite the reported condition of the roof, ceiling, walls and stage, what budget and timeline had been established for rehabilitation, and which officials were responsible for the building’s maintenance.

MCC: ‘Complete Misrepresentation of the Facts’

In a written response, MCC Communications Director Varney Diggs strongly rejected what he described as the narrative presented by FrontPage Africa.

“All of the claims by the FPA are a complete misrepresentation of the facts,” Diggs said.

He argued that Mayor Siafa inherited City Hall, along with other MCC facilities, in a severely deteriorated condition.

According to Diggs, virtually all of the offices at City Hall had experienced leakage when the current administration took over.

He said the Siafa administration has since renovated major sections and offices of the building.

Diggs also pointed to the Fiamah and Stockton Creek transfer stations, saying both were inherited in what he described as “absolute ruins” and that the current administration undertook rehabilitation of the facilities.

He said the administration also inherited a city where garbage disposal was “at a total standstill.”

MCC Acknowledges Theater’s Poor Condition

While rejecting FPA’s broader characterization of the city government’s management of the facility, Diggs acknowledged that the theater was in poor condition when the Siafa administration assumed office.

He said the Mayor has been engaging development partners to secure assistance for a comprehensive renovation of the theater.

“Regarding the much-publicized theatre, the Mayor inherited it in ruins, but he has since demonstrated practical leadership by reaching out to partners for the full renovation of that section of the City Hall,” Diggs said.

He further claimed that renovation work was ongoing at the theater at the time of his response.

However, during FPA’s on-the-ground visit, it did not observe what appeared to be active renovation work in the deteriorating section.

The conflicting accounts leave questions about the scope and stage of any rehabilitation work and whether the project is being undertaken directly by MCC or with assistance from external partners.

Public Memory of Earlier Administrations

The condition of City Hall has also prompted comparisons with previous municipal administrations.

Liberians interviewed in connection with the investigation contend that portions of the facility were more functional and accessible under earlier administrations, including the periods associated with former Mayor Mary T. Broh and former Mayor Jefferson Tamba Koijee.

Broh, who served as Monrovia’s mayor from 2009 to 2013, became known for aggressive city-cleaning and urban-renewal campaigns. Her administration was also credited with improving the appearance and functionality of several municipal facilities.

“Under Broh, City Hall was a place to go. Everything was functional,” said Abraham Kollie, a resident of Capitol Bye-Pass. “I remember it was in the theater that the motorcyclists met with then- President Sirleaf and then Deputy Police Commissioner Abraham Kromah for a reconciliation meeting. Other programs were held there as well. To see it in such a terrible state is frustrating. It’s a leadership failure.”

Critics say Koijee’s tenure did not replicate all of Broh’s renovation efforts, but City Hall’s grounds and several public areas remained accessible and usable for official and social functions.

“The bathrooms were in use. City Hall was better than its current state,” Beatrice Saylee, a former volunteer at Monrovia City Hall. “There was a beautiful garden people used to visit for entertainment. Everything was not perfect, but it was better.”

Critics argue that the current administration should be judged not only by the condition it inherited but also by the progress it has made in preserving and improving municipal infrastructure.

MCC Rejects Claims of Decline Under Siafa

Diggs dismissed the suggestion that MCC was in significantly better condition before Mayor Siafa assumed office.

He accused critics of advancing politically motivated narratives and described claims that the corporation was previously in better shape as dishonest.

He maintained that Mayor Siafa has made “remarkable progress” during his tenure, particularly through the rehabilitation of municipal facilities and the restoration of services.

The MCC’s position, therefore, is that the deterioration observed at City Hall should be understood within the context of longstanding infrastructure problems inherited by the current administration rather than as evidence of neglect under Mayor Siafa.

Broader Sanitation Concerns

The dispute over City Hall comes amid persistent public criticism of sanitation and waste management in Monrovia.

Former President Ellen Johnson Sirleaf also publicly criticized the condition of the capital earlier this year.

Appearing on the Truth Breakfast Show in April, Johnson Sirleaf described Monrovia as “disgustingly dirty,” “stink,” and “shameful,” and called for stronger action to improve waste management and cleanliness.

Her comments added to growing public pressure on the city government to demonstrate measurable improvements in sanitation.

For critics, the deteriorating condition of portions of City Hall is particularly troubling because the building serves as a symbol of the capital and the municipal authority responsible for maintaining it.

A Question of Responsibility

The competing accounts ultimately raise a broader question: who bears responsibility for restoring and preserving City Hall, regardless of when the deterioration began?

The MCC says Mayor Siafa inherited a severely damaged facility and is now working to rehabilitate it.

FrontPage Africa’s findings, meanwhile, indicate that significant portions of the theater remain in poor condition, while questions remain about the timing, financing and scope of the reported renovation.

For members of the public, the distinction may matter less than the outcome.

City Hall remains one of Monrovia’s most recognizable public landmarks. Whether its deteriorating theater is a legacy of previous administrations, a consequence of years of inadequate maintenance, or a problem now being addressed by the current government, residents say what matters is that the facility is restored before further deterioration makes rehabilitation more costly—or potentially impossible.

Until then, the theater’s condition stands as a visible reminder of the wider challenge facing Monrovia: maintaining the capital’s public infrastructure while delivering on repeated promises of a cleaner, safer and better-managed city.

World.title: Liberia: Prophet Key Signals a New Public Image Following His Release From Prison
World.content:
MONROVIA — Justin Oldpa Yeazehn, popularly known as “Prophet Key,” has emerged from nearly six months of incarceration declaring that his time behind bars has changed him, while simultaneously questioning the legality and proportionality of the 180-day sentence imposed against him by the Supreme Court of Liberia.

By Selma Lomax, [email protected]

Following his release from the Monrovia Central Prison Friday, Prophet Key said his experience in detention had served as a period of rehabilitation and reflection, suggesting that the ordeal had forced him to reassess his conduct, his public utterances and the manner in which he communicates with others.

His comments mark a notable shift from the confrontational public persona that preceded his imprisonment, as he now says he intends to approach his public engagements differently. The Supreme Court ordered his immediate release on August 14, 2026, after he had spent roughly six months in custody.

‘I Have Been Rehabilitated’

Prophet Key’s central message following his release was that his period in prison was not without impact. He said the experience had rehabilitated him, implying that the confinement gave him an opportunity to reconsider his actions and the consequences of his words.

According to him, the man who entered prison is not necessarily the same man who walked out, as the period of incarceration provided time for reflection, discipline and a reassessment of his approach to public discourse. His declaration appears to signal an intention to move away from the style of public communication that contributed to his legal troubles and toward a more measured posture.

The statement comes after the Supreme Court found him guilty of contempt in February and sentenced him to six months in prison following remarks it said were directed against the Chief Justice, members of the Court and the Chief Justice’s mother.

For Prophet Key, therefore, his release is not simply the conclusion of a legal battle but also the beginning of what he portrays as a personal transformation.

His assertion that he has been rehabilitated suggests that he believes the punishment, regardless of the controversy surrounding its length, has changed his outlook. Rather than returning to the same style of public confrontation, he says the experience has taught him lessons about restraint, responsibility and the consequences that can follow public statements.

His position is particularly significant because the Supreme Court had not only imposed imprisonment but also required measures intended to regulate his future conduct, including a behavior bond and public apology requirements.

Prophet Key Questions 180-Day Detention

Despite describing himself as rehabilitated, Prophet Key has also raised a fundamental question about the length of time he spent behind bars. He argues that his rights were violated because, in his interpretation of the country’s contempt laws, he should not have been imprisoned for six months.

His position centers on Section 12.6 of the New Judiciary Law, which provides that punishment for criminal contempt may include a fine of up to US$300 in the Supreme Court or imprisonment not exceeding 30 days. Legal commentary published after his conviction has likewise questioned how the statutory 30-day provision relates to the six-month sentence imposed in his case.

From Prophet Key’s perspective, the distinction between 30 days and 180 days is not a minor technicality but a fundamental issue of his rights. He maintains that if the applicable contempt provision establishes a maximum of 30 days, then keeping him incarcerated for six months amounted to punishment beyond the period contemplated by that provision. His argument is therefore that while the Court had the authority to address conduct it considered contemptuous, the punishment should still have remained within the limits established by law.

This position has also featured in public criticism of the sentence, with legal commentators arguing that Article 74 of the Liberian Constitution provides that contempt penalties are to be fixed by the Legislature and must conform to constitutional fundamental-rights protections.

“According to the Contempt Charge, It Was 30 Days”

Prophet Key’s argument can be understood through his contention that the contempt charge should not have resulted in a 180-day custodial sentence. He points to the statutory language concerning criminal contempt and argues that the law provides for imprisonment “not exceeding 30 days.”

On that basis, he questions why a punishment that he believes should have been limited to one month ultimately became six months. His argument is not necessarily that he should never have faced consequences for his conduct; rather, he is challenging the extent of those consequences and maintaining that punishment must remain within the boundaries established by law.

That argument has generated a wider legal debate beyond Prophet Key himself. An opinion published following the sentence noted that Title 17, Chapter 12, Section 12.6 of the New Judiciary Law provides for criminal-contempt imprisonment not exceeding 30 days, while Article 74 of the Constitution states that penalties for contempt of court are to be fixed by the Legislature and must conform to fundamental-rights protections.

What Prompted His Release

Prophet Key’s release ultimately came through a new decision of the Supreme Court itself. On August 14, 2026, the Judiciary announced that the Full Bench had ordered his immediate release from the Monrovia Central Prison.

The official Judiciary announcement confirms that the release order came directly from the Supreme Court, although the brief public notice does not provide detailed reasons for the Court’s decision.

His release came immediately after the period surrounding the completion of his six-month incarceration, bringing an end to one of Liberia’s most closely watched contempt cases of 2026.

The case had generated a broader national debate about the balance between freedom of expression, respect for judicial authority and the limits of the contempt power. While the Supreme Court maintained that Prophet Key’s conduct warranted punishment, legal commentators and civil society voices questioned whether the six-month sentence was consistent with the statutory 30-day ceiling contained in the Judiciary Law.

With his freedom restored, Prophet Key is now presenting himself as a changed man. His claim that he has been rehabilitated, coupled with his criticism of the length of his detention, places his post-prison narrative on two parallel tracks: acceptance of personal lessons from incarceration and continued questions about the legality and proportionality of the punishment imposed upon him.

World.title: Liberia: Parents, Teachers Decry ‘Deplorable’ Conditions at LAC Plantation Schools; Company Says Rehabilitation Works Underway
World.content:
COMPOUND 3, GRAND BASSA COUNTY — Beneath rusted zinc roofs and ceilings marked by years of deterioration, children attending schools operated by the Liberia Agriculture Company (LAC) have been learning in conditions that parents and teachers say are unsafe, unhygienic and unfit for a modern learning environment.

By Gerald C. Koinyeneh, [email protected]

A FrontPage Africa investigation into schools across the LAC concession in Grand Bassa County found deteriorating classrooms, damaged doors and windows, cracked walls, failing ceilings, inadequate furniture and sanitation facilities in need of urgent attention.

The investigation also found concerns over overcrowding, limited learning equipment and the absence of a functional computer laboratory at St. Joseph High School in Estate One, regarded as the plantation’s leading secondary school.

LAC, one of Liberia’s oldest agricultural concessions, does not dispute that several of its schools require major rehabilitation.

In a response to FrontPage Africa, the company acknowledged that facilities at St. Joseph High School, St. Michael Elementary and Junior High School, Blessed Allamano Junior High School in Estate Four, and several satellite schools require attention.

But LAC says the conditions identified by the investigation are already being addressed through a phased rehabilitation program and that work is underway ahead of the reopening of schools in September.

The company says six schools — St. Joseph, St. Michael, Allamano, St. Francis, Estate Four and Division 4.1 Elementary — are expected to be completed by September 2026.

LAC, however, stopped short of guaranteeing that all identified rehabilitation works across its 11 schools will be completed before the new academic year begins.

That qualification has done little to reassure some parents and teachers, who say the deterioration has been visible for years and that repeated appeals for repairs have not produced improvements quickly enough.

Classrooms Falling Apart

During visits to several LAC-operated schools, FrontPage Africa observed aging classroom buildings showing visible signs of prolonged wear and inadequate maintenance.

At some facilities, classroom floors were bare and deteriorating. Doors were broken or damaged, windows required repair, and portions of ceilings appeared to be deteriorating.

Spider webs were visible across sections of classroom ceilings, while some roofing and ceiling materials appeared loose and in need of replacement.

The conditions were not isolated to a single campus.

Among the schools visited during the investigation were St. Joseph High School in Estate One, St. Michael Elementary and Junior High School, Blessed Allamano Junior High School in Estate Four, and several satellite schools spread across the concession.

Parents and teachers expressed concern that children are being asked to pursue their education in environments that do not adequately protect their health, safety or dignity.

One parent, whose identity is being withheld because of concerns about possible reprisals, said the problem has persisted for too long.

“This is not the kind of school environment any child deserves. Our children are expected to compete with students elsewhere, but look at where they are learning.”

Another parent raised particular concerns about sanitation facilities used by girls.

According to the parent, the poor condition of some bathrooms has forced girls to seek alternative places to relieve themselves.

“The girls are forced to use the bush because of the dirty condition of the bathrooms,” the parent said.

FrontPage Africa is withholding the identities of parents and teachers interviewed for this investigation because of concerns about possible reprisals.

Sanitation Concerns

The condition of sanitation facilities emerged as one of the most troubling findings.

Several schools rely on aging pit latrines, with some facilities requiring rehabilitation to meet acceptable standards of hygiene and safety.

Parents said inadequate sanitation presents particular challenges for female students, who require clean, private and functional facilities during the school day.

LAC acknowledged the concerns.

In its response, the company said all 11 schools have separate sanitation facilities for boys and girls but confirmed that upgrades and bathroom renovations are included in its rehabilitation plan.

Bathroom renovations are specifically planned for schools in Estate Four, Steward Camp, Flos Camp and Forest Camp.

The company said some of the work is expected to be completed before September.

Teachers Say Appeals Went Unanswered

Several teachers and residents told FrontPage Africa that concerns about deteriorating school facilities have been raised repeatedly through school administration and LAC’s management structures.

Two teachers residing in Queensville Camp, the main teachers’ residential area on the plantation, said requests for improvements to classrooms, sanitation facilities and other learning infrastructure have been made over the years.

They described the response as inadequate.

Teachers said they have raised concerns about broken facilities, deteriorating floors and windows, and other infrastructure problems, but improvements have not always followed quickly.

LAC rejected the characterization that teachers’ concerns have been ignored.

The company said teachers are often the first people to identify facility problems and that their reports form part of LAC’s assessment and prioritization process.

However, the company acknowledged that a request for repairs does not necessarily mean work can begin immediately.

LAC said it must assess the condition, determine the urgency, secure materials and coordinate logistics and resources before work can be undertaken.

The company cited Queensville as an example of a case where management responded.

According to LAC, 26 teachers had flagged problems involving tiles and window bars, and the company said the work was completed two weeks before its response to FrontPage Africa.

St. Joseph: Expansion Without Matching Infrastructure

At St. Joseph High School, FrontPage Africa found evidence of an institution that has grown academically without a corresponding expansion of some of its physical infrastructure.

The school was expanded into a full senior high school during the tenure of former LAC General Manager George Mensah, raising expectations that students on the plantation would have access to expanded educational opportunities.

But teachers say the enrollment growth has not been matched by sufficient investment in classrooms and learning facilities.

A teacher described classrooms as overcrowded and difficult to manage.

“It is not easy here, my brother,” the teacher said. “Some classrooms have over 100 students, and you can’t teach well. The classrooms are hot and dusty.”

The investigation found students using green-painted benches in classrooms, with concerns that limited seating capacity can force several students to share desks.

Teachers say overcrowding makes it difficult to provide individual attention and effectively manage classroom instruction.

The company says it plans to provide 170 new armchairs and repair 211 others across the school system. St. Joseph alone is listed for 134 new armchairs and 171 repairs.

The company also plans 92 new student desks and repairs to 161 desks across the schools.

Science Lab in Decline

The science laboratory at St. Joseph High School offers another indication of the challenges facing the school system.

FrontPage Africa observed that equipment acquired years ago appeared outdated, while some apparatus was in poor condition or no longer in active use.

For a senior secondary school, the condition raises concerns about students’ access to practical science education, particularly as they prepare for national examinations.

Teachers said the lack of adequate laboratory resources can undermine students’ ability to translate classroom theory into practical experience.

The problem extends beyond science.

The investigation found no functional computer laboratory at St. Joseph High School, raising questions about the ability of students to acquire basic digital skills.

As computers and digital literacy increasingly become essential to higher education and employment, teachers said students from the plantation risk being disadvantaged when competing with students from schools with better-equipped facilities.

LAC’s Rehabilitation Plan

LAC says the conditions identified by FrontPage Africa are not unknown to management.

The company said it conducts regular inventories and assessments covering classrooms, roofs, ceilings, doors, windows, furniture, sanitation facilities and electrical systems.

According to LAC, deficiencies identified through the assessments are tracked and prioritized according to urgency.

Its rehabilitation plan includes a range of general works across the 11 schools.

These include blackboard painting and general building painting, installation of window screens, repairs to cracked walls, office renovations, bathroom renovations, bookshelves, hand-pump maintenance, window canopies and aprons.

The company has also identified specific replacements and repairs.

Its plan includes 32 sheets of roofing zinc, 40 ceiling replacements, floor repairs at several schools, three door repairs and 15 door-frame replacements across seven schools.

LAC says St. Joseph requires the largest number of ceiling replacements, with 20 listed for replacement.

The company also identified six blackboards at St. Michael, two at Vijay Maira and one at St. Joseph for replacement.

According to LAC, some work can only be undertaken during school breaks, which is why rehabilitation projects have been scheduled for the current vacation period.

Can Everything Be Completed Before September?

With the new academic year expected to begin in September, the timing of the rehabilitation program is now central to the concerns raised by parents and teachers.

LAC said rehabilitation work is already underway in phases and that the company is prioritizing repairs affecting student safety and sanitation.

It said six schools — St. Joseph, St. Michael, Allamano, St. Francis, Estate Four and Division 4.1 Elementary — are expected to be completed by September 2026.

But the company acknowledged that it cannot guarantee that every identified project across the school system will be completed before schools reopen.

“Given the number of facilities across the school system, we cannot guarantee every identified project will be finished on that timeline,” LAC said, while emphasizing that rehabilitation will continue in phases until identified needs are addressed.

That admission is significant for parents who fear that the start of the school year could come before the rehabilitation program is fully implemented.

Some parents argue that the condition of the schools has existed for years and that a few weeks of rehabilitation during the vacation period may not be sufficient to address the accumulated problems.

Who Oversees the Schools?

The investigation also raises broader questions about the management structure of LAC’s education system.

Unlike school systems operated under a dedicated education management structure, LAC’s schools fall under the company’s Human Resources Department, which also controls the education budget.

Several residents and education stakeholders questioned whether that arrangement gives education sufficient institutional priority within the concession’s broader administrative structure.

They argued that education spending may compete with other corporate priorities, potentially delaying investments in classrooms, sanitation, equipment and other learning resources.

LAC did not indicate in its response that it plans to change the administrative structure.

Instead, it emphasized that its existing system allows the company to assess facility needs, prioritize repairs and allocate resources accordingly.

Questions for Government

The investigation also raises questions about the role of the Ministry of Education.

Parents, residents and school stakeholders interviewed said they could not recall frequent inspection visits by education authorities to assess the physical condition of schools across the plantation.

Regular inspection is critical not only for monitoring academic standards but also for assessing whether schools provide safe and appropriate environments for children.

The absence of visible government intervention, residents argue, creates the possibility that deteriorating infrastructure can persist for years without sufficient regulatory pressure for corrective action.

For parents, the issue is bigger than whether LAC eventually repairs the buildings.

They want greater accountability over the quality of education available to children living on a concession that has operated in Liberia for generations.

A Concession Dating to 1959

Established in 1959, LAC is one of Liberia’s oldest rubber-producing concessions.

Generations of Liberians have lived and worked on the plantation, and the company has remained an important economic institution in Grand Bassa.

But residents say the length of the company’s presence makes the state of some of its schools even more troubling.

Community members have for years called for greater investment in education and social services in concession communities.

Some have also raised concerns about the concession agreement itself, including calls for stronger local-content provisions and more clearly defined community development obligations.

Residents argue that communities hosting large-scale commercial operations should see tangible improvements in education, healthcare, infrastructure and other essential services.

They say successive governments have failed to adequately address these concerns.

“The Children Are the Ones Paying the Price”

For former LAC student Wremongar Joe, the deteriorating schools represent more than a maintenance problem.

He said the consequences are ultimately borne by children who have no control over the condition of the institutions in which they are expected to learn.

“For many parents, however, the issue extends beyond contracts and policy. It is about children,” Joe told FrontPage Africa.

“Every broken classroom door represents another reminder that students have been forgotten. Every overcrowded classroom limits a teacher’s ability to give individual attention. Every unusable science laboratory denies students practical learning. Every missing computer reduces opportunities in an increasingly digital world. Every neglected bathroom compromises children’s health and dignity.”

His assessment captures the central concern emerging from FrontPage Africa’s investigation: that the problem at LAC’s schools is not simply about aging buildings, but about whether children growing up on one of Liberia’s historic agricultural concessions are receiving the educational environment they need to compete beyond the plantation.

LAC Says It Welcomes Scrutiny

Despite the concerns raised by the investigation, LAC says it remains committed to improving the schools.

The company said the health, safety and dignity of students are a priority and encouraged parents, teachers and school administrators to continue reporting problems so they can be assessed and addressed.

For parents and teachers, however, the test will not be the rehabilitation plan on paper.

It will be the condition of the classrooms when students return in September.

If roofs are repaired, ceilings restored, bathrooms made usable, furniture replaced and learning facilities improved, LAC’s response will represent a meaningful intervention.

If students return to the same broken doors, deteriorating ceilings, overcrowded classrooms and inadequate sanitation facilities, the concerns uncovered by this investigation will remain unresolved.

For thousands of children on the LAC plantation, the new school year is therefore more than a return to classes.

It is a test of whether years of complaints about deteriorating schools will finally translate into visible change.

World.title: The Politics Can Wait. The Port Security Gaps Cannot
World.content:
A Vice President and a Senate Pro Tempore are both eyeing 2029, and both have reasons to want this port law to go their way. Neither reason has anything to do with fixing the security gaps still sitting inside it

WE DO NOT BEGRUDGE LIBERIAN POLITICIANS for looking ahead to 2029. Every democracy runs on ambition, and a Vice President and a Senate Pro Tempore each positioning for a future national ticket is not, on its own, a scandal. What should concern every Liberian is what sits underneath that positioning: a rivalry between Vice President Jeremiah Koung and Senate Pro Tempore Nyonblee Karnga-Lawrence that appears to be shaping how the port decentralization bill was written, whose interests it serves, and how quickly its unresolved security gaps get fixed, if they get fixed at all. Karnga-Lawrence’s own ambitions in Grand Bassa, and ties surrounding the legislation to the Albayrak Group, raise exactly the kind of conflict-of-interest questions a bill this consequential cannot afford to carry unanswered into 2028.

SET THE POLITICS ASIDE for a moment and read the statute the way this newspaper did. It creates four independent port security forces, one each for Monrovia, Buchanan, Greenville and Harper, with no shared command structure linking any of them. The regulatory Commission meant to oversee the whole decentralized system has a mandate that never once mentions trafficking or narcotics enforcement. Neither the Liberia Drug Enforcement Agency nor Liberia’s Maritime Authority holds a guaranteed seat on any of the four new port boards.

THESE ARE NOT ABSTRACTIONS. They are close cousins of the exact jurisdictional seams that let the IB Atlantic IV sit off Liberia’s coast for the better part of a week this summer, chased eventually by AFL boats too small to catch it, tied to a rejected letter and a now-dismissed port official, under a single centralized system that was supposed to make accountability simple. Multiply that system by four independent authorities with no shared command, and the seams do not close. They multiply.

HERE IS THE UNCOMFORTABLE PART. A rivalry built around who controls the political and economic spoils of a decentralized port system has little natural incentive to close those seams. Four independent port authorities, each answering to a differently composed local board, are more valuable as patronage and campaign infrastructure precisely because they are fragmented — more appointments to hand out, more local relationships to cultivate ahead of 2029, more places to plant loyalists’ years before a single vote is cast.

A UNIFIED COMMAND STRUCTURE, a Commission mandate that puts trafficking enforcement in writing, and guaranteed seats for the LDEA and Maritime Authority would do the opposite: concentrate accountability, reduce the number of levers any one political patron controls, and make the whole system harder to quietly steer. We are not accusing either official of wanting Liberia’s ports to stay vulnerable to traffickers. We are saying the incentives built into this rivalry point toward leaving the gaps alone, and Liberians should not have to take it on faith that ambition and public safety happen to align this time.

THE LAW’S 18-MONTH TRANSITION PERIOD, delaying the new structure until 2028, is the one part of this bill this newspaper has consistently treated as a genuine opportunity rather than a stalling tactic. It is also the only window left to fix what the statute did not. That means the Legislature and the incoming Independent Seaport and Inland Ports Regulatory Authority owe Liberians a public, written answer to three specific questions before the transition period runs out: who commands all four port security forces when a single vessel or shipment crosses jurisdictional lines; where in the Commission’s mandate trafficking and narcotics enforcement is explicitly named as a responsibility rather than assumed as an afterthought; and which seats on each of the four port boards belong, by law, to the LDEA and the Maritime Authority rather than to whichever local board chooses to invite them. None of those fixes require reopening the political fight over decentralization itself. They require the officials who won that fight to spend some of their eighteen months finishing the job properly instead of consolidating position for 2029.

WE WOULD ASK VICE PRESIDENT KOUNG and Senate Pro Tempore Karnga-Lawrence directly: whatever this rivalry is building toward, neither of you can plausibly benefit from being remembered as the official who left a port law standing that made Liberia’s next trafficking failure easier rather than harder to prevent. The Albayrak Group ties attached to this legislation deserve a direct public accounting, not a silence that lets Liberians draw their own conclusions. And any political figure with a stake in how these four ports are eventually run has a straightforward way to prove the security gaps were oversight rather than convenience: help close them, publicly, well before 2028, regardless of what it costs a future campaign to do so.

LIBERIA SPENT THIS SUMMER learning exactly what one jurisdictional gap costs, inside a system that was still centralized. It should not need that lesson taught four times over to understand what happens when nobody outside a political rivalry is minding the space between four separate ports. The 2029 race will happen with or without this newspaper’s opinion on it. Whether it happens on top of ports that are secure is still, for eighteen months, a choice.

World.title: India’s All-Women Peacekeepers Remembered In Liberia
World.content:
Monrovia – Ten years after India’s all-women Formed Police Unit packed up its last tour in Liberia, a new report says their biggest weapon wasn’t a baton – it was an example.

By Emmanuel Weedee-Conway

The report, _”The Legacy and Contributions of India’s All-Women Formed Police Unit (FPU) in UNMIL/Liberia, 2007–2016,”_ was launched Tuesday at the Cape Hotel by the Ducor Institute for Social and Economic Research in collaboration with the Indian Embassy.

Brigadier General Geraldine Janet George (Rtd), Liberia’s Minister of National Defense, served as Chief Launcher.

The event drew diplomats, security officials, civil society, and researchers to reflect on how 125 Indian women police officers helped reshape post-war Liberia.

First of Its Kind in UN History

In January 2007, India deployed the first-ever all-women FPU to a UN peacekeeping mission. Drawn from India’s Central Reserve Police Force, the officers came mostly from small towns and villages.

For a decade, they conducted patrols, riot control, public order management, training, medical support, and community outreach alongside the Liberia National Police.

Ambassador Manoj Verma said the deployment was historic from day one.

“When they arrived, they were not merely deployed as peacekeepers. They were making history,” he said.

A Bond Between Nations

Ambassador Verma described the FPU as the human face of India-Liberia ties, noting the report launch fell between Liberia’s July 26 and India’s August 15 independence days.

He maintains that both countries share democratic values and South-South cooperation in education, health, and trade.

He also highlighted India’s broader peacekeeping record: more than 300,000 personnel in 50+ missions since the 1950s, with women Indian peacekeepers still serving in DRC, South Sudan, Lebanon and elsewhere.

More Than Security: Changing Minds

Researchers say the FPU’s most enduring impact was social.

For many Liberian girls and women emerging from 14 years of civil war, seeing women in uniform, commanding patrols and managing crises, challenged deep-seated ideas about who could protect a nation.

In her own assessment, Minister George indicated that the unit proved women’s role in peace goes beyond symbolism.

“It demonstrated the vital role women can play in maintaining peace, protecting communities, strengthening public confidence and supporting post-conflict recovery,” she noted.

Minister George then urged policymakers to use the report to guide future Women, Peace and Security initiatives.

The deployment aligned with former President Ellen Johnson Sirleaf’s push to increase women’s participation in security and governance, and with UN Security Council Resolution 1325 on Women, Peace and Security.

One officer, former FPU Commander Seema Dhundia, has since risen to Inspector General of Police in India — a sign, officials said, of how the Liberia mission advanced women’s careers back home too.

The Ducor Institute report, authored by Dr. Aaron Weah, identified gaps in records, oral histories, and archives.

It recommends preserving documents, collecting testimonies in Liberia and India, integrating the FPU story into police training, and building public memorials.

The event also featured a photo exhibition and coincided with a US$1 million IBSA Fund project supporting women legislators in Liberia.

Members of Liberia’s Women Legislative Caucus were in India for a peer-learning exchange during the launch.

Nearly 20 years after the first Indian women peacekeepers arrived in Monrovia, their footprints remain — not just in barracks and patrol routes, but in the aspirations of a generation of Liberian women who saw what was possible.

World.title: India-Liberia Friendship Takes Center Stage as Embassy Marks 80th Independence Day
World.content:
Monrovia — The Embassy of India in Liberia has celebrated India’s 80th Independence Day with a vibrant display of patriotism, culture and diplomacy, bringing together Indian community members, Liberian government officials, diplomats and special guests to celebrate the longstanding friendship between the two countries.

By Patience M. Jones | [email protected]

The celebration on Saturday featured the ceremonial hoisting of the Indian national flag, cultural performances and a reception highlighting growing diplomatic, economic and people-to-people ties between India and Liberia.

The day’s first ceremony was held at the Indian Ambassador’s residence, where Ambassador Manoj B. Verma hoisted the Indian tricolor, known as the Tiranga, and delivered the message of the President of India.

The celebration later continued with cultural performances and social activities that brought Indian and Liberian guests together in an atmosphere of music, traditional performances and fellowship.

Ambassador Highlights Expanding Partnership

Addressing guests at the Independence Day reception, Ambassador Verma, on behalf of his wife, Poonam, and the Embassy of India family, expressed appreciation to the Government and people of Liberia for what he described as the two countries’ longstanding friendship and partnership.

Reflecting on India’s journey since independence from British colonial rule in 1947, Verma paid tribute to the country’s freedom fighters and founding leaders, whose sacrifices, he said, helped lay the foundation for India’s emergence as a vibrant democracy, strong economy and respected member of the international community.

He also congratulated Liberia on its election as a non-permanent member of the United Nations Security Council for the 2026–2027 term, wishing the country success in carrying out the responsibility.

According to Verma, India-Liberia relations have expanded across several areas, including technology, agriculture, health, mining, energy, trade and investment, education and capacity building.

He particularly welcomed Liberia’s recent inauguration and opening of its Embassy in New Delhi, describing the resident diplomatic mission as a significant milestone that is expected to further strengthen bilateral relations.

Nyanti’s India Visit Deepens Engagement

The Ambassador also highlighted the official visit of Liberia’s Foreign Minister, Sara Beysolow Nyanti, to India on August 13, 2026.

During the visit, Nyanti held bilateral discussions with India’s External Affairs Minister, Dr. S. Jaishankar, providing an opportunity for both countries to review their broad partnership and identify new areas of cooperation.

The two sides also exchanged views on regional and multilateral issues and discussed strengthening cooperation at international forums in support of peace, development and a stronger voice for the Global South.

India Expands Opportunities for Liberians

Verma said capacity building remains a central component of India’s development partnership with Liberia.

Under India’s Indian Technical and Economic Cooperation (ITEC) program, annual training opportunities for Liberians have been doubled from 70 to 140, while scholarships under the Indian Council for Cultural Relations (ICCR) have increased to 24.

He disclosed that 20 Liberian students have received scholarships this year to pursue master’s and doctoral programs at leading institutions in India.

More than 150 Liberians travelled to India last year for education, scholarships and professional training, while specialized training was also provided to 30 Liberian mining officials, geologists and engineers.

The Ambassador also highlighted development cooperation through the India-Brazil-South Africa (IBSA) Fund for South-South Cooperation, which is supporting Liberia’s Women’s Legislative Caucus.

Bilateral Trade Hits US$390 Million

Economic ties between the two countries are also expanding.

Verma disclosed that bilateral trade between India and Liberia reached approximately US$390 million in 2025–2026, while Liberia’s exports to India more than doubled to nearly US$45 million.

He said the figures demonstrate significant potential for the two countries to expand and diversify their economic partnership.

Beyond trade and investment, Verma emphasized the importance of cultural and people-to-people exchanges.

He cited the participation of a Liberian cultural troupe at the Surajkund International Crafts Mela in India earlier this year as an opportunity for Indian audiences to experience Liberia’s cultural heritage.

He also pointed to initiatives such as the International Day of Yoga, Study in India, tourism cooperation and youth outreach as avenues for bringing the people of the two countries closer.

‘A Friendship Built on Mutual Respect’

Ambassador Verma said India and Liberia share a friendship rooted in mutual respect, shared values and a common desire for peace, prosperity and development.

He reaffirmed India’s commitment to deepening the multifaceted partnership for the benefit of both countries.

The Ambassador also commended the Indian community in Liberia for contributing to the relationship through their businesses, professional activities, goodwill and engagement with Liberian society.

The celebration concluded with appreciation to Indian and Liberian colleagues at the Embassy who helped organize the event, followed by messages of goodwill marking India’s Independence Day.

“Happy Independence Day to all Indians and friends of India. Jai Hind,” Verma said.

The celebration provided not only an occasion to mark India’s 80th Independence Day, but also a reflection of the growing diplomatic, economic, educational and cultural ties between India and Liberia.

World.title: Maoma Says Hichilema Victory Safeguards Zambia’s Democracy
World.content:
United Party for National Development (UPND) National Chairman, Collins Maoma has said re-electing Mr Hakainde Hichilema to preside over the affairs of Zambian for the next five years means protecting the country’s democracy, peace and continued development.

Speaking shortly after Mr Hichilema was declared President-elect by Returning Officer for the presidential election, Mwangala Zaloumis at Mulungushi International Conference Centre Kenneth Kaunda Wing in Lusaka in the early hours of today, Mr Maoma said Mr Hichilema is a sober-minded leader who values peace.

He thanked all Zambians, UPND Alliance Partners and other political stakeholders for their peacefulness during the campaign period and throughout the electoral process leading to the August 13, 2026 general elections.

And UPND Alliance Partners said the re-election of the party and Mr Hichilema is the right decision Zambians have made for it will translate into bettering their lives through building on the strong foundation which the president-elect built during his first term in office.

Peter Chanda of the New Congress Party said Zambians have reaffirmed peace, democracy and stability of the nation through the August 13, 2026 polls.

And Lesley Chikuse of the Republican Progressive Party said choosing Mr Hichilema means actualising benefits that were promised to Zambians.

Meanwhile president of the opposition Party of National Unity and Progress (PNUP), Highvie Hamududu congratulated the UPND for having Members of Parliament from each of the ten provinces of Zambia.

Miles Sampa, the Patriotic Front president, noted that Mr Hichilema has been re-elected because of his remarkable performance as Head of State in the past five years.

Mr Hichilema has been re-elected after amassing 2,965,326 votes from the just ended polls, beating his closest rival, Brian Mundubile of the National Reconciliation Party for Unity and Prosperity (NRPUP) who garnered 1,856,217 ballots in an election which was contested by 13 presidential candidates.
