World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018892/‘Just So Easy’: Why China’s Gen Z Prefers Credit Without the Card
World.title: ‘Just So Easy’: Why China’s Gen Z Prefers Credit Without the Card
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018892/‘Just So Easy’: Why China’s Gen Z Prefers Credit Without the Card
World.content:
Yan Bowen’s only attempt to get a credit card came during her first year at university. The bank rejected her because she had no income, reinforcing her belief that cards were meant for “people with stable incomes.”

Then, at 22, she found herself in debt anyway.

Last October, she realized she owed around 3,000 yuan ($400) — more than her entire monthly student allowance. With the debt weighing on her, she cut daily expenses, took on part-time work, and borrowed from friends to pay it down.

The debt had built up through apps she used every day to order takeout, buy groceries, and shop online, each offering the option to pay later or split purchases into installments.

Even so, Yan sees the relatively low limits on app-based credit as a safeguard against getting in too deep. “It keeps the risk manageable, nothing big enough to shock my parents,” she said. “A credit card would just mean higher risk.”

That wariness extends well beyond Yan. By the end of March 2026, China had about 687 million credit and combo cards in circulation, down roughly 120 million from their 2022 peak, according to central bank data.

Yan is one of 12 people aged 20 to 26, including students, job seekers, and office workers, whom Sixth Tone interviewed in July. Of them, nine had never owned a credit card. Many knew little about how cards worked and worried most about missing repayments. The few who did use cards tended to do so for specific reasons, such as overseas travel or managing cash flow.

More than 60 credit card subcenters closed across China in 2025, according to state-run People’s Daily, while some banks folded their card businesses and standalone apps into broader retail operations.

Yet outstanding balances on bank cards have remained relatively stable, said Jiang Jiajun, an associate professor at Fudan University’s School of Economics, in Shanghai. That suggests many of the cards being canceled were dormant rather than evidence that consumers had stopped borrowing. Even so, he said, “at least from the data, there is a clear trend of people avoiding credit cards.”

The traditional selling points — higher limits, longer interest-free periods, and richer rewards — may simply matter less to younger consumers. Those perks “are not necessarily what Gen Z cares most about,” Jiang said.

Yan’s first encounter with borrowing came through a food-delivery coupon. During her sophomore year, Chinese delivery app Meituan offered her a discount worth less than 1 yuan, but only if she activated its pay-later service. She did.

Before long, she had signed up for Huabei, a credit service inside Ant Group’s Alipay payment app, and Baitiao, a similar product from e-commerce giant JD.com. “They’re just so easy,” Yan said. “Even when traveling, hotels let you stay first and pay later.”

Even with enough money in the bank, Yan sometimes chose to pay later or in installments rather than watch her balance fall. Small debts piled up across different apps, and she often did not know the total until the monthly bill came due.

Her biggest current debt comes from a 6,500-yuan laptop. To be eligible for a student discount, Yan had to pay through Baitiao, so she split the cost into six monthly installments of more than 1,000 yuan. As of Aug. 5, she still owed more than 5,600 yuan.

Unlike credit cards, which require a separate application, app-based credit is built directly into services young consumers already use, often with lower limits and fewer steps between browsing and borrowing.

Jiang said the difference comes down partly to “mental accounting” — the way people sort spending into different mental buckets. Small, frequent purchases through apps like Huabei can feel like part of a “convenient lifestyle” rather than “financial debt.” Credit cards, by contrast, make the borrowing harder to ignore.

“They make users acutely aware that they are borrowing money, which naturally triggers resistance,” Jiang said. “These two things sit in completely different mental accounts for young people.”

For some young consumers, credit cards begin to look more useful as purchases get bigger and finances more secure.

Wang Xuanren, 23, works in finance in the eastern city of Nanjing and applied for her first and only credit card in 2024 ahead of an overseas trip. She already had more than 500,000 yuan in a fixed-term deposit at the bank, helping her secure approval the same day; the card arrived five days later.

She now saves it largely for electronics and luxury goods. For big-ticket purchases, Wang said installments can turn a 40,000- or 50,000-yuan expense into much smaller monthly payments, automatically deducted from her debit account.

“I keep a lot of cash on hand,” she said. “Using a credit card interest-free is basically borrowing someone else’s money and paying it back later.”

Zheng Yuxin, a 21-year-old university student in Shanghai, is far less comfortable with that bargain. She has no plans to apply for a credit card or use app-based credit anytime soon. “Nothing in life is free,” she said.

Even generous sign-up bonuses make her wary. Credit cards feel “very distant and risky,” she said. “I worry about falling for a scam because I can’t tell what’s real.”

In 2023, Zheng activated Huabei after agreeing to an authorization screen and completing facial verification. It then became her default payment method, allowing later purchases to be charged through the service without her actively choosing it each time.

She realized what had happened only when roughly 100 yuan was deducted from her bank account on repayment day. “Seeing unexpected money disappear gave me this empty, unsettled feeling,” she said. Since then, she has stuck to a simpler rule: buy only when she already has the money.

From Sept. 30, China will require a clearer separation between paying and borrowing online. Non-bank payment providers will no longer be allowed to present loans as payment options or market lending products through their payment services, with companies required to adjust their practices before the rules take effect.

Jiang said such rules should make borrowing more transparent and give users clearer warnings before they take on debt. The goal, he said, is not to eliminate app-based credit, but to make sure consumers know when an ordinary purchase has become a loan. “This protects consumers and helps platforms earn long-term trust,” he said.

Those preferences may change with age. Higher incomes, more travel, and larger spending needs could eventually make the higher limits and longer interest-free periods of credit cards more useful. “The same group of people might develop completely different habits 10 years from now,” said Jiang.

Zhang Xinyun, 24 and from the northeastern city of Harbin, is currently unemployed and remains deeply wary of credit cards after watching a relative struggle with card debt when she was a teenager. “Spending ahead always comes with bad temptations,” she said. High limits look more like added risk than freedom, and sign-up gifts do little to reassure her.

But Zhang can imagine her needs changing. Once she starts working or running a business, she said, a card could become useful for managing cash flow or traveling overseas.

Jiang underscores that banks cannot rely on that change happening on its own. “They need to improve convenience, embrace fintech, and create use cases that resonate with younger consumers.”

At the bank where Zhao Wei works in the northeastern city of Shenyang, signing up new credit card users is part of the job. She is expected to bring in dozens each year and, last year, even opened her own first card partly to help meet the target.

Many customers worry about missing repayments and damaging their credit records, Zhao said. Others simply see little need for a card when mobile payments and app-based credit are already woven into daily spending through digital services such as WeChat Pay, Alipay, and Huabei.

Banks have responded with incentives. Zhao’s gives new cardholders 150 yuan in spending credits, along with gifts ranging from rice and cooking oil to household appliances. Elsewhere, welcome offers can include health checkups, airport lounge access, fuel vouchers, coffee coupons, and cash back on purchases.

Zhao is blunt about how far such incentives can go. “People who are put off by credit cards won’t open one just for that,” she said.

More recently, her bank began offering customized cards printed with customers’ pet photos, along with discounts on pet supplies.

Even that has not made Zhao optimistic. “Credit cards are being squeezed by more convenient products,” she said. “If they can’t build stronger ties to daily life, becoming obsolete is not impossible.”

Editor: Apurva.

(Header image: VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018887/Lost, Looted, Crumbling: The Vanishing Temple Murals of Yu County
World.title: Lost, Looted, Crumbling: The Vanishing Temple Murals of Yu County
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018887/Lost, Looted, Crumbling: The Vanishing Temple Murals of Yu County
World.content:
A Chinese county known as the home of over 400 temple murals dating back to the Ming dynasty (1368–1644) is facing a heritage restoration crisis, with many of its murals stolen, destroyed, or marred by thieves.

In an investigation published Wednesday, Shanghai-based news outlet The Paper visited 16 fortified villages in Yu County in the northern Hebei province and found that many of the area’s temple murals had been stolen, destroyed during temple collapse, or weathered beyond recognition. Remaining fragments often bore looters’ cut marks.

A major cultural relic hub, the county served as a military and commercial crossroads during the Ming and Qing dynasties (1644–1911) and is home to more than 1,600 registered cultural heritage locations, including numerous fortified villages. The accompanying temples feature murals depicting Taoist, Buddhist, and folk religious elements.

Danhou Village — inscribed on China’s official list of traditional villages in 2016 — is one of the county’s most popular tourist destinations. The village’s Guandi Temple was once home to extensive murals, but only fragments remain today.

When The Paper visited, the temple was under renovation for leaking roofs, missing wooden components, and cracked walls after years of neglect. Work began in April and is projected to be completed by the end of the year.

Of the 16 villages The Paper visited, only those officially considered “traditional villages” or protected sites received restoration and care. The report noted that overall neglect of the fortified villages stems from their abandonment, as villagers have mostly lived outside the sites since the 1980s, leaving the buildings to decay.

A member of the county’s cultural relics management office told The Paper that he recently inspected a temple on a visit to his hometown.

“I went there around noon, and the wall was still standing,” he said. “But at around 2 p.m., I got a call saying the western wall of that temple had collapsed. If I had gone any later, I might have been buried under it.”

Another obstacle to upkeep is funding. Under China’s cultural relics law, their owners or users must preserve them, with government subsidies provided where possible. But in Yu County, most low-level relics are owned by villages that can’t afford maintenance, placing the burden on the county.

The cultural relics worker described how every village has an appointed relic steward, but with no subsidy budget, the role falls to village cadres as an additional duty. With heavy workloads and no stipends, protection relies on individual goodwill.

Yet government investment has been considerable. Over a decade ago, Yu County built a 12,000-square-meter museum for 10,000-plus movable relics, free to the public, costing the county nearly 4 million yuan ($600,000) annually. In 2023, state and provincial funds for restoration projects totaled 14.6 million yuan.

Despite the investment, Yu County’s neglected relics expose gaps in China’s heritage architecture protection, a problem that it has been working to solve in recent years.

In July 2024, the Finance Ministry created a lottery-funded program for unlisted ancient buildings. Upon submitting a proposal, local authorities whose heritage architecture and restoration projects are deemed to serve the public good are given priority. The program will run through 2027.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: Murals at an ancient temple in Yu County, Hebei province, June 20, 2026. VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018886/The Forgotten Legacy of China’s Greatest Explorer
World.title: The Forgotten Legacy of China’s Greatest Explorer
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018886/The Forgotten Legacy of China’s Greatest Explorer
World.content:
During the opening decades of the 15th century, a eunuch from China’s imperial court led seven epic voyages across Southeast Asia and the Indian Ocean, pushing westward as far as the Red Sea and the shores of East Africa.

The expeditions were astonishing feats of engineering and navigation. Setting sail decades before Christopher Columbus or Vasco da Gama, Zheng spent years crossing the oceans at the head of a vast fleet of 200 ships. Some of the vessels measured up to 70 meters long — three times the size of Columbus’ ships.

For many, Zheng deserves to rank among history’s greatest explorers. Yet, much about the voyages — and Zheng himself — remains shrouded in mystery. He barely features in the official records left by China’s Ming dynasty (1368–1644), with court historians dismissing his expeditions as impressive, but ruinously expensive. Even the place and date of Zheng’s death are unknown.

The Ming court’s assessment still colors views of Zheng centuries later. Today, the great admiral is well known in China, with generations of schoolchildren learning about his amazing treasure ships that brought giraffes, lions, zebras, and other exotic beasts back from Africa. But the voyages tend to be presented as a historical curiosity that had little lasting impact.

Zou Zhenhuan is on a mission to change that. The 69-year-old — now a distinguished professor at Shanghai’s Fudan University — has spent decades studying Zheng He, and his research has played a significant role in shifting perceptions of the explorer and his legacy. His latest book, “Monsoon Asia and Africa: Cultural Exchange and Zheng He’s Voyages,” is his most comprehensive look at the subject yet.

For Zou, Zheng’s voyages were far more influential than often assumed. Far from a flash in the pan, they opened up a new era of maritime trade between Asia and Africa, as merchants took advantage of the navigational technologies and sea routes pioneered by Zheng. He even believes they helped pave the way for the European Age of Discovery that followed.

In this interview, Zou, who is also a research fellow at the Shanghai Research Institute of Culture and History, explains why Zheng He is often so misunderstood — and why his voyages should be seen as a harbinger of globalization. The text has been edited for brevity and clarity.

Sixth Tone: You have studied Zheng He for more than 20 years. What drew you to this subject in the beginning?

Zou: My interest in Zheng He began in my boyhood. What captivated me most was his extraordinary perseverance — seven voyages spanning more than two decades. Such marvelous experiences are enough to stir the imagination. As the Portuguese poet Luís de Camões wrote in “Os Lusíadas,” the true and marvelous deeds of brave men surpass all fantasy and legend. I was a sickly boy, but I harbored an intense hero complex, and Zheng He’s exploits answered it perfectly.

It was this interest that led me to study Zheng He once I became a historian, and it is this same interest that has sustained my research for so many years.

Sixth Tone: After all these years of research, what kind of person is Zheng He in your mind?

Zou: As my research has deepened, the image of Zheng He in my mind has grown ever richer. Take his religious faith, for example. Many people might assume Zheng He was simply a Muslim. He was indeed born into a Muslim family; his grandfather and father both made the hajj to Mecca. But he was also a devout Buddhist who was accepted as a disciple by an eminent monk, receiving the Dharma name “Fushan,” and supervising the construction of the Great Bao’en Temple in Nanjing. At the same time, Zheng He was also an adherent of Confucianism. Historical records describe him as “endowed with the talent to govern and versed in the teachings of Confucius and Mencius.”

The most famous material testimony to Zheng He’s plural faith is the trilingual stele he erected in the kingdom of Ceylon (present-day Sri Lanka) during his second voyage in 1409. The stele, commonly known as the Galle Trilingual Inscription, is carved in three scripts: the Chinese text praises the Buddha and records a list of offerings; the Tamil text glorifies the Hindu god Shiva; and the Persian text extols Allah. Paying tribute to the deities of three great religions on a single stone tablet is, in my view, the most vivid expression of Zheng He’s cosmopolitan, all-embracing spirit.

Sixth Tone: It seems “plurality” is a keyword when it comes to Zheng He.

Zou: Exactly. Zheng He was a man of all-around talent. To begin with, he possessed exceptional organizational and managerial abilities — commanding a fleet of more than 27,000 men was in itself an enormously complex feat of systems engineering.

He also had the metaphysical learning of a Confucian scholar and was equally adept at practical, technical matters: during the voyages he spread the Chinese calendar, rituals, weights and measures, and architectural techniques to other countries, and with superb diplomatic skill he mediated disputes between Siam and Malacca, and between Annam and Champa.

Plus, he even displayed outstanding military talent: on his very first voyage he defeated Chen Zuyi, a pirate chief who commanded tens of thousands of followers in the Strait of Malacca, wiping out more than 5,000 pirates.

Sixth Tone: When I was reading your book, what impressed me most was Zheng He’s nautical technology — especially his precise understanding and ingenious use of the Indian Ocean monsoons.

Zou: That’s right. The fleet’s seven expeditions were deeply embedded in the monsoon, which is the main reason I titled the book “Monsoon Asia and Africa.”

The regions the fleet traversed — East Asia, Southeast Asia, and the Indian Ocean — are among the areas of the world where the monsoon phenomenon is most pronounced. And in an era without modern propulsion, the monsoon was the “engine” that drove this enormous armada on its long voyages.

The fleet usually departed China in winter, between October and March, riding the northeast monsoon southward. By the time it reached the Indian Ocean, the summer southwest monsoon would be blowing, allowing a smooth voyage home. The whole round trip took about a year and a half.

To visit more places efficiently, Zheng He would dispatch detached squadrons along the way; after completing their missions, these squadrons would regroup at designated rendezvous points in accordance with the monsoon patterns.

But here’s the thing: the monsoon and the compass could carry the fleet forward, but they could not tell the crew exactly where they were on the open sea. To do this, the fleet mastered a refined technique known as “guoyang qianxing,” or star-observation navigation, using an instrument called the “qianxing,” or star-measuring, board to determine a ship’s latitude according to stars’ altitude above the horizon. Zheng He’s fleets also compiled these observations into dedicated star charts, creating a reusable navigational database.

One could say that Zheng He’s fleet fused three techniques — the monsoon patterns, star-observation navigation, and the magnetic compass — into a single, world-leading navigational system for its time. I believe these sea routes, nautical technology, and geographical knowledge helped lay the intellectual and technical foundations for the arrival of European explorers more than half a century later. However, this topic needs further research.

Sixth Tone: Since you mention the European explorers who came later, I have to raise a common critique: that unlike the explorers who launched Europe’s Age of Discovery, Zheng He’s expeditions — for all their grandeur — were a mere flash in the pan that left no lasting imprint. How do you see it?

Zou: This view is indeed very common. I would point out that Zheng He’s seven voyages were not merely official acts of diplomacy by the Ming court; they also facilitated exchanges of goods, species, and technologies between Asia and Africa on an unprecedented scale.

The exotic animals the fleet brought back from foreign lands — giraffes, lions, ostriches, zebras — and the rare plants and fruits such as pepper, sappanwood, and durian greatly enriched China’s native stock of species. Wherever it went, the fleet shared nautical and astronomical knowledge with local peoples, deepening mutual learning among the civilizations of Asia and Africa.

The most representative example of all this is blue-and-white porcelain. Zheng He’s fleet carried large quantities of porcelain into the Islamic world, while the cobalt pigment needed to produce blue-and-white ware, known as “Sumali blue,” originally came from Persia. This pattern of “bringing finished products out and importing raw materials in” was itself a cross-cultural dialogue of technology and aesthetics.

As the Ming dynasty’s most sought-after export in overseas markets, blue-and-white porcelain was among the important gifts carried on every mission. Pieces dating from the period of Zheng He’s voyages have been unearthed at Fustat in Egypt, at Aydhab in Sudan, at Aden on the Arabian Peninsula, and elsewhere.

The huge overseas demand, in turn, stimulated a massive increase in early Ming porcelain production: according to historical records, in 1433 alone the court ordered the firing of 443,500 pieces in a single decree.

What does this tell us? It shows that nearly a century before Columbus set sail, Zheng He’s fleet had already opened up the east-west sea routes of the Indian Ocean and built a regional network of trade and cultural exchange. I call this the “Zheng He exchange.”

Sixth Tone: That concept readily brings to mind the “Columbian exchange” — the massive exchange of people, plants, animals, and diseases between the Americas and Afro-Eurasia that opened up after Columbus’ voyages.

Zou: I did indeed borrow the theoretical framework of the “Columbian exchange,” but my concept points to an earlier wave of civilizational interaction — one that unfolded between Asia and Africa. In many respects, Zheng He was a key catalyst on the eve of globalization.

Of course, while the “Zheng He exchange” and the “Columbian exchange” share many similarities, their purposes were fundamentally different. Zheng He’s voyages never established colonies overseas, and they were extremely restrained in their use of force.

As you mentioned, many Chinese people feel rather regretful about this, believing it caused China to miss a golden opportunity to dominate the globe. Liu Cixin’s short science-fiction story “Xiyang” (“The Western Ocean”) expresses exactly this sentiment through an alternate-history framework: in the story, Zheng He’s fleet sails farther west from the East African coast, rounds the Cape of Good Hope, and eventually reaches Europe, defeats the combined Anglo-French forces, and conquers the European continent, turning China into an empire on which the sun never sets.

But in my view, Zheng He radiates the light of pacifism and cultural pluralism — and that is precisely where his example can offer inspiration for our own time.

(Header image: A statue of Zheng He in Hangzhou, Zhejiang province, 2024. 500px Essential)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018882/An AI Actress Sold Contact Lenses. China Isn’t Buying It.
World.title: An AI Actress Sold Contact Lenses. China Isn’t Buying It.
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018882/An AI Actress Sold Contact Lenses. China Isn’t Buying It.
World.content:
“My contact lenses are comfortable even after wearing them all day. Do you want to try them?”

So says a young woman in glasses with transparent lenses, in response to a friend who says her contacts are painful. She then takes a contact box out of a black handbag, offers it, and says, “You can blink without worry.”

The endorsement seems genuine enough — except neither woman is real.

This , featuring the popular AI actress Fang Taozi endorsing colored contacts, has recently sparked controversy in China over whether an AI character can vouch for a product’s quality.

Released in late July on Douyin, the Chinese version of TikTok, by domestic contact lens brand Nutnutlook, the ad was taken down without comment last week.

In response, Chinese netizens criticized the  for using an AI avatar instead of a human actress. “What makes me uncomfortable is that someone without eyes now has the right to speak about eyes,” one user commented.

“AI doesn’t even know what it feels like to actually wear the product,” another wrote.

Neither the company behind the AI actress, Guangzhou-based World Media Film and TV Culture, nor the contacts brand has responded to the controversy.

The fictional 20-year-old Fang Taozi was unveiled in the AI short drama “The Laid-off Girl” in June this year. The series, which tells the story of a small-town girl moving to a fictional city to pursue a modeling career, has been viewed more than 320 million times on Douyin.

In the months following the series’ release, directed by popular content creator Fei Feifei, Fang’s personal Douyin account — created by companies to boost AI actors’popularity — gained more than 470,000 followers. Her account posts content ranging from so-called “behind-the-scenes” footage during the show’s production to snippets of her supposed daily life, such as making breakfast.

Fang has been lauded by fans for having, unlike many AI characters, moles and blemishes, giving her an imperfect and realistic appearance. In “The Laid-off Girl,” she struggles with relatable Chinese workplace challenges, such as pressure to attend business dinners and getting bullied by her colleagues.

Domestic media reported that on Juliang Xingtu, Douyin’s influencer marketing platform, Fang Taozi’s advertising rates are 168,000 yuan ($24,900) per video for clips under 20 seconds, 208,000 yuan for videos between 21 and 60 seconds, and 258,000 yuan for videos over 60 seconds — significantly higher than ad rates charged by most human influencers.

Ma Lihong, a senior partner at Beijing DHH Law Firm, told domestic media that, despite AI avatars not being considered people under Chinese law and therefore not legally considered  endorsers, the video could still constitute false advertising.

Ma added that advertisers are responsible for the truthfulness of their content and that by making a first-person claim about experiencing a product, the AI character could be seen as fabricating user experience. As such, the brand and the ’s producer could potentially be in violation of the law.

Compounding the severity of the issue, colored contact lenses are classified as Class III medical devices under China’s regulatory system, reserved for items that pose the highest risk to consumers. Actors are prohibited from recommending such products in s, a rule aimed at preventing brands from misleading consumers.

This is not the first time Chinese brands have experimented with AI-generated figures in advertising. Major bottled water company Nongfu Spring made headlines last year for using AI-generated images in promotional posters, while companies ranging from yogurt brands to office chair suppliers have collaborated with various AI-generated actors to endorse products and use slogans. Tutorials on using AI-generated videos for livestream commerce have also become common.

Entertainment law expert Qiu Zhimiao said AI-powered endorsements will become increasingly common, and regulating them is a new frontier. As s endorsed by virtual influencers exist in a legal gray area, he said, there is a need for clearer regulations.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: A screenshot of the AI actress Fang Taozi in the  promoting colored contact lenses. From Weibo)

World.title: FACT CHECK: Post cites 2025 SC ruling to falsely claim VP Sara impeachment trial to be halted
World.content:
The Supreme Court's 2025 ruling barred Duterte's impeachment then as the fourth complaint violated the one year bar rule; the ongoing impeachment trial is a separate proceeding that began in 2026

Claim: The ongoing impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte may be halted after the Supreme Court (SC) declared unconstitutional the fourth impeachment complaint against her.

Rating: FALSE

Why we fact-checked this: The reel bearing the claim was posted on July 25 and has already received 158,000 views, 11,100 reactions, 1,100 shares, and 330 comments as of writing. It shows a photo of Duterte’s defense counsel, including lawyers Sheila Sison, Michael Poa, Carlo Joaquin Narvasa, and Mark Vinluan.

Background audio was attached to the reel, in which a narrator can be heard saying, “Breaking news! Impeachment trial posibleng ipatigil ng Supreme Court matapos idineklara ng Korte na labag sa Konstitusyon ang ikaapat na reklamong impeachment laban kay Pangalawang Pangulo Sara Duterte. Ang litratong ito ay galing mismo sa Supreme Court ng Pilipinas.”

(Breaking News! The Supreme Court may halt the impeachment trial after declaring the fourth impeachment complaint against Vice President Sara Duterte unconstitutional. This photo comes directly from the Supreme Court of the Philippines.)

Several Facebook users believed the claim. One comment reads, “Yes, thank you lord and thank you, your honors, the Supreme Court of the Philippines!”

The facts: While the SC did issue a ruling stating that the fourth impeachment complaint against Duterte was unconstitutional, it concerned the first impeachment drive against the Vice President in 2025. Contrary to the claim, it does not apply or nullify Duterte’s ongoing impeachment trial, which is based on a new set of complaints filed in February 2026.

During the the first impeachment drive in 2025, the SC barred Duterte’s impeachment, saying that the fourth complaint against her already violated the one year bar rule. At the time, Duterte faced four complaints; the first three did not materialize and she was impeached on the fourth complaint.

The High Court held that the House’s failure to act on the first three complaints meant they were effectively dismissed, and they were therefore deemed terminated on February 5, 2025.

After a year, new complaints were filed against Duterte in February 2026. The third and fourth complaints were found to be sufficient in form and substance. Duterte was impeached again by the House in May. These new articles of impeachment are currently being heard in the Senate, convening as an impeachment court, since July 6.

Since the second impeachment drive is based on fresh complaints filed in 2026, the 2025 SC ruling concerning a previous impeachment complaint has no connection to the current proceedings and does not bar the ongoing trial.

The Senate trial continues its deliberation on the four articles of impeachment against Duterte, particularly her alleged misuse of confidential funds, unexplained wealth, bribery, and grave threats.

AI-generated: Artificial intelligence (AI) detector tools flagged the reel as AI-generated. Hive Detect rated the video as 99.9% likely to contain AI-generated content and 98.9% likely to have AI-generated audio. Undetectable AI also flagged the video as AI-generated with 97% confidence on its analysis.

A reverse image search also did not show any credible photo issued by the Supreme Court that matches the image presented in the Facebook reel.

Previous fact checks: Rappler has previously fact-checked similar false claims about Duterte’s impeachment:

– Angelee Kaye Abelinde/Rappler.com

The impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte — the first Philippine public official to be impeached twice by the House of Representatives — began at 2 pm on Monday, July 6.

World.title: [Vantage Point] Companions in power: When Ramon Ang goes up against Ramon Ang
World.content:
His personal investment in Lopez Inc. is not necessarily a conflict of interest. But there are red lights.

There is nothing inherently wrong with Ramon S. Ang investing his own money. But his 25.68% stake in Lopez Inc. creates a corporate-governance question that has attracted surprisingly little attention: where does Ramon Ang, the independent private investor, leave off and Ramon Ang, the chairman and chief executive of San Miguel Corp. (SMC), step in?

His personal investment is not necessarily a conflict of interest. But there are enough red lights to make the longer answer important.

Ang acquired the stake through his wholly owned investment vehicle Illumina Investment Holdings Inc. SMC did not buy the shares, and even clarified in an official disclosure to the Philippine Stock Exchange (PSE) that Ang had acted in his personal capacity.

That is an important distinction, but it does not resolve potential conflicts.

Consider the numbers.

Lopez Inc. owns 54.74% of Lopez Holdings, which owns 60.67% of First Philippine Holdings (FPH). FPH, in turn, owns 67.84% of First Gen Corporation (First Gen)’s common shares. Trace Ang’s 25.68% through those ownership layers and you will see that he has roughly 5.79% look-through economic exposure to First Gen.

That is not a direct holding or voting right. But Ang now has a personal economic interest in one of the biggest power groups in the Philippines, while continuing to head another conglomerate that dominates much of the same industry.

The Energy Regulatory Commission (ERC)’s numbers make that overlap difficult to brush aside. At end-2024, SMC accounted for 6,079.6 megawatts (MW) of attributable installed generating capacity, or 22.44% of the national total — the country’s largest share. First Gen ranked third with 3,583 MW, or 13.22%.

These are not two companies that may eventually collide in the same line of business. They already inhabit the same electricity market. They may compete for power plants, renewable-energy projects, liquefied natural gas (LNG) and other fuel contracts, electricity customers, financing, and government-awarded energy opportunities.

This is where the conflict becomes real. (READ: ERC scrutiny adds a new wrinkle to Ramon Ang’s Lopez, Inc investment)

The many what ifs

What if an attractive generating asset is offered for sale and First Gen wants it as badly as San Miguel? Suppose they pursue the same hydropower project or power-supply contract. Imagine commercially sensitive information obtained from one side potentially giving an advantage to the other.

Which Ramon Ang would then show up?

Philippine corporation law anticipated this problem.

Section 30 of the Revised Corporation Code addresses directors who acquire personal or pecuniary interests that conflict with their duties.

Section 33 goes further: when a director, by virtue of his office, takes for himself a business opportunity that should belong to the corporation and profits at its expense, he must account for those profits, unless stockholders representing at least two-thirds of outstanding capital stock ratify the act.

The law contains an especially relevant qualification: the corporate-opportunity rule applies even when the director risked his own funds.

Caveat: this does not mean that Ang breached either provision by buying into Lopez Inc.

There is no evidence that SMC wanted Crème Investment Corp.’s 25.68% stake, that the opportunity was first offered to San Miguel, or that Ang diverted an SMC opportunity into Illumina. It would be a step too far to call the acquisition itself unlawful.

Ang’s Lopez stake carries an implied value of roughly P11.56 billion based on his P45-billion valuation of Lopez Inc. Piki Lopez has described him not merely as an investor but as a “partner” whose expertise could help grow Lopez businesses.

Why governance matters

The corporate relationships are meanwhile becoming more intertwined. ABS-CBN is raising P6 billion in fresh equity, including P3.5 billion from I&C Holdings Corp., a newly incorporated investment company formed by senior bankers associated with Fortman Cline Capital Markets.

Fortman Cline is hardly a stranger to San Miguel. Its published transaction history shows it advised SMC on acquisitions that helped transform the conglomerate into a major power and infrastructure player, including transactions involving Meralco, Sual, San Roque, Ilijan and, more recently, the NAIA concession.

None of this establishes that Ang owns, finances or controls I&C. There is presently no documentary evidence that he does. But it illustrates how closely Philippine corporate circles can intersect — and why governance matters as personal investments, advisory relationships and corporate partnerships overlap.

Does that mean Lopez companies should now avoid businesses where San Miguel operates?

No.

That would effectively create a private non-compete zone around SMC. First Gen should not abandon a project merely because San Miguel wants it. The governance burden falls principally on Ang and the decision-making process.

Disclosure and recusal

When interests collide, disclosure and recusal become essential. Confidential information cannot travel from one side to benefit another, and an opportunity properly belonging to SMC cannot be redirected toward an enterprise in which Ang has a personal financial interest.

The problem could also run in reverse. We still do not know what governance rights accompany Illumina’s 25.68% Lopez Inc. stake. If Ang or his nominees obtain board seats, veto rights or direct participation in strategic decisions, fiduciary obligations could arise on both sides.

That is why the next crucial disclosure is not another percentage.

It is governance.

And there is one coincidence worth putting on the table.

On August 3, before I&C emerged publicly, the market was abuzz with speculations that an Ang-led investor group was preparing to inject P3.5 billion into ABS-CBN for a 39% economic interest. ABS-CBN subsequently denied that Ang and Manuel V. Pangilinan were negotiating to take over management.

Eleven days later, the disclosed transaction involves I&C investing exactly P3.5 billion for what our calculations suggest could become roughly 38% of enlarged ABS-CBN.

The numbers are remarkably close.

But coincidence is not evidence. Nothing disclosed so far establishes that Ang owns, finances or controls I&C. The parallel is nevertheless difficult enough to ignore — and important enough for investors to keep watching.

None of this presumes wrongdoing. Good governance exists precisely because legitimate business interests sometimes collide.

The scale makes complacency difficult. SMC held 22.44% of attributable national installed generating capacity at end-2024; First Gen had 13.22%. Between them sits Ramon Ang—SMC chairman and CEO on one side and, through Illumina, owner of 25.68% of the holding company above the other.

Those interests can coexist.

The test comes when they want the same thing.

And when that day arrives, the question will no longer be whether Ramon Ang bought his Lopez stake with his own money.

It will be which Ramon Ang has the fiduciary duty to step away.

I welcome your views on these and other issues where decisions made in power shape the country’s economic future.

World.title: [OPINION] Will AI take Filipino jobs? The answer depends on what we do now
World.content:
The future of Filipino jobs is not waiting for us in 2027. We are shaping it now.

Will artificial intelligence take our jobs? It is a question many Filipino workers are asking. It was also central to discussions at the 2026 Future of Work Forum organised by the European Chamber of Commerce of the Philippines (ECCP).

AI and clean energy may appear separate, but they raise the same question: can the Philippines turn technology and investment into better jobs and better lives?

Prosperity requires skills, strong institutions, productive businesses — and shared benefits.

The better question is whether the Philippines can prepare people for new opportunities while protecting those most at risk.

The evidence calls for neither panic nor complacency. The International Labour Organization’s 2025 global assessment finds that one in four workers is in an occupation with some exposure to generative AI. Yet only 3.3 per cent of global employment is in the highest exposure category. AI is therefore more likely to change jobs than remove them entirely.

AI can handle routine tasks, but judgement, accountability, communication and trust remain hard to replace. Technology should help people, not displace them.

For the Philippines, the stakes are high. ILO research estimates that 12.7 million jobs — more than one-quarter of employment — have some potential exposure to generative AI. Women face greater exposure because many work in clerical, administrative and service occupations.

But exposure does not mean job loss. Philippine firms can use AI to move from repetitive transactions to higher-value services. Our advantage cannot continue to rest on lower costs. It must increasingly come from Filipino skills and services that clients trust.

Young people face a challenge. The ILO’s Global Employment Trends for Youth 2026 estimates that 6.1 per cent of jobs held by people aged 15 to 29 are in occupations highly exposed to AI-related change. Many are middle-skilled jobs that provide entry into work. Meanwhile, jobs in science, engineering, health and information technology are growing. Young people need clear routes from learning into expanding occupations.

Clean energy presents an opportunity. The World Bank’s 2026 Philippines Economic Update estimates that, compared with a constrained pathway, a fully implemented, least-cost power transition could generate about 161,000 jobs by 2030. But without skilled workers, these opportunities may be delayed or lost.

This is why skills policy is economic policy — and youth policy. Investments do not automatically become Filipino jobs. Employers need skilled workers. Young people need apprenticeships, employment services and paths from learning into work. Government must provide standards, responsive training systems and support during difficult transitions.

Yet, businesses, government agencies, training institutions, and workers’ organizations often work separately. Training can remain disconnected from investment, while employers struggle to find qualified people. The problem is not Filipino talent. It is sustained coordination and delivery.

The Philippines’ roadmap under the United Nations Global Accelerator on Jobs and Social Protection for Just Transitions responds by bringing partners together around decent jobs and stronger social protection.

The proposed Better Energy Alliance could put this approach into practice in clean energy. It would bring companies, business organisations, government, training institutions and workers’ organisations around one table. Together, they could identify new occupations, update training standards, develop apprenticeships and recognised certification, improve workplace safety, and remove barriers to investment and job creation.

Led by the private sector, anchored in government and shaped through social dialogue, the Alliance would connect industry demand with national training. Workers’ organisations would help ensure that plans reflect workers’ needs. The ILO can contribute technical knowledge and international experience.

The Alliance should not become another short-term training project. It should become a lasting bridge between clean-energy investment, the national skills system and decent jobs.

The future of Filipino jobs is not waiting for us in 2027. We are shaping it now. Technology will not decide whether these changes widen inequality or create better jobs and shared prosperity. Our choices — and our ability to work together — will. – Rappler.com

Khalid Hassan is the director of the International Labour Organization’s country office for the Philippines.

World.title: 2 dead in Ateneo de Zamboanga shooting: What we know so far
World.content:
CAMPUS SHOOTING. An investigator stand near the body of a student inside one of the classrooms at Ateneo de Zamboanga University in Zamboanga City on Tuesday morning, August 18, 2026.

(7th UPDATE) Zamboanga Mayor Khymer Olaso tells ANC that the shooter was a 'very bright student' but was reportedly a 'Roblox fanatic'

ZAMBOANGA, Philippines – At least two students were killed in a shooting at a building of Ateneo de Zamboanga University on Tuesday morning, August 18.

Ateneo de Zamboanga University confirmed the two deaths inside its junior high school campus. One of those who died was the shooter himself.

Outside the school in Zamboanga City, a crowd gathered, mostly worried parents, waiting anxiously for word about their children.

Police said the incident occurred at about 7:45 am at the university’s Tumaga campus in Barangay Tumaga.

Authorities said the suspect was a minor, while the victim was a 10th grader, also a minor.

Initial police findings showed that the shooter went to Room 404 of the campus building and shot the other student, killing him. He then ran down to the third floor, shouted, and then shot himself.

Gun from Bureau of Customs

Police said they found 9mm pistols at the crime scene, and that it looked like a case of premeditated attack.

The father of the shooter was the Enforcement and Security Service District commander of the port of Zamboanga, according to Bureau of Customs chief Ariel Nepomuceno.

He also confirmed that at least one of the guns used by the shooter had been issued by BOC.

“I had to relieve him immediately to have an impartial investigation,” Nepomuceno told Rappler.

Details of the campus shooting remained sketchy, and people, including reporters, were barred from getting inside. This report will be updated as more information becomes available.

Philippine National Police chief General Melencio Nartatez Jr. said authorities in Zamboanga were establishing the circumstances surrounding the shooting.

“The situation is now under control,” he said even as he called for calm.

Father Guillrey Anthony Andal, AdZU president, said students had to be evacuated to a safe place immediately after the gun attack took place, and teachers took care of them.

Ironically, he said, the shooting occurred shortly after the university’s security team conducted simulation exercises to prepare for such incidents.

“We are deeply, deeply saddened by this incident,” Andal said.

Roblox fanatic?

Over ANC News Channel, Zamboanga Mayor Khymer Olaso said the suspect killed himself after shooting at a teacher and another student. He said the teacher was unscathed but the other student was fatally hit in one of the classrooms.

He said at least three others were reportedly hurt.

Olaso said the shooter, a 7th grader, was armed with two firearms, one a high-caliber weapon and a short arm.

He told ANC that the shooter was a “very bright student” but was reportedly a “Roblox fanatic.” The online gaming platform has recently faced increased scrutiny in the country over child safety, sexual grooming and the risk of violent extremist radicalization targeting minors.

Olaso said it was time for Congress to ban violent online games in the country and urged parents and guardians to keep firearms out of their children’s reach.

Classes at the AdZU have been suspended following the incident, he said.

‘Gravely concerned’

The Department of Education (DepEd) said it was “gravely concerned” over the reported shooting at the university’s campus.

DepEd said it was ready to provide support and assistance to affected students, families and school personnel, and was coordinating with mental health partners to provide psychological first aid and psychosocial support.

It urged the public not to spread unverified information or share sensitive photos, videos or other details about the incident, particularly because minors were involved.

The circumstances surrounding the shooting were not immediately clear.

In a statement, the university said it was saddened by the incident inside its junior high school campus.

“As of now, we confirm that there are two fatalities. As for other information, we are coordinating with authorities for the full report with full details to be provided as soon as possible,” AdZU said.

It said the safety of its students was its top priority, and it has already coordinated with parents and guardians to pick up their children while ensuring the safety of those remaining on campus.

AdZU said it has set up official communication channels even as it urged the public to refrain from sharing unverified information, photos, and videos “as these will only bring further harm to those involved and may hinder the ongoing investigation of the incident.”

The university also appealed to the public to respect the privacy of all those affected.

“We pray for the quick resolution of the situation and for the safety of all,” AdZU said.

Call to action

The Alliance of Concerned Teachers (ACT) expressed sympathy to the families of the students who died and called for a thorough investigation into the shooting, including how a minor gained access to a firearm.

The group said the incident showed the need to strengthen mental health and psychosocial services in schools, improve support for teachers and students, and address what it described as a culture of violence. It also urged Congress and the Marcos Jr. administration to prioritize education and basic social services in next year’s budget.

The shooting followed an attack in June at a public high school in Tacloban City in which at least three students were killed and about 20 others injured when two of their schoolmates opened fire on campus.

School ​shootings are rare in the Philippines, which has relatively strict gun ownership regulations, including background ‌checks ⁠and psychological evaluation requirements, although illegal firearms remain in circulation.

The school is a five-story building on an 8-hectare site that houses the university’s grade school and junior high school students, according to its website. – With reports from Pia Ranada, Reuters/Rappler.com

World.title: DILG seeks P332 billion for 2027, with PNP getting biggest share
World.content:
'SAFE' CITIES.Several individuals, including drunk people, shirtless residents, and minors, were arrested by Manila Police District officers during patrols in barangays in the Ermita and Malate areas of Manila on Tuesday evening, April 7, 2026.

The DILG is looking to increase the PNP’s funding while reducing allocations for the NAPOLCOM, the Early Childhood Care and Development Council, and the National Commission on Muslim Filipinos, among others

MANILA, Philippines – The Department of the Interior and Local Government (DILG) is asking for P332.5 billion for its 2027 budget, with the lion’s share going to the Philippine National Police (PNP) at P242 billion, according to the National Expenditure Program (NEP).

In 2026, the DILG received a budget of P308.2 billion, with the PNP getting the largest share at P225.8 billion, followed by the Bureau of Fire Protection (BFP) at P36.2 billion and the Bureau of Jail Management and Penology (BJMP) at P31.3 billion.

In April, the DILG and the PNP drew heavy public criticism over the implementation of the Safer Cities Initiative in Metro Manila, which later became a nationwide policy that resulted in the arrest of minors and residents, primarily those from impoverished communities.

Human rights groups called the implementation of the initiative “anti-poor” and a misuse of taxpayers’ money.

For the upcoming fiscal year, the DILG is looking to increase the PNP’s appropriation by at least P15 billion, with the majority going toward its Crime Prevention and Suppression Program.

Here’s how much the agencies under DILG would likely get in 2027:

Philippine National Police (PNP): P242,109,847,000

Bureau of Fire Protection (BFP): P38,105,387,000

Bureau of Jail Management and Penology (BJMP): P34,428,339,000

Office of the Secretary (OSEC): P9,940,619,000

National Police Commission (NAPOLCOM): P2,315,855,000

Philippine Public Safety College (PPSC): P1,237,473,000

National Commission on Muslim Filipinos (NCMF): P1,177,539,000

Local Government Academy (LGA): P553,133,000

National Youth Commission (NYC): P295,914,000

Philippine Commission on Women (PCW): P177,552,000

Early Childhood Care and Development Council (ECCDC): P123,846,000

Under the Office of the Secretary, the department is seeking P10 million for its Bantay Korapsyon (BK) Program, the DILG’s flagship anti-corruption initiative since 2018.

The department, through its Local Government Academy, is also looking to appropriate P76 million to conduct training programs for local governments on climate change adaptation and disaster risk management frameworks.

Some of the agencies under the DILG are expecting reductions in their appropriations for 2027.

NAPOLCOM, the agency responsible for monitoring and investigating police anomalies and irregularities, had its proposed 2027 new general appropriation drop from P2,465,656,000 in 2026 down to P2,315,855,000 — a P149.8-million decrease.

The NCMF, which advises the President on policies and issues concerning Muslim Filipinos, also faces a decrease from its 2026 budget of P1,313,603,000 to P1,177,539,000 — a P136.06-million drop.

The ECCDC, the key governing body on the development of policies, coordination, and implementation of early childhood care and development programs in the Philippines, faces the highest decrease in the DILG’s proposed 2027 budget.

From its 2026 appropriation of P356,793,000, the ECCDC is expecting to get P123,846,000 for 2027 — a P232.94-million reduction or a -65.3% change from its previous year.

The House appropriations committee is set to tackle the proposed DILG budget on August 27. – Rappler.com

World.title: Flood control, climate-tagged budget: Are we getting close to resilience?
World.content:
Flood control projects are intended to help Filipinos adapt to the impacts of climate change

MANILA, Philippines – The Department of Public Works and Highways is seeking P107.4 billion for flood control projects in 2027, after the government canceled new funding for such projects in 2026.

Some, if not all, flood control projects are classified as climate change expenditures, many of which have been found to be substandard or incomplete.

Environment groups noted that climate change spending fell in 2026, when no new funds were allocated for flood control. Climate network Aksyon Klima said this was “largely due to the redirection of billions of pesos from flood control projects that were plagued with corruption and mismanagement,” and “climate action should never be a casualty of corruption.”

For the proposed 2027 budget, climate change-tagged expenditures for mitigation and adaptation totaled P692.7 billion.

Rappler’s Iya Gozum tackles the issue here. – Rappler.com

World.title: Kazakhstan Opens 5.2 Million Hectares for Carbon Projects. Will Investors Follow?
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan has identified 5.2 million hectares of non-forested land within its 31-million-hectare state forest fund as having potential for carbon projects, opening new opportunities for investors in emissions reduction and carbon absorption projects, Ecology and Natural Resources Minister Yerlan Nyssanbayev said.

“This opens new opportunities for investors to participate in projects to reduce and absorb emissions and generate carbon units,” Nyssanbayev said at a seminar on developing Kazakhstan’s carbon project market under the Paris Agreement.

The opportunity comes as Kazakhstan seeks to attract climate investment while meeting its international commitments. The country has pledged to reduce greenhouse gas emissions by 15% by 2030 and 17% by 2035, compared with 1990 levels, reported Kazinform on Aug. 13.

According to Nyssanbayev, the country’s potential is concentrated in forestry, agriculture and energy efficiency. The government is also considering Article 6 of the Paris Agreement as an additional mechanism for attracting investment in emission-reduction and carbon-absorption projects.

Nyssanbayev previously told The Astana Times that developing carbon sequestration sites could help restore degraded pasturelands, expand green areas and increase carbon absorption. He also noted that such sites could allow farmers to participate in the carbon market through carbon farming.

The move is significant because Kazakhstan’s existing greenhouse gas regulation system, including the free allocation of emission quotas, does not provide sufficient incentives for technological modernization, the minister said.

A clearer framework for investors

A revised version of Kazakhstan’s rules on state regulation of greenhouse gas emissions and absorption entered into force on Aug. 10. The changes establish detailed procedures for climate projects under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement.

The updated rules define key concepts, including validation, verification, monitoring, authorization, baseline scenarios and internationally transferable mitigation outcomes. They also establish the process for transferring verified emission-reduction or absorption results internationally.

Participation in Article 6 mechanisms is voluntary. Developers must first submit a project concept for review by relevant government authorities. If approved, the project proceeds to registration and preparation of project, monitoring and sustainable-development plans.

The documents then undergo validation and examination. After implementation, project results are monitored and verified before being recorded in the relevant registry.

International transfer requires separate authorization. Project approval therefore does not automatically allow investors to transfer all future results abroad; each subsequent reporting period requires new verification and authorization.

The new framework gives investors a clearer route from project development to internationally transferable carbon units. However, land availability alone will not determine whether the market develops. Reliable monitoring, transparent verification, predictable approval procedures and the ability to demonstrate genuine emission reductions or increased carbon absorption will also be important.

Why the market matters for exporters

Kazakhstan’s carbon market could also become increasingly important for companies trading with the European Union. Kazakhstan’s aluminum, iron and steel sectors are among those most exposed to the EU’s Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM), which puts a carbon cost on certain imports.

The International Trade Center has estimated that accurate emissions monitoring and reporting could significantly reduce potential CBAM costs for Kazakh exporters. Strengthening domestic carbon pricing and verification systems could therefore serve two purposes: attract investment into climate projects while helping businesses adapt to stricter international carbon requirements.

For Kazakhstan, the next test will be whether the new rules can turn the country’s large land and emissions-reduction potential into credible projects that attract investment, generate verifiable carbon units and support the country’s climate commitments.

World.title: Beyond Oil: Why New Resources Will Decide Global Power
World.content:
While the prevalent discourse in the 20th century centered on the importance of oil pipelines, gaining access to oil reserves and spotlighting countries controlling energy supplies ranging from OPEC states to European giants such as Norway for economic resilience, the current, global, geopolitical environment points to a new trend.

Supply side shocks impacting the international energy market due to militarization of strategic maritime chokepoints such as the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab El Mandeb Strait, is shifting attention towards countries controlling materials essential for powering domestic industries clean energy transitions, defense equipment, transistors, integrated circuits, diodes and solar cells. Regions less reliant on oil but have deposits of lithium, processing facilities, rare earths, copper reserves and uranium deposits are now increasingly relevant as this translates into greater strategic and economic influence.

Competition between the EU and China on the electrical vehicles front requires access to nickel, cobalt, graphite and rare earths whereas renewable energy systems warrant aluminum, silicon and rare earth magnets to sustain a workable ecosystem. Advanced electronics also require materials such as gallium and germanium whereas military industrial complexes seeking to counter adversaries need specialized minerals for aircrafts, radar systems, reconnaissance equipment and satellites. As a result, critical minerals are increasingly tied to national security.

The International Atomic Energy Agency in its recent Global Critical Minerals Outlook 2026 for example, underlines demand for minerals powering clean energy technologies growing exponentially in the next few decades as supply chains remain incredibly constrained and limited to certain economic regions. As per the IEA’s 2026 assessments, demand for lithium is projected to more than triple by 2040, which benefits countries such as China who dominate processing and refining of critical minerals. However, lessons from increased dependence on oil underlines an irrefutable fact- countries which rely on a few suppliers risk facing strategic challenges as supply chains remain volatile.

In light of this, Central Asia gains traction as a potential hub for global supply chain management. Kazakhstan for example remains one of the world’s largest uranium producers with extensive reserves of zinc and titanium alongside lithium and chromium at its disposal. The country’s national atomic corporation, Kazatomprom places Astana’s global uranium production in 2025 at 39% while accounting for 20% of global supplies. These unique advantages can be capitalized on if investments in refining, manufacturing, processing, research and technology to build domestic industrial capacities and support domestic resource bases become more pronounced.

Sitting at the confluence of Russia, China, Europe, the Middle East and South Asia the entire region is also a potential node for regional connectivity where minerals can aid supply chain management as an alternative to riskier routes. This includes the Middle Corridor for diversification of supply chains where the Trans Caspian International Transport Route continues to gain coverage in key policy circles ranging from capitals such as London to Beijing to address bottlenecks from reliance on maritime chokepoints in the Middle East.

However, mineral deposits prove valuable only if they manage to reach international markets.

This warrants the avoidance of the ‘resource trap’ in the current, global, geopolitical environment. Cases such as the Democratic Republic of Congo in Africa quintessentially point at how lack of requisite infrastructure and targeted investments can prevent realization of true economic potential. While Central Asia’s case differs significantly, indigenization remains the key. Selling of copper ores for example, while importing finished products creates economic imbalances domestically which can only be addressed if production of copper components for finished products indigenously is achieved. Similarly, developing relevant knowledge on nuclear technology to channelize uranium ore deposits is the correct approach for domestic prosperity amid increased global demand. For Central Asian states, this requires investments in advanced mining technologies, partnerships with countries specializing in producing finished commodities, development of human capital and institutional collaborations.

Yet despite challenges, few can doubt that Central Asia can act as a bridge particularly as global competition for minerals heats up ranging from the United States to Europe, seeking to invest in domestic capacities and build partnerships with resource rich states to counter China on battery supply chains and rare earth technologies. The Trump administration for example, is treating access to critical minerals as tied with issues of US national security. What is commendable is that from Uzbekistan to the Kyrgyz Republic, all five states alongside Azerbaijan have adopted multi vector, multipronged foreign policies in the absence of camp politics which allows the region to position itself as a credible, reliable supplier and a partner in technological development.

For the region, this constitutes an opportunity in 2026 to move beyond being a mere supplier of resources to becoming a key driver of the global economy provided that targeted investments take place to convert natural resources into innovation and economic resilience.

The author is Hamzah Rifaat, the president of Initiate Futures, a policy think tank. He is also an author for the Trends Group in Abu Dhabi and is cooperating with Nightingale Int.
