That is why, in his view, a Western investor sees the port’s construction, European integration, democratisation and restoration of territorial integrity as parts of a single strategy.

Gvaramia believes the port of Ochamchire could also become part of this economic space in the future. This would make cooperation with Georgia serve Abkhazia’s economic interests.

Limits of compromise and a governance model

In the interview, Gvaramia says resolving the conflict will require concessions from both sides. However, he does not propose a specific model for future political governance.

The discussion touched on the experiences of Lebanon, Bosnia, Northern Ireland and Cyprus. Some of these examples show that allocating government positions and powers along ethnic lines can make state institutions ineffective.

Gvaramia does not rule out an agreement covering Abkhazia’s special legal status, the distribution of political powers, the return of displaced people and property issues:

“Reconciliation is impossible without concessions.”

At the same time, he noted that Georgia is a state recognised under international law. Therefore, creating a new state “from scratch” should not become a necessary condition for resolving the conflict.

Gvaramia sees the European Union as the key foundation for a possible agreement. In his view, the EU accession process could provide security guarantees for Abkhaz people while preserving the principle of Georgia’s territorial integrity.

Enguri HPP: cryptocurrency mining and corruption allegations

In the final part of the interview, Gvaramia discussed electricity supplies and cryptocurrency mining in Abkhazia. He made serious corruption allegations against the government and Bidzina Ivanishvili personally.

According to Gvaramia, a significant share of the electricity generated by the Enguri HPP goes to Abkhazia free of charge. However, he says a substantial portion of this resource goes not to meet people’s needs but to power cryptocurrency mining farms:

“They supply them with twice as much electricity as they need, yet they still face shortages. It is astonishing. Why? Because this electricity goes to crypto farms — to the ability to make money literally out of thin air.”

He alleges that this scheme benefits groups operating in Abkhazia’s de facto authorities, Russian interests and people linked to the Georgian government.

He also criticised possible fuel supplies to Abkhazia from Georgian-controlled territory. According to Gvaramia, it remains unclear how such shipments are documented, who pays for them and where exactly the fuel goes.

In his assessment, there is a risk that the fuel could serve the needs of Russian military infrastructure in Abkhazia. Gvaramia also considers the issue in the context of Russia’s war against Ukraine.

Tamta Mikeladze’s assessment: an important vision and unanswered questions

Tamta Mikeladze, head of the Centre for Social Justice, described the interview as an expression of a rational and pragmatic political vision. She said Gvaramia had moved beyond established political rhetoric on Abkhazia and linked the issue of territorial integrity to the country’s development strategy.

Mikeladze particularly highlights his comments on overcoming traumatic memories, rejecting the false choice between war and capitulation, the European Union’s appeal and the possible role of the Anaklia port in strengthening security.

In her view, an important part of the interview is the challenge it sets for the opposition: alongside criticising the government, it should offer the country a comprehensive alternative project.

Tamta Mikeladze

However, Mikeladze sees several problems with Gvaramia’s approach. The first is the possible overemphasis on economic interests.

She notes that in ethno-political conflicts, economic benefits do not always outweigh fears of losing one’s identity, nationalist narratives and the idea of independence.

Therefore, Tbilisi should offer solutions on protecting Abkhaz identity, language and political autonomy. A promise of prosperity alone will not be enough.

The second issue is the Russian factor. According to Mikeladze, Gvaramia’s model relies heavily on a weakening of Russia.

It remains unclear what would happen if Moscow maintained its influence and military bases in the region. Under such circumstances, economic appeal cannot replace alternative security guarantees.

The third issue concerns efforts to overcome trauma. Mikeladze notes that Pashinyan’s approach has caused serious divisions within Armenia.

Some sections of society see his policies not as overcoming trauma but as a national defeat. Such changes therefore require long-term democratic, social and cultural work with communities affected by the conflict.

The fourth issue concerns the model for sharing power. According to Mikeladze, this aspect has often undermined previous peacebuilding efforts. The political status of Abkhazia, its representation and the distribution of powers are therefore far from secondary details.

Despite these questions, Mikeladze considers the interview an important basis for public debate. She believes other politicians should also offer democratic, future-oriented alternatives rather than build their positions around the traumas and confrontation of the past.

She also calls on the media to exercise caution. According to Mikeladze, if Georgian Dream uses territorial integrity to justify political or economic interests, the opposition should provide a well-grounded response.

Mikeladze’s main message is that the debate on Abkhazia should no longer focus solely on memories of war, mutual accusations and general calls for reconciliation.

Public policy should answer difficult questions: how will Abkhaz identity be protected, who will guarantee security, how will power be shared, and under what conditions can a common political space be created?

Peaceful return of Abkhazia to Georgia

World.title: The future of Abkhazia: from preserving the language to building a civic nation. View from Abkhazia, video discussion
World.content:
Abkhaz language and civic nation

The editor of the newspaper Chegemskaya Pravda, Inal Khashig, and political scientist Astamur Tania discuss the challenges and state policy regarding the Abkhazian language, the shift in historical narratives surrounding the Georgian-Abkhaz conflict, as well as the necessity of building an inclusive civic nation for the sustainable future of Abkhazia.

Main theses and arguments:

Preservation and Development of the Abkhaz Language — The language issue is viewed as the foundation of national identity, requiring not merely electoral campaigns, but a long-term state program encompassing education, ideology, and administrative measures. Overcoming Formalism in Language Policy — Existing legislative initiatives and laws (such as the 2007 law) face implementation problems; there is a risk that successive delays and amendments will boil down to a formalistic approach without real results. Balance Between the State Language and Interethnic Harmony — Grace periods for non-Abkhaz citizens to master the Abkhazian language are aimed at preventing discrimination and fostering a unified civic platform under conditions of inevitable bilingualism (Abkhaz and Russian). Countering Historical Revisionism — Attempts to rewrite the history of the conflict are observed in the Georgian information space (including the promotion of the pseudoscientific “Ingorokva theory” and the interpretation of the 1992 war exclusively as Russian aggression), which relieves Georgia of responsibility and hinders a peaceful settlement. Abkhazia’s Agency and the Reduction of Hate Speech — Abkhazia emphasizes its status as an established nation and an active subject of relations; both sides acknowledge the destructiveness of “hate speech” in the media, as a resumption of the conflict would be catastrophic for everyone. Formation of a Civic Nation and the Rule of Law — The key challenge is the transition from ethnic self-awareness to an inclusive civic nation that unites all ethnic groups in Abkhazia on the basis of shared values, legal order, security, and consensus.

Inal Khashig: Hello, Chegemskaya Pravda is on the air. Today, we are going to speak again about the very same topics that concern our Abkhaz society. This prolonged discussion regarding the Abkhaz language, the standards of proficiency in this language, the state language for members of parliament. At the parliamentary hearings, the parliamentary committee rejected – that is, did not recommend – the draft constitutional amendments proposed by the president. But, nevertheless, legally this does not mean, as I understood, that the issue has been removed from the agenda; one way or another, it can be included in the agenda of the parliamentary session, even without this recommendation from the profile committee. Our guest today is Astamur Tania.

Astamur Tania: Good day.

Inal Khashig: Good day. Generally, what do you think about this whole situation that has arisen with these amendments to the constitutional law?

Astamur Tania: Here, the topic of the Abkhaz language is periodically raised in the form of certain information campaigns, usually during some pre-election period or in connection with certain events. It is also impossible to manage without information campaigns. It is necessary to sharpen public attention on this problem.

I hope that this information campaign will not have an independent significance of its own, but will transform into some programmatic actions. Because, probably, everyone understands—both supporters of one approach and supporters of the second approach—that in itself this decision means little. Because here it should still be about a state program.

This program is both educational and ideological, because much rests even on questions of self-awareness. Because it is clear that with the help of the Abkhaz language it is impossible to obtain the volume of information necessary to participate in any competition. So, there must be some other incentives. Just like that, in a natural way, unfortunately, it will not work.

These must be administrative measures and measures of an ideological nature. The Abkhaz language is inextricably linked with issues of identity. This is a big task on all fronts.

Now, regarding the presidential initiative specifically: to be honest, I consider it rational. Some argue that it involves an unequal approach, but I believe it is not aimed at discrimination.

On the contrary, its purpose is to address potential concerns so that advancing the Abkhaz language development program is not perceived as discriminatory by non-Abkhaz residents. After all, preserving interethnic harmony, maintaining consensus, and building a unified civic platform are fundamental for our society.

From this perspective, the approach is entirely sound. However, we must ensure this does not lead to endless postponements. The state must actively work on this by defining clear criteria in legislation to specify what constitutes fluency in the Abkhaz language.

This requirement should apply not only to the parliament but also to the executive branch. Implementing it within the judiciary will be more complex, as it requires extensive work to adapt the full body of legal terminology, which demands highly specialized legal expertise.

Inal Khashig: There are terminologies. All of that exists.

Astamur Tania: I know that preliminary work has been carried out—mostly at the level of compiling dictionaries of legal terms, as far as I am aware. However, implementation within the judiciary is far more difficult purely due to professional constraints.

That is why I believe the presidential initiative reflects today’s realities. It creates a space for compromise among political participants and allows us to develop proper criteria for assessing Abkhaz language proficiency.

If we fail to reach an agreement and leave everything as it is—which could easily happen if the president’s proposed law fails to pass—we will remain at a standstill. The entire process could degenerate into a formalistic routine, similar to what we witnessed during the presidential elections, and only spread further.

Therefore, as an initial step, I view this approach as very reasonable. Since there is no discrimination involved, I see no basis to claim it is unconstitutional.

Inal Khashig: I have my own perspective on this, though doubts constantly trouble me. The initiative grants a deferment to non-ethnic Abkhazians, but I am convinced that in five years, by 2032, we will find ourselves with the exact same results.

Astamur Tania: That certainly cannot be ruled out.

Inal Khashig: Indeed. But my concern is the formalistic approach toward the Abkhaz language itself. For instance, the language law was adopted in 2007 and was meant to take full effect in 2015, requiring the entire Abkhaz bureaucracy to be fluent in the state language.

Yet, even if a good half of them are fluent today, we should consider ourselves lucky—especially since no actual testing or measurements were ever conducted.

Astamur Tania: If at least a “bad half” had command of it.

Inal Khashig: Yes, yes. I am afraid that, strictly speaking, we will simply do this—formalize the commission itself, which we will bring to formal absurdity. Like, here is a good guy, he knows 10 words.

Astamur Tania: If we do not change our attitude toward our state, then in the Abkhaz language, and in security, and in the economy, we will have roughly the same result. You are right. This is a broader question than the Abkhaz language. It is just that now it is at the peak of relevance due to the debates in parliament and in society. In fact, this is a question of our attitude.

Various arguments are brought up that the quality of parliamentarism may drop from this. It seems to me that despite the absence of this norm, the quality of our parliamentarism was declining anyway. So the problem, after all, is not only in the Abkhaz language. This is a hackneyed phrase that we always get the government we deserve, that it is a reflection of our society. Therefore, this is a giant societal problem. But it must be dealt with.

First of all, the authorities, you see—to change the quality of authority, those in power must work on changing the quality of society as well. This goal must be set. Not simply to sit out one’s tenure in parliament or executive power. It is necessary to influence society, its enlightenment, its self-awareness, its creative potential. Therein lies the main task. Otherwise, you are right, it will drift on its own, like everything else.

Inal Khashig: It seems to me that the situation around the Abkhaz language is indeed much broader. It shows, probably, our attitude toward the law in general. This applies not only to the Abkhaz language.

We have passed very many all sorts of legislative acts, proper laws, but then we tried in every way to bypass them. An active advertising campaign is taking place on the internet: acquire Abkhaz real estate, and so forth. So many lances were broken over this law on apartments, and still they sell Abkhaz real estate to foreigners. It is possible, it can be acquired.

Astamur Tania: Yes, that is also—you know what the matter is? It is impossible to contain the onslaught; it can only be directed into some profitable channel. Of course, it is possible for some time to contain the natural course of events with prohibitions. But we must nevertheless forecast how we can direct these investments, where our weak zones are.

Simply sitting like a dog in the manger will not work. Therefore, we must understand how in this harsh reality—what is our place. Today one hole was plugged, in another place it tore open. We must have some clear program of action, at least for the short term.

This concerns the economy, security, foreign policy, everything. What I am saying is very banal, but unfortunately, we always have a reactive response to something, to already accomplished facts. Although it was not difficult to predict that the course of events was leading to this. And we live for today. If an individual person can live for today like that, the state should not live like that.

Inal Khashig: The state somehow manages to.

Astamur Tania: It should still plan its future, the society.

Inal Khashig: I would like to switch to another topic now. Periodically, we are reminded of the unresolved Georgian-Abkhaz conflict, which continuously remains at a dead end. Last time, we discussed how Georgian perceptions of Abkhazia and the Abkhaz people have changed, particularly through the influence of Pavel Ingorokva’s theory, which took a strong hold in Georgian thought.

Shortly after our conversation, I watched an interview with the Georgian historian Tsurtsumia on a Georgian YouTube channel. He noted that Ingorokva’s theory is actually marginal and lacks official state support.

Nevertheless, just the day before yesterday, I came across a vividly animated video. It was set in Sukhumi on the embankment, depicting peaceful civilians in a setting reminiscent of 1992, when a Russian military aircraft suddenly swoops in and begins bombing. The people are shown fleeing the embankment, trying to escape by ship or heading into the mountains.

Astamur Tania: Those are slightly different scenes, probably. Maybe it is one pie, but different slices.

Inal Khashig: Yes, but you see, this is proceeding very actively – why I understood this is not only Ingorokva’s theory about who the Abkhaz are and what their origin is, but in Georgian society the understanding of what the Georgian-Abkhaz conflict was is changing very actively. And what happened 33 years ago, 34 years ago. How the war started.

According to this cartoon… A cartoon is a certain part of upbringing. It also has its own audience. Directed at a certain audience. At children. It is important for me to understand why the Georgians converted this conflict into a conflict not between Georgians and Abkhaz, but a certain conflict between Russia and Georgia.

Astamur Tania: That is completely understandable, as acknowledging it would require admitting responsibility for starting the armed conflict. By the way, Shevardnadze did admit this responsibility—and while he claimed Kitovani was to blame, Kitovani was not the Defense Minister of Russia, but of Georgia. Everyone remembers, and archival footage still shows, how this war began and how the local Georgian population reacted.

Acknowledging this would require erasing entire sections of history. Instead, there is an effort to reshape the narrative of 1992 and merge it with the events of 2008, framing everything around legislation and the narrative of post-2008 occupation. Yet, a detailed examination—including the report by the International Fact-Finding Commission led by Heidi Tagliavini—confirmed that responsibility for initiating military action in both instances lay with the Georgian side.

Naturally, there is a desire to obscure this in the media space to advance narratives about occupation, aiming to shape international opinion to justify a forceful resolution or delegitimize the Abkhazian state.

We must react to this. The fact that animated videos are being produced on this topic shows an intent to pass this worldview down to the next generation. If we carry such a perspective into the future, achieving a peaceful settlement or joint progress will be extremely difficult. This is why it is essential to present the fullest possible picture, starting with the factual timeline.

Regarding Zura Tsurtsumia’s comments: first, it is positive that Georgian-Abkhaz relations are being examined at a solid academic level, attempting to move beyond today’s propaganda clichés toward a historical assessment of the conflict’s roots.

However, claiming that Ingorokva’s theory is marginal ignores reality in the Georgian media landscape, where it remains the most widespread view on the origins of the Abkhazian people. While prominent Georgian scholars considered it pseudoscientific—such as Javakhishvili, who noted that ancient Adyghe tribes inhabited Western Georgia prior to the Kartvelians and recognized the Apsilals and Abasgs as direct ancestors of modern Abkhaz—these classical works are largely ignored by mainstream media.

Instead, hate speech dominates the discourse among commentators—and we must acknowledge that hate speech exists on the Abkhaz side as well. Neither side benefits from this.

Objectively, neither we nor Georgia have any interest in a renewed armed conflict, which would yield disastrous consequences for both. Some in Georgian society may assume their larger population makes it an easy victory, but that is far from reality. We cannot afford to trigger such a dangerous cycle.

Both sides are equally served by abandoning hate speech and language that demeans human dignity and belittles culture, especially given that all human cultures, including Abkhazian and Georgian, are products of historical interaction and symbiosis.

Finally, addressing Tsurtsumia’s assertion—which is not unique to him—that the Abkhaz nation was deliberately engineered by Soviet authorities to counter Georgia: while Soviet policies influenced the development of both the Georgian and Abkhazian nations in the late 19th and 20th centuries, it is vital to recognize that the Abkhaz national identity was not an artificial creation.

In fact, during the 1930s and 1940s, deliberate repressive measures were used in an effort to suppress the formation of the Abkhaz nation.

Inal Khashig: That was when schools were closed.

Astamur Tania: Schools were closed, and the destruction of the intelligentsia—the bearers of this very idea—took place at that time. This inflicted a serious trauma.

But one must understand that this process is accomplished. It is an accomplished fact. And in dialogue with the Abkhaz, everyone must proceed from the premise that this is not simply an ethnos, but a formed nation. With its own ideas about borders, policy, with its own national mythology. This is not always equal to history. Here there is a completely different approach.

As I once spoke with an Abkhaz, he said in his heart: why did Gurandukht, the daughter of the Abkhaz king, marry Gurgen, the ruler of Tao-Klarjeti? Since then, the unification of the Abkhaz state with the Georgian one began. That is the feudal era. It is an accomplished fact. We can only look at it like that. It sounds like a parody.

The same applies to this issue. It is closer to us. These are already accomplished facts. We must take them into account. Proceed from the fact that this is a given. Second, there were in fact certain inaccuracies there.

I do not want to delve into that now. In itself, this attempt to approach the understanding of the origins of the Georgian-Abkhaz conflict with a cool head, using academic material—if this happens more or less regularly, in the same calm atmosphere, then it seems to me that both societies can win from this.

Inal Khashig: On the other hand, it seems to me, given that this seems to be a recent event—the war is relatively a historical event, only 30 years ago—nevertheless, judging by what I read in social networks, certain articles, certain speeches of politicians or experts…

Astamur Tania: Very much so.

Inal Khashig: I still see a lot of statements specifically adjusting to the political opportunism of the moment. If you remember, in the 80s, in the 90s after the war, what were we called? Abkhaz separatists. Now you practically do not hear this term.

Astamur Tania: By the way, they started calling us Abkhaz separatists back during the war, and before that—Gudauta separatists. Although during that period Abkhazia had not yet declared that it was ceasing any relations with Georgia and was not going to live with it within common borders.

In its time, on the initiative of Georgian figures, the process of all kinds of division began in Abkhazia. They separated the Georgian sector from the Abkhaz State University. Then they withdrew the football team. Then they withdrew the Georgian faction from the Supreme Council. They began to sit separately. That is, they apparently assumed that gradually they would somehow paralyze things. And here the question arises: who was the separatist?

And the same with this term. And, by the way, “Gudauta separatists”—later this very term migrated into the documents of the United Nations. And for some time after the end of the war, when our authorities were already located in Sukhumi, they continued to call us Gudauta separatists. I think for the Abzhua Abkhaz this is a bit offensive. Gudauta-Abzzua separatists would have been sound better.

Inal Khashig: But, nevertheless, this term somehow went out of circulation. And we have already been switched to the idea that Abkhazia is a territory occupied by Russia. And at the same time, as for the Abkhaz—let us leave aside those social networks where we generally came down from the mountains, according to the Georgian version—in official rhetoric nothing is said about us anymore.

Astamur Tania: “Came down from the mountains” is also quite amusing, because on most of the coast, based on climatic conditions and the unhealthiness of this climate, it was practically impossible to live permanently. Even if you open the press of, say, the late 19th and early 20th centuries, it is evident that the affluent portion of the residents of the city of Sukhumi left Sukhumi for the summer period. Precisely when there was the peak of this disease, people left for the foothills, because living here was a bit dangerous.

Inal Khashig: And the most prosperous ones lived there.

Astamur Tania: Generally, we have a perception as if in the Middle Ages communications in Abkhazia—this applies to everything, we are talking about Abkhazia—ran along the coast like that; there was the Ancient Roman railway running, next to it the Byzantine highway, but in reality all communications passed through the foothills and across the ridges. It was later, with the arrival of the Russian Empire, that this network of communications familiar to us began to develop. And psychologically we begin to tie our perception of the past to what had already taken shape in the 19th and 20th centuries. There was no railway at the beginning of the 20th century yet.

Inal Khashig: This highway that exists now.

Astamur Tania: For example, construction of the Black Sea railway continued in 1918 still. The Russian Empire no longer existed, but it was unclear what would happen. But they continued to build it in the Gagra region in 1918. And now it seems that it was always there.

Inal Khashig: But nevertheless, I tried to understand. Why do they depict Abkhaz who did not participate in this conflict, or played some secondary role in this Georgian-Abkhaz conflict? In the war that took place in 1992-1993.

Astamur Tania: A moment is omitted. What quantity of weapons was transferred to Georgia under the Tashkent Agreement on the eve of the conflict? The Russian authorities of that time were far from being, to put it mildly, pro-Abkhaz.

This is evident from everything. This is visible if one reads at least the transcript of September 3 of the meeting of Shevardnadze, Yeltsin, Ardzinba, representatives of the North Caucasus, representatives of our various parliamentary deputations. Not only should documents be studied, one should read the transcript.

But why did Georgia start armed conflicts? It received at its disposal several motor rifle and tank divisions of the Transcaucasus Military District. Therefore, in their joy, they thought that it would be possible to quickly finish this business.

Inal Khashig: But nevertheless, why am I saying all this—I read an interesting Georgian perspective on why this is happening, that Abkhaz are being excluded from this conflict, that through such an exclusion—and, say, when a certain image of the enemy is removed from the Abkhaz in this conflict, in this war, if the Abkhaz played a non-primary role, it means they are not enemies. There is a hypothetical possibility they retain that later at some point we will make peace with them.

Astamur Tania: That is very hypothetical. In my opinion, it is impossible to do that. Because how can one take a segment of a section of thinking and take something out of there… It seems to me this is very much a laboratory theory.

Inal Khashig: But this is laboratory on the one hand, and on the other hand the Abkhaz themselves have their own perception of the war.

Astamur Tania: To reiterate: those in Georgia who deal with the Georgian-Abkhaz settlement or seek to study this issue must start from the accomplished fact of the Abkhazian nation’s existence. A nation cannot be treated as a third-party observer—it is an active subject. We are an active subject in our relations with Georgia. Recognized or unrecognized, by our internal structure, we are a nation—with our own statehood and our own distinct perception of both the past and the future.

Our perspectives may not always align, but if we look at history honestly, our centuries-long—even thousand-year-old—relations with various Kartvelian peoples, primarily Megrelians, cannot simply be painted in black-and-white. History saw different periods, including feudal wars, which, it should be noted, occurred internally among those groups as well. There was continuous interaction, symbiosis, and movement back and forth. This is why we find Megrelian surnames in Abkhazia, Abkhaz surnames in Zugdidi, and why Gali in particular serves as a concentrated microcosm where everything is intertwined.

We, too, must draw important policy conclusions from this. But there must be a foundational understanding that if there is a real desire to settle our relations or develop a pragmatic approach—though I do not expect major breakthroughs given our disagreements—it starts with recognizing that a political nation has formed here. Its members are not solely ethnic Abkhazians, but all citizens of Abkhazia. We, too, must recognize this and move away from a narrow communal mindset.

Inal Khashig: But, by the way, it is present.

Astamur Tania: That is natural, because that is where it started. But we must nevertheless move in the direction of a civic nation.

Inal Khashig: Well yes, a political nation. This distinction is crucial because, unfortunately, many people’s perception of the Abkhazian situation and where we stand today was shaped back in Soviet times.

Astamur Tania: In fact, the post-Stalin Soviet period wasn’t all bad. Despite setbacks during that recovery process, it was unthinkable to express such vile ideas in writing back then.

Inal Khashig: My point is slightly different. In Soviet times, the Abkhaz struggle focused on ethnic rights—opening schools, theaters, literary journals, and universities—since few anticipated the collapse of the Soviet Union. The political nation back then was subsumed under the concept of the ‘Soviet people,’ right?

Astamur Tania: Well, ‘the Soviet people’ was an ideological construct, though autonomous frameworks did exist.

Inal Khashig: Yet today, some still take a fragmented approach, viewing society purely as separate ethnic groups—Abkhaz, Armenians, Russians, and so on—rather than…

Astamur Tania: You mean moving toward a unified civic nation?

Inal Khashig: Exactly. That is essential.

Astamur Tania: That requires active political education. Some processes occur naturally: living within the same state fosters shared views on security, peaceful development, and the necessity of an independent Abkhazia. However, we must establish clear criteria for this political nation to avoid repeating the mistakes made in Georgia during the Gamsakhurdia era. As a polyethnic society, we must embed protections that guarantee the survival of the Abkhaz people. Our fellow citizens understand this foundational principle.

That brings us back to language. Over time, our entire society must achieve sufficient command of the Abkhaz language for daily communication. Naturally, our society will remain bilingual due to demographic and geopolitical realities. This is why Russian is constitutionally designated alongside Abkhaz. But ‘alongside’ must not mean replacing Abkhaz. Striking this balance requires preserving the Abkhaz language while maintaining interethnic harmony. We should engage Abkhaz academic circles and draw on international experience—such as the major initiatives used to revive and preserve Welsh alongside English.

Ultimately, we need a sense of proportion in both domestic and foreign policy. Though emotions run high, avoiding extremes is vital. A population of our size can only survive through moderation and consensus.

Inal Khashig: Having come full circle, it seems clear that the survival and development of Abkhazia depend on building an inclusive civic nation that encompasses all ethnic groups residing here as citizens…

Astamur Tania: Including Georgians, of course.

Inal Khashig: …who would also command the state language.

Astamur Tania: Regarding the Gali district specifically, we must rethink our policy. We must acknowledge that regardless of how they identify ethnically, the residents there represent a native Megrelian-Georgian population, many with historical Abkhaz roots.

Inal Khashig: We can dedicate a separate conversation to that topic. But building a civic nation—governed by the rule of law and grounded in our constitutional language framework—is key to securing our future so that we aren’t constantly fearing our own disappearance.

Astamur Tania: Though I think we are destined to sound the alarm for many years to come!

Inal Khashig: Building a civic nation takes time and represents a broader movement toward a state governed by the rule of law.

Astamur Tania: To end on a reassuring note: perhaps artificial intelligence will solve all these problems for us!

Inal Khashig: I hope so! On that note, we will wrap up today’s broadcast. Today, Astamur Tania and I discussed the Abkhaz language, the Georgian-Abkhaz conflict, and why these complex questions persist. Goodbye. Until new meetings. Thank you.

Astamur Tania: Thank you.

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

World.title: “When the state serves an oligarch, people leave” – from a march in Tbilisi. “Protests in Georgia” video blog
World.content:
For more than a year and half – since November 2024 – continuous protests have been taking place in Georgia, with demonstrators demanding that the country return to the path of European integration. The results of the parliamentary elections held in autumn 2024 are still not recognised by part of Georgian society.

Every evening thousands, and often tens of thousands, gather in Tbilisi and several other cities. Over this time dozens of participants have been detained, many have faced criminal charges, and some have been sentenced to prison terms.

For the first time in the history of independent Georgia, the country has up to 150 prisoners of conscience, including women. Among them is Mzia Amaglobeli, founder of the popular outlets Batumelebi and Netgazeti.

In 2025 she was sentenced to two years in prison for slapping a police officer. Protesters demand the release of all political prisoners and the repeal of all anti-democratic laws adopted over the past two years.

To suppress the protests, the ruling Georgian Dream party has increasingly tightened repression against civil society and the media. However, protests in various forms continue.

World.title: 'Equal with any victory': 60 years since the Battle of Long Tan
World.content:
Vietnam War veteran Graeme Davis struggles to find the words to talk about what he went through during the conflict.

"It's almost impossible to describe unless you have been in battle," Mr Davis said.

"Unless you've actually looked down the barrel of a weapon ... and having to make a moral and ethical decision whether to pull the trigger."

Graeme Davis, of the 26 Australians of the 6th Battalion in The Royal Australian Regiment (6RAR), was wounded in the Battle of Long Tan. (Supplied: William James Cunneen, Australian War Memorial)

Mr Davis said despite Australia's ultimate victory at the Battle of Long Tan, it was overall a long conflict that saw the Australians mostly overpowered by their enemy.

And there was a moment on the afternoon of August 18 when he believed they would not survive at Long Tan either.

"Virtually we had less than probably 60 rounds of ammunition between us, we had less than 60 soldiers still alive or wounded, that were able to continue to protect and fight the battle," he said.

" And we virtually thought 'within the next 60 minutes, it will be all over for us, we won't be here'. "

He said it was in that moment that the "reality" of the war came home to him.

"That we were totally outnumbered ... we never had the resources or the people to defend ourselves, or even at that stage do a tactical withdrawal," he said.

A significant day

Fought in a rubber plantation called Long Tan, the battle was one of the most significant engagements involving Australians during the war.

The first Australian soldiers of the Royal Australian Regiment's D Company had arrived in south Vietnam in May of 1966, and within two months, some were of them were at Long Tan.

The villagers of Long Tan and Long Phuoc had been relocated by the Australians to secure a new base, prompting Vietnamese troops to attack in a bid to recover them.

Australian troops, alongside soldiers from New Zealand and the United States, were victorious at Long Tan. (Supplied: Australian War Memorial)

The Australians were joined by New Zealand's 161 Field Battery and soldiers from the US in what would become a victory over the Vietnamese.

As a result of the battle, 18 Australians were killed and 24 wounded.

By the time it was over on the evening of August 18, the North Vietnamese suffered hundreds of casualties.

Remembering the fallen

Uniformed military personnel lay wreaths at the ceremony in Canberra. (ABC News: Caitlin Maloney)

Today, 60 years on, veterans and their families laid wreaths to honour those who died in the conflict at the Australian Vietnam Forces National Memorial in Canberra.

Governor-General Samantha Mostyn, Veterans' Affairs Minister Matt Keogh and Australian War Memorial director Matt Anderson were among those who attended the ceremony.

The anniversary coincides with Vietnam Veterans' Day, something that is meaningful for many who fought in the conflict.

ACT Vietnam Veterans Federation president Ward Gainey said the ceremony was a chance to commemorate those who served in the war, and their families.

"We take this opportunity to remember, to understand the families who are involved, those who returned and are still trying to live with their memories and making sure we support them as they grow older," he said.

ACT Vietnam Veterans Federation Ward Gainey at the commemoration of the Battle of Long Tan. (ABC News: Caitlin Maloney)

Mr Gainey said the day was a reminder that serving in the defence force was not just "putting on your suit and going to work".

"It's important, I think, that we don't forget what people do," he said.

"These are hardships … we go away, and we know that we're going to a place that is dangerous.

"But another time, during peacetime, we are still there to be a part of the nation that we love and the nation we have to protect, and we are honoured to do so."

Keeping the stories alive

Reverend Mick O'Donnell, who served in the navy in Vietnam, read the prayer for peace at the memorial.

He said it was vital veterans' stories continued to be told.

"I think of the collegiality, getting together with the colleagues and remembering stories and remembering the days when we were all together and doing various things, but also just to recognise that we're getting older," he said.

" It's good to keep the memory alive, I think. I love the stories. "

Veteran Mick O'Donnell said he hoped those in power would think of "love instead of war". (ABC News: Caitlin Maloney)

Reverend O'Donnell said he hoped the leaders present remembered the importance of peace and love, as conflicts continue around the world.

"They are in the position where they are making decisions for our involvement in conflicts in the future," he said.

" I hope today that ... they might stop and think about love instead of war. "

'Never been fully accepted'

Graeme Davis with a Red Cross nurse in a military hospital in 1966. (Supplied: Graeme Davis)

To this day, some of those who served in Vietnam still feel the sting of what they perceived as the Australian public ignoring or not recognising their sacrifice and service.

"It was something outside our control and the public were demonstrating against the government of the day and the action of the day, and taking it out on the veterans rather than saying, 'You weren't responsible, you were doing what your nation asked you to do'," Mr Davis said.

He said the Battle of Long Tan was equal to any other major military engagement in Australia's wartime history.

"I think anyone who has studied military history or read military history, you would have been familiar that there's probably been more accounts of Long Tan written equal to the landing at Gallipoli," he said.

World.title: Want to block gambling ads? Soon, this is how you will do it
World.content:
The government is moving to make opting out of gambling ads online as easy as paying a bill.

It is part of a deal with the Coalition to pass gambling ad reform through parliament, legislation that would also include changes to how gambling companies can induce people to place bets, and an ad blackout either side of live sports games.

The government is warning the opt-out mechanism will be complicated to build, and could take a long time to implement.

But in essence, the goal is to allow families and individuals to tell companies and platforms they do not want to see gambling ads when they log in online.

Critics of the government's proposed reform say it goes nowhere near far enough to address real gambling harm, pointing to the vast majority of recommendations from the government's own 'You Win Some, You Lose More' report from 2023 that are not being adopted.

The Greens have gone so far as to suggest the gambling overhaul is purposely convoluted, and have doubted the communications watchdog's ability to manage the opt-out register.

Here is what we know.

How would I opt out of gambling ads?

The details are slim at this stage, but the ABC understands people would be able to opt out by submitting details, such as their email and the platform they hold an account with, to the register.

Anika Wells says the government will introduce a register to opt out of wagering advertising. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

It is not yet clear whether the register would then pass that information to the platforms, or if they would be required to check their lists against the opt-out register proactively.

Ultimately, the idea is that the online platforms would be required to stop showing gambling ads to anyone on the register.

In parliament on Monday, Communications Minister Anika Wells described it as a "one-stop shop" for Australians.

"It is expected that the government's reforms will respond to these concerns by introducing new restrictions on inducement-based marketing and establishing the wagering advertising opt-out register, which will provide Australians with a one-stop shop to opt out of seeing wagering advertising on online platforms," she said.

Doesn't opt-out already exist?

Yes, on some platforms.

For example, SBS has an option to opt-out on gambling ads on its streaming platform.

But the Senate inquiry that looked at the proposed changes to gambling ads heard that only 1 per cent of SBS viewers chose to opt out.

It is likely that, in part, that is because people either did not know it was an option, or found it too hard to figure out how to click the right button.

Anthony Albanese says the changes will help the people most at risk of gambling harm. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

Already, the government's proposal includes what is called a "triple-lock" mechanism.

It would force social media and streaming companies to turn off gambling ads to users 18 and under, and give adults the option to opt out.

That has been criticised as too onerous for the user, with some advocates calling for an opt-in mechanism instead, an idea the prime minister has firmly rejected.

A centralised register, like the one being considered in this deal, would help to make it easier for people who want to turn off gambling ads across all their online accounts in one fell swoop.

The "triple lock" would also remain for people to manually opt out from a specific platform.

BetStop was supposed to protect gambling addicts, but it didn't stop Ravi from losing nearly $70,000 The credibility of the Albanese government's much vaunted wagering self-exclusion scheme BetStop has been called into question after loopholes in the system allowed a Sydney man to lose nearly $70,000 despite signing up to a lifetime ban.

There is also BetStop, a scheme administered by the federal government, for people who want to be stopped from gambling altogether.

BetStop is the national self-exclusion register and allows users to prohibit themselves from engaging in online and phone gambling for a minimum of three months, up to a lifetime.

Gambling companies are also barred from sending marketing messages and offering inducements once someone has self-identified on BetStop.

Who will be in charge of the opt-out register?

The Australian Communications and Media Authority (ACMA) would be in charge of building, administering and monitoring the scheme.

The government has introduced legislation that would require betting companies to pay for it, as they do with BetStop, via a levy.

Initially, ACMA said they had not received extra resourcing to implement the changes coming with whatever version of the bill passes parliament.

But the government has since clarified the regulator will get extra help to regulate the new laws.

The idea behind the scheme is that online streaming services would stop showing gambling ads to people on the register. (ABC News: Stephen Cavenagh)

What don't we know yet?

Quite a lot.

The full details of the deal have not been made public, but we know the Coalition will be asking for more amendments beyond the opt-out register in exchange for their support.

We do not know a whole lot about how the government plans to make the one-stop opt-out shop happen, noting the difficulty of sharing data and matching emails across multiple platforms and services.

The broader changes to gambling ads are expected to take effect from July 1 next year, but it is clear the opt-out register would not be ready by then.

World.title: Pork industry fraud case raises questions about money laundering risk
World.content:
A financial crimes expert says the revelation of large-scale fraud connected to the pork industry raises new questions about the risk of money laundering in food production.

Four people, who are all business owners or representatives in the pork meat industry, allegedly kept $10 million in sales off the books, altered use-by dates on frozen meat products and moved cash interstate in freight vehicles between 2017 and 2026.

They have been charged with a range of fraud-related offences, including fraud, destroying records with the intent to defraud, receiving tainted property and making false declarations.

Pork industry financial crimes charges Police allege about $10 million was funnelled out of businesses in the pork meat industry for personal use.

More than $25 million worth of assets, including $3 million in cash and two motor vehicles, was seized as suspected proceeds of the crimes.

Griffith University Academy of Financial Crime Investigation and Compliance director Andreas Chai said using legitimate trade to disguise the proceeds of crime was a common method of money laundering, but it was rare to see it connected to agriculture.

Andreas Chai says he is interested in the unusual case. (Supplied: Griffith University)

"This is quite interesting … interstate using pork hasn't really come up on the radar before," he said.

"It makes sense [because] there's a lot of this kind of agricultural products moving between states all the time.

"But usually … [it's] high-value stuff like wine."

How cooking the books works

Trade-based money laundering involves falsely reporting the value of goods, either by over-invoicing or under-invoicing.

Billions in cash that can't be accounted for There is no shortage of theories, but little in the way of definitive answers.

Professor Chai said it was often used to create a legitimate "cover story" for money earned through illegitimate or illegal activities.

"Usually what happens is there's an accumulation of dirty money … they need to move the money in a way that is not suspicious," he said.

"When a bank or an accountant or a lawyer might ask, 'Where's this money coming from?' they have paperwork that says this is related to trade … when in fact it is actually dirty money."

The investigation involved the Queensland Crime and Corruption Commission, the NSW Crime Commission, and members of the NSW Police anti-money laundering unit. (ABC News)

The joint investigation involved the Queensland Crime and Corruption Commission, the NSW Crime Commission and members of the NSW Police anti-money laundering unit.

Detective Inspector Gilbert Laverdure said it was a complex cross-border operation.

"Criminal networks that seek to exploit business structures and move illicit funds across state borders should expect to be identified and investigated," he said.

"The NSWPF [NSW Police Force] will continue to work closely with partner agencies to detect, disrupt and prosecute any serious offending."

Authorities have not released the names of the charged individuals or the businesses they were connected to, but did say two were from Queensland and two were from New South Wales.

It is alleged the offending happened between 2017 and 2026. (ABC News)

Professor Chai said investigators would be looking for changes to records to determine the true value of goods, usually through a forensic audit of the companies' systems.

"You've got records in terms of the company that's sending it and the company that's receiving it," he said.

"They would be taking a very close look at the IT systems, when things have been changed, why they've been changed.

"You could probably pick up a pattern … about how these records were being altered over time."

Vulnerable links in the supply chain

Peak industry body Australian Pork Limited (APL) declined to comment while the matter was before the courts, but said all businesses must follow the law.

Australia's pork industry works separately to the wider red meat industry with its own industry body; it conducts its own research and development, and pork is processed through separate speciality meatworks.

The latest industry data published on APL's website showed more than 470,000 tonnes of pig meat was produced in Australia in the March quarter this year.

Australian Pork Limited is the peak industry body for the pork sector. (ABC News: Pip Courtney)

Across the country, there are more than 4,700 registered pig production sites, which, according to APL, contributed $6.9 billion to the economy in the 2024-25 financial year.

New national anti-money laundering regulations have extended the obligation to verify the origin of money and report suspicious transactions beyond banks and casinos to include real estate agents, conveyancers, lawyers and accountants

"There's greater responsibility on company directors to pick this up," Professor Chai said.

"The pork industry and others might have to do some more risk assessment around what the money laundering risks are around these systems."

World.title: What to know about the Tupac Shakur murder trial now underway
World.content:
For almost 30 years, the question of who killed rapper Tupac Shakur has gone unanswered.

At least, in an official sense.

For years, Duane Keith Davis, known as Keffe D, claimed to have played a part in the fatal drive-by shooting.

Those comments led authorities to reopen the case.

Davis, who is accused of providing the gun used to kill Shakur, is now the centre of a murder trial over the attack.

My colleague Dannielle Maguire and I have all the info you need to know.

What happened the night Shakur was shot?

Shakur and Death Row Records co-founder Marion "Suge" Knight were in Las Vegas to watch Mike Tyson knock out Bruce Seldon at the MGM Grand Garden Arena.

Tupac mystery may soon be solved Three decades after the murder of rapper Tupac Shakur, the world may get some answers about who killed the young superstar, and why.

Outside the venue, Shakur, Knight and their entourage got into a brawl with a group that included Davis's nephew, Orlando "Baby Lane" Anderson.

Shakur and Knight were later heading to a nightclub where Shakur was scheduled to perform.

They stopped at a red light near the Las Vegas Strip, where a white Cadillac pulled up beside them, and gunfire erupted.

Authorities say Davis was one of four men in the Cadillac, alongside Anderson, Deandrae Smith and Terry Brown.

Shakur was shot multiple times and died six days later. Knight survived with minor injuries.

Duane Davis was arrested by Las Vegas police in 2023. (Reuters: Las Vegas Metropolitan Police Department/Handout)

Who is Keffe D?

Davis, now 63 years old, is the only person who has been charged in relation to Shakur's murder.

He is the former leader of the South Side Compton Crips, a California gang long suspected of orchestrating Shakur's murder.

He has been awaiting trial in jail since 2023.

Why is the case going ahead now?

It's all due to Davis's own detailed descriptions of the evening.

In a 2019 memoir he co-authored, Compton Street Legend, Davis wrote that Shakur and his entourage had "crossed the line" when they beat up Anderson.

"We couldn't let no record company studio gangsters do us like that," the book reads.

He wrote that he was sitting in the passenger seat of the Cadillac and passed a gun to the back seat, adding that moments before the shooting, Davis and Knight "looked each other dead in the eye" like "two rams locking horns".

A graphic of the alleged Cadillac occupants displayed during the trial. (AP: Steve Marcus/Pool)

The memoir, as well as past interviews with investigators, revived the cold case and led to him being charged.

As the trial got underway on Monday, local time, Chief Deputy District Attorney Binu Palal said Davis was the "one person who has a hard time being silent".

D Dannielle Maguire So, it's been almost 30 years since Tupac died. Is that going to make things harder for prosecutors? E Elissa Fitzgerald You bet. Many eyewitnesses are no longer alive. The three other men who were riding in the Cadillac have died since then, and never faced any charges over the attack. D Dannielle Maguire Does that make Keffe D the only living person who witnessed the murder? E Elissa Fitzgerald Alongside Suge Knight, yes. Here's what Palal said as the trial got underway: "When he says he's the only person who can tell what happened, he's right."

How is Keffe D's legal team defending him?

Davis has pleaded not guilty to one count of murder with the use of a deadly weapon.

His lawyers have argued that any descriptions Davis previously put forward about the night were fictitious, and that Compton Street Legend is not based in fact.

Michael Sanft has argued Duane Davis's descriptions of the night Tupac Shakur died were false. (Reuters: Steve Marcus)

"What they are telling you, they are representing as fact, when it's really fiction," defence attorney Michael Sanft said of the narrative put forward by the prosecution, which leans on Davis's own comments.

Mr Sanft said Davis wasn't previously charged for the 1996 killing because law enforcement knew that he was "full of crap".

D Dannielle Maguire So, can prosecutors use the memoir as evidence? E Elissa Fitzgerald Davis's defence team did fight to have it excluded, but Judge Carli Kierny ruled the memoir, and his related statements, are all admissible evidence.

Mr Sanft also pointed to missing documents in the original investigation and distrust between police departments.

What other evidence do prosecutors have?

The prosecution will also lean on Davis's comments from interviews with authorities through the years.

D Dannielle Maguire Let's dig a little more into those interviews. You say there have been several? E Elissa Fitzgerald That's right. Mr Palal said Davis spoke with the FBI in 1998 and 1999, and admitted he had been in Las Vegas at the time of the shooting. Then we get to a 2008 interview with a federal task force investigating the killing of Biggie Smalls, in which Davis talked about the Shakur shooting and handing the gun to the men in the back seat. And Mr Palal said in 2009, Davis admitted to his role in the killing in an interview with Las Vegas police.

Security footage also shows Shakur and his entourage confronting Anderson hours before the shooting.

The prosecution will call between 35 and 45 people to the stand, including police and technical witnesses.

Knight, who was in the car with Shakur at the time of the shooting, is also on the witness list and may be summoned, but he has said he wants no part in the trial.

Marion Knight is currently serving a 28-year prison sentence in California for running over and killing a man in 2015. (Reuters: Paul Buck/Pool)

Authorities also seized items such as computers and hard drives from Davis's home.

What can we expect from the trial?

It is expected to last up to six weeks.

The outcome will come down to whether the jury believes the narratives put forward by Davis in his memoir and elsewhere.

Davis is not accused of pulling the trigger but could still be found guilty of murder and given a life sentence under Nevada law.

ABC/AP

World.title: New mental health unit needed at Prince Charles Hospital, inquest hears
World.content:
A nurse has told an inquest into a cluster of patient suicides at a large Brisbane public hospital that "a whole new mental health unit" is needed.

Warning: This article contains references to mental health and suicide.

The registered nurse, whose name cannot be published, was on shift at The Prince Charles Hospital on the day Kendal Quicke, 31, died by suicide in November 2023.

A coronial inquest is examining the deaths of Ms Quicke and two other patients, Barry Ellery, 77, and Miranda Meyer, 37, who also took their own lives at the facility the same year.

The Mental Health Facility at Prince Charles Hospital north of Brisbane. (ABC News: Michael Lloyd)

The inquest heard that on the day Ms Quicke died, a protocol was in place for nurses to visually observe her every 15 minutes.

The nurse witness was asked extensive questions about whether those observations were done.

She was asked about records showing Ms Quicke was in the toilet when the nurse checked on her at 3:10pm.

"It says in my statement I called out to Kendal are you okay and she immediately responded that she was," the nurse said.

She confirmed she did not actually see Ms Quicke.

Counsel then asked the nurse: "The correct way in which to do therapeutic observation is to directly visualise a patient isn't it?"

"Not all the time — you have to respect their dignity," the nurse replied.

The registered nurse was also asked if she had any recollection of Ms Quicke's former partner warning her, in person when delivering a bag of belongings, that the patient had been googling methods of suicide while in hospital.

"No, I don't recall," the nurse replied.

She also did not recall if the patient's former partner specifically suggested an item should be removed for safety reasons.

The nurse told the inquest that physical changes made to bathroom doors since the cluster of suicides had made the unit safer and there had been improvements with staffing and the freeing up of nurse team leaders from some duties.

The nurse told the inquest the current facility has "blind spots". (ABC News: Michael Lloyd)

However, when asked what more could be done to improve the facility, the nurse said: "Can I just be really broad and say we need a whole new mental health unit?"

"There's blind spots, there's so many things, I could go on and on and on, I would like a purpose-built mental health unit," the nurse told the court.

She was also asked if the facility was full most of the time.

"Yes, absolutely," she answered.

More questions on search history

A different mental health nurse who worked at the hospital in 2023 recalled her interactions with Ms Quicke on the morning she died.

A lawyer representing the families of the deceased patients asked the nurse if she was aware Ms Quicke's former partner had informed the ward that she had been googling self-harm methods.

The nurse also responded that she wasn't aware.

When asked if information about such google searches would have been "relevant to your opinion on her risk" the nurse replied "yes, it would have".

Inquest into suicides at Prince Charles Hospital A coronial inquest has begun into three patient suicides within a seven-month period inside the mental health unit of a major Brisbane hospital.

The nurse also agreed that had she known about the patient's internet searches she would have been more alert to looking for safety risks in her room and informing other nursing staff.

However, the registered nurse also said the 31-year-old appeared "quite calm" and had "no visible signs of distress" when she had a conversation with her that morning.

"And that is why I handed over that we had a very good, plus lengthy, conversation in my email and I remember leaving that day thinking that it was a good conversation," said the nurse who can't be named.

The inquest before coroner Megan Fairweather is due to run for two weeks.

It will examine the appropriateness and adequacy of the mental health care and treatment provided by the Metro North Hospital and Health Service at the time of the three deaths.

World.title: Why South Koreans thought Trump's drill decision was 'fake news'
World.content:
In a strikingly friendly meme posted on Truth Social, United States President Donald Trump shared a photo of North Korea's Kim Jong Un asking a simple question: "Hey Donald, we cool … right?"

According to Mr Trump, they are more than cool.

A meme featuring North Korean leader Kim Jong Un that US President Donald Trump posted to his Truth Social account on August 18, 2026. (Truth Social: Donald Trump)

He told reporters at the White House that Mr Kim has "always treated me with great respect".

North Korea's leader had also responded to requests for a conversation, and it was "very positive", Mr Trump said.

"I understand him. He understands me."

An AI-generated image of Donald Trump and Kim Jong Un the US President shared to his Truth Social account on August 18, 2026. (Truth Social: Donald Trump)

The comments come after Mr Trump ordered the Pentagon to scale back joint military exercises with South Korea on the day they began.

He had said the exercises sent a "totally inappropriate and hostile" signal to North Korea and the US president believed what he was doing was "making it much safer".

"[Mr Kim] didn't like [former US president Joe] Biden. He didn't like [former president Barack] Obama. He didn't like anybody," he said.

" But I get along with him very well. "

To visit Kim, Xi made an exception Xi Jinping and Kim Jong Un's bilateral talks in North Korea were a big departure from the Chinese president's usual diplomacy playbook because, for this first time this year, he was the one travelling abroad to make the meeting happen.

The military drills, which will involve 18,000 South Korean troops over 11 days, are designed to practise responding to an attack by North Korea.

But they also act as a show of force and deterrent to Pyongyang.

The annual exercises are still proceeding, but Mr Trump's late call to "substantially reduce" them has prompted speculation he is courting a meeting with the North Korean leader.

Trump's friendly overtures to Kim

In the past week, North Korea has fired two ballistic missiles into the sea toward Japan in what has become an almost standard pre-emptive response to US and South Korean military drills, which it denounces as an "invasion rehearsal".

Despite Mr Trump tying his military drills decision to South Korea's lack of assistance in Iran, it is being widely viewed as an overture to Mr Kim.

Donald Trump has ordered the Pentagon to scale back joint military exercises with South Korea. (Reuters: Kevin Lamarque)

During his first term, Mr Trump held meetings with the North Korean leader in a bid to get Pyongyang to disarm, but the regime has accelerated its nuclear program in the years since.

Retired South Korean Lieutenant General In-bum Chun said North Korea has no intention of giving up its nuclear weapons and he didn't think "curtailing of the [military] exercises is going to help at all".

"The only way you're going to get Kim Jong Un to the table is by announcing that we recognise Kim Jong Un and North Korea as a nuclear weapons state."

In response to Mr Trump's original social media post, South Korea's presidential office said it "hopes that the friendly relationship between the US and North Korean leaders will lead to meaningful dialogue between the two countries, opening discussions aimed at advancing peace and stability on the Korean Peninsula".

South Korea's president, Lee Jae Myung, recently made his own call for talks with North Korea, proposing they try to meet and officially end the Korean War.

Lieutenant General Chun said his "biggest concern" was not Mr Trump reducing the military exercises, but that a "progressive government in South Korea" might support the position, "weakening our position to negotiate with North Korea".

North Korea fires ballistic missile towards Japan as region boosts military A short-range ballistic missile was fired over the Sea of Japan, according to Japan and South Korea's militaries, a day after Pyongyang criticised Japan's military build-up in the region.

"This kind of gesture of goodwill will only be perceived by North Korea — and the Chinese and the Russians and the Iranians — as a weakness of the United States," he said.

The potential of another round of talks with the US comes as North Korea strengthens its military relationship with Russia, and amid speculation it will send more troops to fight in the War in Ukraine.

Some are viewing the interest in dialogue from Mr Trump as a way of impeding those growing ties.

James Acton, the co-director of the Carnegie Nuclear Policy Program, said he was "very sceptical" Pyongyang would agree to speak about denuclearisation.

"If the goal is somewhat less ambitious, if the goal has some form of risk reduction, slowing or conceivably halting North Korea's development of nuclear weapons, I think that is a potentially more productive thing to talk about."

He is also concerned that South Korea's "entirely reasonable loss of trust in the US" could strengthen voices in "South Korea who are interested in acquiring their own nuclear weapons".

Allies questioning US reliability

After almost four decades in South Korea's army, Lieutenant General Chun has seen military exercises changed for diplomatic reasons before.

But he concedes the timing of Mr Trump's message was "surprising" and the delivery method "a bit concern[ing]".

"Many Koreans initially thought it was fake news," he told the ABC.

Lieutenant General Chun said having a significant change "announced publicly and linked to a personal relationship with Kim Jong Un" would have allies "questioning" the US' commitment.

"It's all our problem — Japan, Australia, everybody — that this kind of unpredictability and notion of discussing these … very important issues through public channels, does not give predictability or confidence in the collective defence decision-making process," he said.

The US president has linked his call to scale back the military drills with the fact South Korea has not assisted with the war in Iran, saying "all I want is fairness".

"I said [to South Korean President Lee Jae Myung]: 'Would you like to give us a little hand? We don't need help with Iran. But if you'd like, give us a hand with Iran.'

"He said, 'No, thanks.'"

Mr Trump pointed to the US troops stationed in South Korea "guarding you from Kim Jong Un, your next-door neighbour" when questioning why "you're not going to help us on a very easy military operation in Iran?"

Analysts have pointed to South Korea's limited ability to assist, its distance from the Middle East and the fact it "has its hands full" with North Korea and China.

Mr Acton said extended deterrence against nuclear threats depended on trust and US allies would now be "seriously question[ing]" whether the "United States would actually come to their defence in the event that they were subject to attack".

"President Trump has always been very clear that he doesn't value alliances," he said.

" He treats them like a geopolitical protection racket. "

Lieutenant General Chun said it was an "unsettling message to America's allies in Asia" that commitments may be "viewed through a transactional lens" and could "potentially be adjusted according to the President's relationship with an adversary".

But despite the "damage" to the "reliability of the US as an ally", he said it "does not mean the US alliance system in Asia is collapsing".

"The military relationships, treaties, and shared strategic interests remain substantial," he said.

Questions in Asia

Just days before Mr Trump's call to reduce the military drills, the US pulled its last aircraft carrier out of Asia.

The USS George Washington left the Pacific to replace a ship deployed in the Middle East as part of operations against Iran.

It has been viewed by some analysts as evidence of a US retreat from the Asia-Pacific.

Donald Trump met Kim Jong Un three times during his previous term. (AP: Evan Vucci)

Malcolm Davis, a senior analyst in defence strategy at the Australian Strategic Policy Institute, said while the withdrawal was viewed as a "concerning signal" and "not helpful", he does not think the US is "thinking in terms of a wholesale drawdown of forces" from the region.

"They understand that China is the main threat in the region, that China ultimately wants to see the US excluded from the region," he said.

"So I don't see the US essentially giving China what it wants."

He points to the 2026 US National Defense Strategy, which stated South Korea should "take primary responsibility for deterring North Korea with critical but more limited US support".

But while he does not think there is a broader shift away from Asia, he said South Korea would be "seeking clarification" from the Trump administration.

"I think the South Koreans will be wanting signs of reassurance that this is not the beginning of a longer-term trend, which would see the US turn away from one of its most important allies in the region," he said.

"From an Australian perspective, we will continue to see America as one of our most important allies and partners.

"They can't be replaced in that sense. There's no alternative to the United States."

About a dozen Australian Defence Force personnel are taking part in the military exercises on the peninsula, working as part of the United Nations command.

Australia's deputy prime minister and defence minister, Richard Marles, will meet with his Japanese counterpart in Canberra today, as the two countries continue to strengthen their security ties.

Lieutenant General Chun said he expects Mr Trump's call to reduce the military drills will be discussed.

"I am sure it will be, and it should be," he said.

World.title: Former support worker gives evidence during inquest into death of boy sleeping in skip bin
World.content:
The former manager of an Aboriginal support service has told an inquest into the death of a 13-year-old boy, that she felt police and child protection authorities were "beating her up" over not doing a good job of managing children in the regional South Australian city.

WARNING: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander readers are advised that this article contains the name and image of an Indigenous person who has died, used with the permission of their family.

Budda Spencer, as his family would like him to be known for cultural reasons, died in May 2021, after the industrial skip bin he was sleeping in was tipped into a rubbish truck during a routine collection.

Two young boys, aged 11 and 12 who were under the Department for Child Protection's (DCP) care, were also sleeping in the bin, but they were unharmed.

Budda Spencer was not under the department's care.

Budda Spencer was sleeping in an industrial skip bin before he died. (Supplied)

The former manager of Port Lincoln's Aboriginal Family Support Services (AFSS) Angela Backman told the inquest on Tuesday she felt both SA Police and the child protection department did not understand her service's therapeutic approach to encourage children to return to their families.

"I went to a meeting and I just felt like DCP and SAPOL were saying that we weren't doing our job because the children were constantly going missing," Ms Backman told the court.

Ms Backman said AFSS's role was to support parents and help keep Port Lincoln families together.

"At one point we were driving around behind these young people, following them everywhere in town — to the point that it was putting them at risk where they were jumping out in front of cars … we had to pull back," she told the inquest.

"That is not how we work, our role working with children is to build relationships and work in a therapeutic manner.

" At one point SAPOL said we should put barbed wire around a residential service, so I thought that was quite … not productive. "

Angela Backman was a former manager of Port Lincoln's Aboriginal Family Support Services. (ABC North and West SA: Jodie Hamilton)

Counsel for SAPOL Ben Garnaut questioned Ms Backman whether that sentiment was on one or multiple occasions.

"One occasion," Ms Backman replied.

"I think [the police] were frustrated."

Support from the department

Ms Backman told the inquest her former service would provide "voluntary" parenting programs, and offered Budda Spencer's mother Deborah Betts support, but she did not attend due to illness.

She told the court AFSS provided regular support to Budda Spencer's two friends related to the inquest, and became familiar with the 13-year-old through them.

Ms Backman explained DCP would enlist her service to read out to families needing support, and she would provide programs to support those families who chose to join — and if families did not engage, she would refer the "risk" back to DCP.

Police at the scene after the 13-year-old boy died in May 2021. (ABC News)

Counsel assisting Rebecca Schell asked Ms Backman if she felt there should be more overarching support from the DCP, including departmental staff physically attending meetings with AFSS staff.

Ms Backman agreed, adding DCP were "the ones that have the powers to enforce participation, we don't have any of that".

The former manager also told the inquest DCP generally were not visiting at-risk children.

"They're supposed to have a relationship with the children, they never visited the children — so they didn't quite understand what we had to deal with on a day-to-day basis," she said.

Concerns raised before his death

During her opening statements, counsel assisting Rebecca Schell told the court Budda Spencer's mother became "increasingly worried about her son", which she had reported to multiple agencies.

Ms Schell said a notification was raised with the DCP in March 2021 that Budda Spencer was an "adolescent at risk".

"On one occasion, [Budda] Spencer had attempted to hitchhike to Ceduna — that was at the end of March 2021," Ms Schell said.

"On another occasion, his family had reported him missing on Facebook and to the police."

Budda Spencer's mother and maternal grandmother attend the inquest this week. (ABC Eyre Peninsula: Jodie Hamilton)

Ms Schell said a week before Budda's death, Ms Betts attended Port Lincoln Health Services to seek assistance for her son.

"[Budda] Spencer had lost weight and by this stage his attitude was said to be poor," Ms Schell said.

"He would run away from family when they saw him.

"Deborah Betts thought she was losing control of her son."

Ms Schell said there were a series of notifications raised between the end of March 2021 and to [Budda] Spencer's death two months later.

"These notifications to the Department for Child Protection will be explored as a part of this inquest," she said.

"Concerns were raised about his general wellbeing at a meeting on 4 May 2021, which was only six days prior to his death," Ms Schell said.

The court heard the meeting was attended by various agencies which included West Coast Youth support services, Youth Justice, AFSS, SA Police and the Department for Human Services.

World.title: In her final months, Hayden Panettiere chose to be 'brutally honest'
World.content:
In the final months before Hayden Panettiere's death at 36, the actor spoke candidly of her traumatic experiences and shared messages of inspiration.

The former child star, known for her roles in TV shows such as Heroes and Nashville, was found unresponsive in an apartment in Greenville, South Carolina, and was pronounced dead at the scene on Sunday, police said.

The cause of death is yet to be established, but police said there were no signs of foul play.

Her death came just months after the publishing of her memoir, This Is Me: A Reckoning — a book in which she decided to be "brutally honest" about "every aspect of my life, from childhood to now".

"I had to learn not to be afraid of what people would think about it. Or if they would judge me," she told The Independent newspaper in May.

Panettiere experienced numerous hardships during her decades in the spotlight, including the death of her younger brother Jansen Panettiere in 2023.

This is what the actress has said about growing up as a child actor, struggling with substance abuse and battling with her mental health.

On being a child star

Panettiere grew up as a child actor, performing in s and soap operas before landing a voice acting role as Princess Dot in the 1998 movie A Bug's Life.

Her mother, former soap opera actor Lesley Vogel, started taking Panettiere to commercial auditions when she was an infant.

Hayden Panettiere shot into mainstream fame at a young age. (Reuters: Andrew Kelly)

In her memoir, Panettiere wrote of how the traumatic storylines she portrayed in soap operas as a child led her to associate "catastrophe with adoration".

"Grown-ups gave me positive attention when — as an actor — I failed, got sick, screamed and cried, killed, grieved, and suffered," she wrote.

" Is it any wonder why I've faced so many real struggles in my life? I've often wondered whether — unintentionally — I've brought on my traumas because I'm wired to think they're good for me. "

Panettiere reached mainstream fame in 2006 for her role as a cheerleader with supernatural powers in the TV show Heroes, a role that led her whole family to relocate to Los Angeles.
