"My mum bought an apartment for me when I was 16 and my whole family lived in it. So again, it was just that very strange, uncomfortable feeling of the role reversal and desperately wanting to still feel like the kid and still feel like I had parents to lean on," Panettiere told host Jay Shetty on his podcast, On Purpose.

Hayden Panettiere's brother Jansen died in 2023. (AP Photo: Dan Steinberg)

She said she couldn't remember a time when her mother wasn't acting as a "momager" — a word referring to a mother who also manages the career of their famous child — and she feared disappointing her.

"She was my boss, that's how I saw her. Even if she was the most supportive person when I did what I was supposed to do and did it well and was the one cheering me on, it did feel like it was what I had to do to get her love."

On postpartum depression

In 2014, 25-year-old Panettiere welcomed her daughter Kaya with her then-partner, former professional boxer Wladimir Klitschko.

After giving birth, Panettiere was haemorrhaging and needed seven blood transfusions as well as surgery, she said in an interview to Momé in July.

When she got to see her baby after the operation, Panettiere said she "felt nothing".

Hayden Panettiere with ex-fiance Wladimir Klitschko. (Reuters)

"I had always heard that mums feel an instant rush of love, but I didn't — and I had no idea why," she told Momé.

After trying to self-medicate with alcohol, Panettiere sought help and finally received a diagnosis of postpartum depression.

Panettiere first opened up about her postpartum depression in 2015 on the US morning talk show Live with Kelly and Michael.

Gaps in postnatal depression support Each year in Australia, up to 100,000 families will be affected by postnatal depression or anxiety after birth. However, only a fraction receive treatment.

"When they tell you about postpartum depression, you think about, 'Okay, I feel negative feelings towards my child, I want to injure my child, I want to hurt my child,'" she said.

"I've never ever had those feelings and some women do, but you don't realise what broad of a spectrum you can really experience that on, and it's something, I think, that needs to be talked about and women need to know that they're not alone.

"There's a lot of misunderstanding and I feel like there's a lot of people out there who think that it's not real, that it's not true, that it's something that's made up in their mind.

" It's something that's completely uncontrollable and it's really painful and scary. "

In her interview with Shetty, Panettiere said cosmetics brand Neutrogena cancelled a decade-long endorsement deal with her after she spoke of her postpartum depression, citing a morality clause.

"Of all the things I had been caught doing, that being the thing where they drew the line, was shocking to me," Panettiere said.

On 'self-numbing' her anxiety

On the set of her TV show Nashville, Panettiere said the struggles of her character Juliette closely mirrored what was happening in her private life, including writing around her pregnancy, substance abuse and struggles with parenthood.

"I was suffering from debilitating anxiety and an addiction I couldn't shake, and I had to live through it twice. First at home, as Hayden, and then in front of millions as Juliette," she wrote in her memoir.

Hayden Panettiere said the plot lines in Nashville closely mirrored her personal life. (Supplied: Lionsgate)

"I didn't know where Juliette ended and Hayden began," she told Jay Shetty.

"I couldn't come up to air from it."

To soothe her anxiety and manage her panic attacks, she turned to substances.

"I was self-medicating and looking for relief at the bottom of a bottle … I needed to self-numb."

On losing custody of her daughter

When Panettiere and Klitschko split in 2018, their daughter, who was two years old, began living full-time in Ukraine with her father.

At the time, Panettiere was in the depths of battling her problems with substance abuse.

Hayden Panettiere pregnant with daughter Kaya in 2014. (Invision/AP: Jordan Strauss, file)

"It wasn't a decision I made lightly, nor was it a decision I even wanted to make," she told Momé.

"I was going through a really challenging time in my life … I knew I needed to be able to put her first so that I could get the help I needed and be the mum she needed me to be," she said.

"I love my daughter, and I'm so proud of the young woman she is becoming. I talk to her all the time, and I feel so connected to her."

On leaving behind abuse

In her interview with Shetty, Panettiere spoke of the support she needed to leave an abusive relationship she had been in.

"At one point I thought I had gotten out of it and gotten away from it," she told Shetty.

"Abusers, they weave themselves like weeds into your life and there's always something that they left behind. There's always something they have to come back for, there's always something that they find to keep that connection, keep you on the hook.

"I thought I was capable of doing it by myself but I needed an incredible amount of support and back-up in order to make sure that there was no way for him to find his way back in."

In her final post on Instagram on July 27, a photo of Panettiere with photographer Randall Slavin, Panettiere wrote: "Good times and good friends".

Loading Instagram content

In her memoir, Panettiere described herself as an "optimist to the core" who refused to be defined by tragedy.

World.title: Drinks in the city used to mean waiting for a taxi home. Now people catch the bus
World.content:
NationalQueenslandPublic Transport Drinks in the city used to mean waiting for a taxi home. Now people catch the bus Felicity Caldwell August 18, 2026 — 4:04pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Brisbane’s “tram-like” Metro is prompting revellers to ditch taxis and Ubers on Friday and Saturday nights, the council says. Brisbane City Council released figures showing trips on the M2 Metro, which replaced the Route 66 bus in January 2025, surged 161 per cent on Fridays and Saturdays from 7pm to midnight, compared with the previous 13 months. On those nights there are also 58 more services on the route, which connects UQ Lakes with the Royal Brisbane and Women’s Hospital. Lord Mayor Adrian Schrinner says the Metro has been very popular. Courtney Kruk Brisbane Lord Mayor Adrian Schrinner said international research showed people wanted to use a “tram-like” service, and it was the most affordable way to roll out mass transit, particularly with the Olympic and Paralympic Games on the horizon.



“When you provide 24-hour services on the weekend, people use them, so there’s great demand for it,” he said. “A lot of people are now shifting their habits. They’re using public transport instead of Ubers, and that is a great thing.” The surge has been supported by the introduction of 50¢ fares, which began as a trial under the former Labor government in August 2024. The Brisbane Metro launched in October 2024, before being quietly stopped a month later, with the M2 line then launching on January 28, 2025, and the M1 line on June 30, 2025.



Coinciding with the M1 line, there was also a shake-up of the bus timetable on June 30, 2025. Schrinner said the Metro was a trunk service, so at night people might, for example, ride it to Garden City and catch an Uber for the remainder of their journey, but the council worked with the state government to expand services where there was demand. The lord mayor said he caught the Metro at night on the Ekka public holiday with his son, expecting it would be quiet. “It was so crowded, and it’s a great thing,” he said. “In past years, you would see not so many people using public transport on public holidays, and the frequency would have normally been right down.



“But Metro comes every five to 10 minutes on public holidays.” Another route to become more popular was the 425 from Kenmore Village to the CBD, which had a 37 per cent increase in weekend patronage. QPAC executive director Rachel Healy said more than one in three patrons now arrived at its South Bank venues by public transport, and it was perfectly located near bus, train and ferry stops. “It is crazy to bring your car into central Brisbane,” she said.



The council also announced its business case for an expansion of the Brisbane Metro would be finished by August next year, with new funding from the state government meaning it was now funded by all three levels of government. Only $12 million from the federal government contribution was needed for the business case, allowing $38 million for early works. Related Article Public Transport It’s been talked about for years, but Brisbane’s third CityGlider still hasn’t arrived Schrinner said current Metros were bi-articulated vehicles produced by manufacturer Hess, but new technology had emerged, and the council would investigate the next generation of Metros while the business case was developed. This masthead previously revealed a full expansion of the Brisbane Metro was unlikely to be delivered before the 2032 Olympic Games, according to a leaked draft of its updated transport legacy plan.



The expansion was set to feature 22 new stations and stops, south to Springwood, east to Capalaba, and north to Carseldine and the airport. In response, Schrinner argued the Metro expansion could not happen without federal funding. Labor council opposition leader Jared Cassidy said the lord mayor said in February 2025 he could start on a business case after the federal government contributed $50 million, but Cassidy said progress had been delayed. World.title: Alan Jones trial live updates: ‘Complainant C’ has emotional outburst during cross-examination after suggestions of fabricating allegations as indecent assault, sexual touching trial continues
World.content:
Warning: Graphic content

Hello and welcome to our live coverage of day 10 of Alan Jones’ criminal trial on charges of indecent assault and sexual touching. My colleague Perry Duffin will be bringing you the latest from the courtroom today.

The NSW Local Court in Sydney’s historic Downing Centre court building will hear further evidence from complainant “C”, the second of six men who have accused the former 2GB host of unwanted touching and kissing over a 20-year period.

Alan Jones outside the Downing Centre Local Court on Tuesday. Steven Siewert

Jones denies the claims and is entitled to the presumption of innocence.

Jones is charged with indecently assaulting “C” eight times over a five-month period by touching and kissing him without his consent.

“C” told the court yesterday that he broke down sobbing when he told then-2GB host Ray Hadley about the alleged assaults.

He said last week that he told Jones “no” repeatedly before the then 2GB host kissed him for the first time in the lift of the broadcaster’s harbourside apartment, but the “extraordinary” power imbalance stopped him speaking out as the alleged assaults continued.

He also told the court that Jones touched him under the table on the penis over his clothing at a lunch in Sydney in front of other guests. He said one guest asked him after the lunch if he had “copped a feel”, a remark that left him “deeply embarrassed”.

The Crown alleges that Jones indecently assaulted or sexually touched six men without their consent between 2003 and 2020, and is seeking to prove 22 charges against him.

Jones’ barrister, Gabrielle Bashir, SC, said during her opening address to the court that the credibility and reliability of the complainants’ evidence would be tested.

Support is available from the National Sexual Assault, Domestic Family Violence Counselling Service at 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732) or the Men’s Referral Service on 1300 766 491.

World.title: Hit team captured surveilling gang boss’s house hours before attempted murder
World.content:
Breaking NationalVictoriaCrime Hit team captured surveilling gang boss’s house hours before attempted murder Isabel McMillan August 18, 2026 — 3:59pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The hit team responsible for gunning down crime boss Fadi Haddara surveilled his Altona North home for an hour before the execution attempt in his driveway on Sunday night, police say. The 48-year-old remains in a critical condition in hospital with several bullets still lodged in his body. He has not regained consciousness. Loading With the investigation into the brazen murder attempt in its second day, police are calling on the public to help identify a vehicle of interest in the shooting. A white Holden Commodore with a rear spoiler was captured on CCTV repeatedly driving past Haddara’s family home on Marigold Avenue, in Melbourne’s west, hours before a gunman opened fire.



Police say whoever was in the car had been keeping a close eye on the home, driving past it several times between 4.48pm and 5.45pm on Sunday afternoon. They also said it was “at times parked in the vicinity for an extended period”. Less than three hours later, Haddara was found lying in a pool of his own blood on the ground next to his black BMW. Residents reported hearing loud bangs before emergency services descended on the property. “Police are keen to speak to anyone who can identity the vehicle and its owner or occupants,” police said in a statement on Tuesday afternoon. “Detectives are also urging anyone with dashcam footage who was travelling through the Marigold Avenue area on Sunday afternoon and evening to contact police.” Fadi Haddara outside court two years ago. Jason South



Haddara remains in Royal Melbourne Hospital with life-threatening injuries, according to a friend of the family, who said the crime boss had recently undergone an MRI. The friend told this masthead that Haddara had been shot in the neck – not the face, as originally believed – and the bullet had “ricocheted through to his cheek”. Haddara was ambushed in his driveway on Sunday evening. PENNY STEPHENS Surrounded by family in hospital, the crime boss will soon undergo surgery to remove three bullets still lodged in his body, including two in his shoulders. Although he is breathing normally and is in a stable condition, the friend said Haddara’s life would probably be permanently altered by the attack.



“There is still a big feeling of surprise,” he said. “He hasn’t done anything in the last couple of years. His family is clearly distressed, including his children. Related Article Exclusive

Crime When the head of a crime family found trackers on his car, he knew the game was up “He’s been living a low-key life, looking after his kids.” Haddara was accused of holding a commanding position over the illicit tobacco trade in Melbourne – which he has always denied – but was allegedly squeezed out by a new gangland boss, Kazem “Kaz” Hamad, in early 2024. Despite his reputation, neighbours said Haddara was friendly, often waving as he drove along the street.



Detective Inspector Adam Tilley, from the Victoria Police armed crime squad, on Monday said police would remain on alert for retaliatory attacks after the failed execution. “We hope this isn’t the start of any ongoing feud,” he said. “The difference between someone receiving a non-fatal injury [and] a homicide is only a matter of centimetres.” Anyone with information or dash-cam footage is urged to contact Crime Stoppers on 1800 333 000 or online at www.crimestoppersvic.com.au Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Is being frugal really such a bad thing?
World.content:
August 18, 2026 — 3:55pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Your recent column stopped me in my tracks. You suggest that an “attachment to frugality” can limit your financial growth, and propose gradually increasing your capacity to spend, with the goal of “find[ing] yourself more inspired to want to create more wealth”. Huh? Might I ask you to have another think about your proposition? The experience of Warren Buffett suggests the nexus between frugality and limited financial growth is not fixed. If someone is content with their frugal lifestyle, why upend this? First, a correction: I suggested increasing one’s capacity to enjoy spending money. I’m not saying to spend more – I’m saying to enjoy spending more. You can spend $100, happily or unhappily. For those attached to frugality, every expense hurts. This is what I was addressing. The key difference isn’t in the amount you’re spending – it’s the mindset with which you’re spending it. Simon Letch Second, you are correct. If someone is content with their frugal lifestyle, and has no desire to change this, there’s no need to upend anything. I was not writing for that person. I was writing for the person who wants to continue to pursue more financial growth. Now, I don’t know Warren Buffett, but I have coached multimillionaires who are wealthy on paper and still feel constrained, anxious, scared to spend, or unable to experience the level of enjoyment and freedom you truly desire.



They’re not frugal because they enjoy it or want to be – they’re frugal because it’s become a habit they can’t break. So, while Warren Buffett is celebrated for being a frugal billionaire, is that admirable, in and of itself? But presumably your point was that you can be frugal and pursue financial growth. You can do both. Technically, it is possible. However, frugality can also be a constraint. Do you really not enjoy spending money? Or are you just scared of spending it? I want you to imagine you have “enough”. Maybe you have a fully paid-off home, you have enough in investments to cover a comfortable lifestyle. Now, would you choose to do the work to keep pursuing financial growth – even if you didn’t “need” more? For many people, the answer is “no”. Why keep going, if you don’t need more? You wouldn’t. Unless – there is a level beyond need. After you are financially secure, the next level isn’t defined by need. No one needs to be rich. No one needs first-class flights or an extra bedroom. Those aren’t needs. They’re desires.



But if you’ve spent the past few decades being “financially responsible”, curtailing all your “wants” and only allowing yourself “needs”, then you might not have a great relationship with desire. You might be so conditioned to suppressing your desires, squashing them before they can even surface, that you might not even feel desire any more. This might even feel like contentment. Editor's pick Opinion

Ask an expert I’m making good money. So why does everything still feel like a slog? Paridhi Jain Money contributor This takes some introspection. Are you really content? Or did you just suppress all desire? Do you really not enjoy spending money? Or are you just scared of spending it? Is there really nothing you want to spend money on? Or has frugality become an identity you’re attached to? I’m not suggesting one should pursue growth beyond what they need. I’m not saying it’s wrong to live a life of frugality. It’s your life. Live it how you want. What I’m saying is – if you do want to pursue a higher level of financial growth, being overly attached to frugality might become a constraint if it robs you of any inspiration to pursue further growth. You might find it easier and more enjoyable to continue pursuing growth if you gave yourself permission to enjoy the rewards of your work along the way.



This is applicable to many areas of life. If you have a sedentary lifestyle, you might lack any real motivation to pursue higher levels of fitness. Sure, it’s “good for you” – but that’s not a compelling source of motivation. However, if there’s something you’re actually excited to do – such as climb a mountain with a friend, get in shape for your wedding, compete in a sport you enjoy – now you have a personal, compelling reason to pursue a higher level of fitness. The difference is that when it comes to money, the dominant narrative is that spending is bad, and the goal should always be to spend less. If that’s your world view, then the idea of enjoying spending will feel triggering because spending isn’t to be enjoyed – it’s to be eliminated. But the point isn’t to spend or not spend. The point is to experience life more fully. Does this require you to spend more? No. But does it mean it might be beneficial to stop grasping so tightly to money because you’re terrified to spend it? Yes. And when you do, might the natural consequence of this be that you end up spending more? Maybe, but not necessarily. The key difference isn’t in the amount you’re spending – it’s the mindset with which you’re spending it.

World.title: Men run the AFL and it is time they fixed its dark underbelly
World.content:
SportAFLAFL off-field behaviour Opinion Men run the AFL and it is time they fixed its dark underbelly Angela Pippos Contributor August 18, 2026 — 3:54pm

August 18, 2026 — 3:54pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

When Sydney Swans CEO Matthew Pavlich addressed the media on Monday about the alleged sexual assault scandal enveloping his club, he said he was “shocked and disappointed” that the players have “found themselves in this situation”. The “situation” he was referring to was that after their game against Essendon on Sunday, five Swans players had been out drinking to 3am then invited women back to their rooms at the Pullman Hotel, which were paid for by the AFL. Swans CEO Matthew Pavlich. Sitthixay Ditthavong Pavlich’s language bizarrely implies that the players somehow stumbled into a situation not of their making. At least one woman has since made an allegation of sexual assault about what unfolded in that hotel room. Eight police officers attended the hotel and are investigating. To date, none of the players have been formally interviewed or charged.



We don’t yet know what happened in that hotel room but at a bare minimum, sexual assault allegation aside, by bringing two women back after a night drinking the players involved have apparently shown no regard towards their partners, their teammates, and their AFLW team. It’s staggering professional athletes who have had so much training about acceptable behaviour in their positions as role models to young men, who have access to club welfare and support officers, thought this would be deemed acceptable. But more important than the players’ apparent selfishness is the disturbing, all-too familiar response to the latest sexual assault allegation to rock the AFL. The knee-jerk reaction from some in football has been to erase the alleged victim/s from the picture. Clockwise from left, the Swans players involved in the hotel scandal: Chad Warner, Riley Bice, Isaac Heeney and James Jordon. Michael Howard Instead, the focus has been on the five players and the inconvenient timing of the allegation at the pointy end of the season. When Pavlich addressed the media with his carefully worded comments, he should have found space to mention that all women have a right to safety, as several other public figures have. Instead his players “found” themselves in the situation, not “put” themselves in it.



Related Article Updated

AFL 2026 ‘Extremely disappointed’: Cox breaks silence as police release update on Swans investigation Language matters in cases as serious as this. Sexual assault is a grossly underreported crime in Australia and one of the reasons why people don’t go to police is they know they’re in for an avalanche of victim-blaming if they do. But it’s not only the response from the Swans that has a Groundhog Day feel about it. Just two weeks ago, former footballer and television host Sam Newman said on a podcast that the woman raped by AFL players’ agent Ralph Carr “might have had some buyer’s remorse”.



Comments like this are sadly predictable, ill-informed and dangerous in a society where gendered violence is a national crisis. For decades, women have done all the heavy lifting in shifting the culture of sport. We’ve been the ones who have spoken out about the dark underbelly, often to the detriment of our mental health and careers. We’ve been the ones who have shouldered the conversations about basic decency and respect. We’ve put ourselves in the firing line because we want the culture to change so girls and women feel safe and respected, and have properly resourced pathways, facilities, and elite competitions to be their sporting best. And my god, at times it has been ugly.



I’ve worked in both sport and politics and women in both spheres are subject to abuse, but there’s something particularly vile about the abuse women in sport cop – it’s next level, visceral, and it comes from a belief that women don’t belong in sport. Like clockwork, this latest allegation has brought with it the “boys will be boys” defence on social media and unleashed a toxic torrent of abuse towards women who dare to question the culture and show empathy towards the alleged victim or victims. And, with it, a barrage of rape jokes. It’s time for men in football – senior figures in the AFL, retired players, current players, leaders at local clubs, commentators and journalists – to take a proactive stand against the dark elements of sporting culture in a hypermasculine team sport. It’s time for them to do their bit. And by “do their bit”, I simply mean call out and educate the community about sexist and demeaning behaviour – the kind of behaviour that excuses and validates gendered violence.



It’s time for men to wrap their heads around the misogyny pyramid, which shows how sexist jokes and banter at the bottom create the social context to excuse the more egregious behaviour that sits at the top. It’s not too much to ask. Related Article Exclusive

AFL 2026 Swans players set to be punished under AFL rules as police investigation continues I’ve seen sport change over the past three decades. The introduction of the AFL Women’s competition has brought with it a sisterhood unafraid to challenge the status quo. But there’s a limit to how much can be achieved when your views aren’t equally respected and you don’t have the same decision-making clout. Unfortunately, there is no magic wand that will get rid of deeply entrenched sexism and disrespect towards women, but the reality is we cannot affect real change without men.



Men in football have the power to create a safer and fairer environment for women, if the will is there. I’d even go a step further and say men have a responsibility to fix it. It breaks my heart but here’s another opportunity. Let’s see if they take it. Angela Pippos is a veteran sports journalist, writer, filmmaker and former political adviser. World.title: Changing fortunes: Is Biotech giant CSL’s $10 billion write-down a comeback story?
World.content:
BusinessCompaniesBiotech Opinion Changing fortunes: Is Biotech giant CSL’s $10 billion write-down a comeback story? Elizabeth Knight Business columnist August 18, 2026 — 3:51pm

August 18, 2026 — 3:51pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Rarely has an Australian company booked a write-down of the magnitude of biotechnology giant CSL’s $10 billion. It is almost as extraordinary to see the share price of a company the size of CSL – $74.2 billion – leap by more than 16 per cent in an hour. Both happened on Tuesday. CSL’s share price found a strong pulse. Eamon Gallagher History tells that only BHP and Rio have had bigger write-downs than CSL – the former thanks to a disastrous foray into US shale assets, the latter thanks to its ill-conceived takeover of Canadian aluminium producer Alcan. In all three cases the companies succumbed to the folly of hubris and wildly overpaid for a business, only to feel the time-delayed sting of buyer’s remorse and shareholder anger. The achilles heel for CSL has been the 2022 acquisition of specialty pharmaceutical firm Vifor, which is responsible for the lion’s share of the write-down it reported in its 2026 financial year.



Vifor’s sales grew in 2026 but are forecast to fall by 25 per cent in the current financial year, due in part to competition from generic products, while the performance of CSL’s vaccination business Seqirus has felt the headwind of lower vaccination rates, particularly in the US. But even more significantly, CSL’s underlying sales and profit were both down slightly in 2026, having been hit by a mix of changes in its operating environment and own goals. CSL has also felt the pain of blood plasma division Behring’s struggle with an oversupply of plasma stock in the US, an issue that it is now attempting to address. So why did CSL’s share price race ahead after Tuesday’s disclosure of its mistakes and mishaps? It’s because after the recent history of earnings disappointments, management upheaval and the negative shifts in the competitive landscape, CSL offered an unexpected peek into the beginnings of a change of fortunes.



Everyone loves a comeback story. Related Article Opinion

World markets Red alert: This chart says Wall Street is ready to crash Make no mistake, the home-grown biotechnology company that for decades had allowed Australia serious boasting rights is still a long way from redemption. The rush of positive feedback from Tuesday’s earnings announcement said more about the expectation that it would be worse. Analysts were clearly caught off-guard by the better-than-expected second-half profit performance and the promise of a return to profit growth. The 2026 result came in well ahead of all expectations and sufficiently so to prompt a decent upgrade to their financial models.



For decades CSL shareholders had faith in banking double-digit gains in annual profit, and can now look forward to underlying profit growth of about 5 per cent for the 2027 financial year. The improvement will be driven by Behring, its largest business, which is expecting mid-single-digit revenue growth. The overall performance in 2027 will also feel an easing of the headwind of immunisation rates that is now stabilising in all markets but the US, where the rate of decline is slowing. Coupled with this is the axe CSL has taken to its cost line. The company called it a reset and a clear growth signal but it could more aptly be described as the first step in a tough fightback.



Its share price responded very positively to the spectre of earnings green shoots and was up more than 16 per cent to about $156.80 by lunchtime. Remember: this was a company trading above $311 only two years ago, and would have resided in most people’s superannuation funds. Those shareholders will still be disappointed. But those who picked up the stock at its June low of $90 are already in the winner’s circle. The Market Recap newsletter is a wrap of the day’s trading. Get it each weekday afternoon.

World.title: It’s old, leaking and falling apart. Yet, this humble pool could help determine who governs Victoria
World.content:
Bass Coast residents are fighting to make the Wonthaggi pool upgrade a central election issue.

Elections can be decided on hyper-local issues. In the highly marginal Bass electorate, it is not just potholes, but pools, that will help determine the outcome.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

In its day, the Wonthaggi pool was ahead of its time. When it opened in 1980, there were few indoor pools in regional Victoria. But the pool’s heyday ended long ago. The 25-metre pool, about 140 kilometres south-east of Melbourne, is primitive by modern standards. The separate children’s pool is a cramped and brutalist concrete square. Last week, the heat pump failed, forcing the cancellation of popular classes such as water aerobics. The Wonthaggi pool has long passed its use-by date. Simon Schluter Bass Coast Shire mayor, Brett Tessari said without a major upgrade the pool faced certain closure. “We’ve got bits of material falling off the walls all the time,” he said. “It’s the only pool we have. So when this does finally die, our community has no pool.” From Port Fairy in the state’s south-west, to Bendigo and Bairnsdale, regional communities have long fought to save their pools when they fall into disrepair.



Now, the Bass Coast Shire is hoping to leverage Wonthaggi’s location in one of the state’s most marginal state seats, Bass, to secure funding pledges before the November state election. Pool users Marilyn Crump and Amy Hodson. Simon Schluter In the 2022 state election, Labor won Bass by just over 200 votes on a two-party-preferred basis. Pool advocates want the upgrade to become a local election issue. “We have been advocating to all sides of the political spectrum, asking for an election promise,” Tessari said. The council has committed $15 million to the upgrade, but wants $15 million each from the state and federal governments. Tessari said the council was told about 11 years ago that the pool had a 10-year lifespan. “It’s evaporating, losing water at an incredible rate. So, it’s costing a fortune to keep the doors open.”



Despite the pool’s dilapidated state, it remains immensely popular. Figures supplied by the pool’s management show the facility had 15,000 visits a month and about 610 members. It provides lessons for about 380 students a week. Wonthaggi lies within one of Victoria’s most marginal state electorates. Simon Schluter The council wants to widen the existing 25-metre pool and build a spa, sauna, cafe and new changing rooms. It also wants a new children’s pool and another heated pool geared towards older swimmers. The council also hopes to upgrade the centre’s existing indoor sports facilities, including a gym and multipurpose rooms. The council expects demands for the aquatic centre will continue to rise. The Bass Coast Shire’s population has already surpassed 41,600, but is set to exceed 47,400 by 2036. That population growth could also influence the outcome in the Bass electorate in November. Monash University political scientist Zareh Ghazarian said winning Bass could prove crucial for whichever side wins the election.



He said Labor faced an uphill battle to form majority government without seats like Bass. Likewise, Ghazarian said, the Coalition would struggle to win without taking Bass from Labor. The dilapidated first aid room is one of the areas due for an upgrade. Simon Schluter “There’s a lot riding on Bass,” he said. “It could be one of those handful of seats that determines who wins government.” Ghazarian said candidates in Bass would have to balance the interests of diverse communities, from growth areas on Melbourne’s outskirts to more established rural areas, including Phillip Island, Inverloch and Wonthaggi. That means election promises have to be finely tuned to local communities within Bass to be successful. “They will have to be tailor-made for Bass.” Bass Labor MP Jordan Crugnale announced last year that she would not contest the November election, robbing Labor of the advantage of incumbency. Labor has preselected former Latrobe Valley Authority chief executive Chris Buckingham to contest the state election. The Liberals preselected former Bass Coast Shire mayor Rochelle Halstead.



A spokesperson for the Victorian government said the Bass Coast deserved world-class sport and aquatic facilities, and the government was working with the council to explore how it could support a redeveloped Wonthaggi pool. The spokesperson said Labor had spent $106 million on regional aquatic facilities since 2014 because people in communities like Bass should not have to travel for essential services. The opposition did not respond to a request for comment. Jordan Crugnale (far left) is retiring from state parliament. Joe Armao Inverloch resident Marilyn Crump uses the pool three times a week for water aerobics and socialising. She loves the classes and cups of tea and coffee afterwards. “If anybody’s got a problem, everybody chats about it,” she said. “It helps mentally to get past it.” Amy Hodson, 14, trains five times a week in the pool with the South Gippsland Bass Swimming Club. But the swimmers cannot compete there because it is not suitable for competition. Nor can they practise diving because the pool has no starting blocks.

World.title: One Nation’s reform is economic vandalism disguised as compassion
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

One Nation’s Barnaby Joyce and Pauline Hanson have apparently discovered a brilliant economic principle: if Australians cannot afford to live today, let them spend the money they will need tomorrow (“Chalmers warns of Hanson threat to super after One Nation leader calls system ‘broken’”, 17 August). Joyce wants broader access to super for housing and hardship; Hanson says the system is “broken”. What’s broken is their logic. If people cannot afford food, rent or a home, tackle those problems – don’t hand them a crowbar and point them towards their retirement savings. COVID should have taught us the danger of treating super as readily available cash: more than $36 billion was withdrawn, much of it by people who could least afford to sacrifice future returns. Existing early-access provisions cover cases of genuine hardship. Every dollar raided today means less at retirement and years of lost returns. It simply shifts today’s problem into the future and makes it bigger. Nor does it fix housing affordability. It doesn’t build a single home; it just pours more money into the market, pushing prices higher. One Nation’s apparent unfamiliarity with what drives inflation is becoming something of a theme. It is painfully clear that Hanson and her clueless treasury spokesperson understand remarkably little about superannuation. Tackling hardship at 40 by helping create poverty at 70 isn’t reform – it’s economic vandalism dressed up as compassion. Denise McHugh, Tamworth One Nation leader Pauline Hanson and Barnaby Joyce want access to super made easier. Alex Ellinghausen What the likes of Liberal senator Andrew Bragg, and now Pauline Hanson, don’t get is that while superannuation may be “our money”, it has strings attached. It is intended for retirement and is not freely available. If it was, you might as well not have superannuation at all. Similarly, a term deposit might be your money, but you don’t expect free access it without incurring a penalty. As for people taking lump sums from super and then falling back on the age pension, blame former Liberal treasurer Peter Costello, who made all withdrawals from superannuation after the age of 60 (including lump sums) tax-free. If needs be, make incomes more attractive than lump sums (as is already happening) rather than scrapping the whole system. Talk of higher taxes on superannuation is just scaremongering. If it does happen, it will probably be on those with big accounts, which is reasonable. How much do people need to live on in retirement, and is it reasonable for the rest of the taxpayers to subsidise concessions to the rich? Australia’s compulsory superannuation system is the envy of many other countries. So much for a “public policy failure”. David Rush, Lawson Of all the subjects that could gain the attention of our political leaders, compulsory superannuation should be at the bottom of the pile. Question time, government and media focus is being wasted on a non-issue. Superannuation provides for people in their retirement and, with reduced levels of tax on their income and investment earnings, it reduces the call on other taxpayers to fund the aged pension. It significantly reduces pensioner poverty and provides a national investment fund for the future. Where is the problem? The real agenda should include gambling addiction, the budget deficit, caring for people with a disability and funding of the NDIS, artificial intelligence, poor housing affordability, the energy transition and climate change. David Hind, North Sydney As One Nation continues to enjoy strong support, Pauline Hanson and de facto deputy Barnaby Joyce are continuing to muddle their policies publicly. Apart from immigration (“One Nation in a migration muddle over visa numbers”, August 18), superannuation and taxes so far, there are no signs how the party will manage our economy. Our younger generation is smart enough to recognise the dangers of having One Nation elected to government. Peng Ee, Castle Cove Don’t opposition politicians realise the negative reaction they provoke when they criticise simply for the sake of criticising? There are plenty of legitimate reasons to hold a government to account, and that is an essential part of any democracy. But when every announcement, proposal or decision is automatically condemned, regardless of its merits, the criticism begins to lose its force. Opposition for opposition’s sake doesn’t make politicians look effective. It makes them look predictable – and eventually people stop listening. Gregory Sale, Saratoga



Ideology first Catholic Schools NSW chief executive and Liberal Party powerbroker Dallas McInerney gave the game away when he said that various conservative Coalition operatives he employed directly or indirectly “were aligned to the ideological positions of Catholic Schools NSW” (“He’s never been called an idiot”, August 18). It is not the task of Catholic Schools NSW to promote a political ideology, but to promote Catholic teaching. Given the Coalition’s persistent refusal to take climate change seriously, this puts their ideology at odds with the teaching of Pope Francis in his two teaching documents, Laudato Si’ and Laudate Deum. McInerney’s position was indeed ideological, but certainly not fully Catholic. He has no place leading a Catholic institution. Neil Ormerod, Kingsgrove Catholic Schools NSW chief executive Dallas McInerney is giving evidence at the Independent Commission Against Corruption. Internet Old boys are still boys How fitting that a group of “old boys” from Scots College have reportedly come to the defence of three current students charged with sexual assault (“Text messages emerge in Scots College rape case amid calls for principal’s resignation,” August 18). The term “old boy” prompted me to think that I have never heard of an “old girls” network from private single-sex schools. Is this because, generally speaking, women grow up more compassionate and develop meaningful relationships within other friendship groups without clinging to the old school tie? This seems so different to those boys, educated in privileged private schools, who never grow up and cling to the notion that they are the special few born to rule, to whom society’s laws and values just don’t apply. Rob Asser, Balmain East It’s great to see my tax dollars at work. Some private schools buy up city blocks and others grapple with the fallout of students allegedly committing serious crimes. May I suggest that sexual consent activist Chanel Contos be appointed to clean up the mess (“When the accused in sex crimes are children, school leaders must wake up to a toxic culture”, August 18)? Mark Paskal, Austinmer I’d like to remind readers and correspondents that there is no such thing as consent for anyone under 16. It’s a moot point whether Scots College embraces sexual consent education in the context of the recent allegations and charges. Jenny Greenwood, Hunters Hill



Current affairs addict that I am, I undertook a quick pre-bed scroll of the news. I wish I had rather just brewed some chamomile tea. The top three stories were about male violence. Scots College teens allegedly assaulting a young girl, Swans players allegedly involved in a sexual assault (“The Swans players who could be stood down on finals eve”, August 18) and the Alan Jones allegations, currently in court (“Jones accuser told Ray Hadley, Peter FitzSimons about alleged assaults”, August 18). I love men. I despair men. Christine Northam, Cronulla It seems that the three Scots students who were charged with sexual assault are out on bail. Despite new laws, 85 per cent of children refused bail in NSW are Aboriginal. Homeless children are also very unlikely to be allowed bail. It seems not all children are equal under the law. Jennifer Killen, St Peters Educational imbalance When discussing the private versus public education question, examine the facts. As private education has proliferated, Australia’s world rankings in student performance has continued to decline. Australian students once ranked near the top in most areas. Sadly, our misguided leaning towards private schooling has destroyed our performance. Very few other countries support private schools as Australia does, and guess what? They outperform us massively. How could we have got it so wrong? Ian Roberts, St Ives Off target Does anyone believe that the proposed gun buyback is effectively targeted (“The Sydney stockpiles targeted in major new surrender scheme”, August 17)? Are politicians too focused on the next election instead of trying to solve social issues properly? Do they really believe that the illegal and nefarious users will hand in their guns? Does anyone think that community gun reduction might be better aimed at the source rather than the end user? Effective change takes time, and targeting the vendors, importers, manufacturers, illegal makers and retailers might just better reduce the number of guns circulating in this country. Can the politicians please apply their minds to more effective measures? That is why we vote you in. I live in hope. Peter Singh, Dubbo The new gun buyback scheme will launch in NSW in November, six weeks before the first anniversary of the Bondi Beach attack on December 14. Craig Sillitoe



We are told Australia has more guns now before the Port Arthur shooting. It would thus appear that the current legislation to control guns has failed, with police just rubber-stamping applications. Tighter gun laws are required. Allowing farmers to possess 10 firearms and individuals four is simply too many. Are we going to have expensive buybacks every 20 years, or tighter controls on the number of firearms owned and entering our country? Brian McDonald, Willoughby Transport cost doubts The latest step towards Sydney-Newcastle high-speed rail does little to dispel “deep community scepticism” surrounding a project estimated at $90 billion (“High-speed line design right on track”, August 18). With Newcastle and the Central Coast having a combined population of about 700,000, that equates to almost $129,000 per resident. That makes the “build it and they will come” case rather ambitious. Before committing taxpayers, shouldn’t we ask whether a more sensible path exists? Tilt-train technology, which allows trains to take corners faster than standard trains and is proven globally, could allow faster services using the existing Sydney-Newcastle rail corridor, particularly through the curves north of Hornsby. Australia already knows it works on the Rockhampton-Brisbane route. Upgrading existing infrastructure could avoid much of the cost of new tunnels, bridges and land acquisitions. While high-speed rail could cut the journey to about an hour, a NSW parliamentary inquiry found tilt trains could do it in roughly one hour and 45 minutes. Is saving less than an hour really worth $90 billion? By all means investigate the project, but with $90 billion at stake, surely the cheaper alternative deserves serious consideration. As transport professor David Levinson put it: “Until they show us the money, it’s not real.” John Kempler, Rose Bay The Productivity Commission has found that “heavy vehicle transport is vital to Australia’s economy, but road freight physical productivity has stalled for more than a decade” (“Electric trucks ‘can deliver productivity boost’ ” 18 August). This means that governments have spent many billions on main roads over the past 30 years for a limited return. Two questions need to be asked: why hasn’t the commission looked at rail reform for more than 20 years? And why are there still more than 5000 heavy trucks travelling each day, in each direction, between Sydney and Melbourne? Chris O’Rourke, Bathurst Three is enough No, no, no, John, Dennis and Bipin – a thousand times no (Letters, August 18). Even if the federal pollies could just legislate four-year terms without a referendum, why should we not pass judgment regularly on our representatives? Those who want to face the will of the people less often should ring a loud warning bell. The old canard about three years not being long enough to get things done is nonsense. We see various programs (e.g. the NDIS) playing out over many years and decades, utterly unimpeded by election cycles. But longer terms would deny us the ability to remove a government quickly if it was damaging our nation and was on the nose. Ask yourself how you’d feel if a government with which you disagreed spent an extra year legislating for policies you find objectionable? You’d be happy with that? Three years is plenty of time to persuade us that you deserve another three years to continue. The fact that you can’t legislate some things quickly – indicating significant opposition among Australians and their representatives – is a good thing, not some problem to be done away with. Chris Mangan, Bracken Ridge (Qld)

World.title: Drinks in the city used to mean waiting for a taxi home. Now people catch the bus
World.content:
NationalQueenslandPublic Transport Drinks in the city used to mean waiting for a taxi home. Now people catch the bus Felicity Caldwell August 18, 2026 — 4:04pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Brisbane’s “tram-like” Metro is prompting revellers to ditch taxis and Ubers on Friday and Saturday nights, the council says. Brisbane City Council released figures showing trips on the M2 Metro, which replaced the Route 66 bus in January 2025, surged 161 per cent on Fridays and Saturdays from 7pm to midnight, compared with the previous 13 months. On those nights there are also 58 more services on the route, which connects UQ Lakes with the Royal Brisbane and Women’s Hospital. Lord Mayor Adrian Schrinner says the Metro has been very popular. Courtney Kruk Brisbane Lord Mayor Adrian Schrinner said international research showed people wanted to use a “tram-like” service, and it was the most affordable way to roll out mass transit, particularly with the Olympic and Paralympic Games on the horizon.



“When you provide 24-hour services on the weekend, people use them, so there’s great demand for it,” he said. “A lot of people are now shifting their habits. They’re using public transport instead of Ubers, and that is a great thing.” The surge has been supported by the introduction of 50¢ fares, which began as a trial under the former Labor government in August 2024. The Brisbane Metro launched in October 2024, before being quietly stopped a month later, with the M2 line then launching on January 28, 2025, and the M1 line on June 30, 2025.



Coinciding with the M1 line, there was also a shake-up of the bus timetable on June 30, 2025. Schrinner said the Metro was a trunk service, so at night people might, for example, ride it to Garden City and catch an Uber for the remainder of their journey, but the council worked with the state government to expand services where there was demand. The lord mayor said he caught the Metro at night on the Ekka public holiday with his son, expecting it would be quiet. “It was so crowded, and it’s a great thing,” he said. “In past years, you would see not so many people using public transport on public holidays, and the frequency would have normally been right down.



“But Metro comes every five to 10 minutes on public holidays.” Another route to become more popular was the 425 from Kenmore Village to the CBD, which had a 37 per cent increase in weekend patronage. QPAC executive director Rachel Healy said more than one in three patrons now arrived at its South Bank venues by public transport, and it was perfectly located near bus, train and ferry stops. “It is crazy to bring your car into central Brisbane,” she said.



The council also announced its business case for an expansion of the Brisbane Metro would be finished by August next year, with new funding from the state government meaning it was now funded by all three levels of government. Only $12 million from the federal government contribution was needed for the business case, allowing $38 million for early works. Related Article Public Transport It’s been talked about for years, but Brisbane’s third CityGlider still hasn’t arrived Schrinner said current Metros were bi-articulated vehicles produced by manufacturer Hess, but new technology had emerged, and the council would investigate the next generation of Metros while the business case was developed. This masthead previously revealed a full expansion of the Brisbane Metro was unlikely to be delivered before the 2032 Olympic Games, according to a leaked draft of its updated transport legacy plan.



The expansion was set to feature 22 new stations and stops, south to Springwood, east to Capalaba, and north to Carseldine and the airport. In response, Schrinner argued the Metro expansion could not happen without federal funding. Labor council opposition leader Jared Cassidy said the lord mayor said in February 2025 he could start on a business case after the federal government contributed $50 million, but Cassidy said progress had been delayed. World.title: Alan Jones trial live updates: ‘Complainant C’ has emotional outburst during cross-examination after suggestions of fabricating allegations as indecent assault, sexual touching trial continues
World.content:
Warning: Graphic content

Hello and welcome to our live coverage of day 10 of Alan Jones’ criminal trial on charges of indecent assault and sexual touching. My colleague Perry Duffin will be bringing you the latest from the courtroom today.

The NSW Local Court in Sydney’s historic Downing Centre court building will hear further evidence from complainant “C”, the second of six men who have accused the former 2GB host of unwanted touching and kissing over a 20-year period.

Alan Jones outside the Downing Centre Local Court on Tuesday. Steven Siewert

Jones denies the claims and is entitled to the presumption of innocence.

Jones is charged with indecently assaulting “C” eight times over a five-month period by touching and kissing him without his consent.

“C” told the court yesterday that he broke down sobbing when he told then-2GB host Ray Hadley about the alleged assaults.

He said last week that he told Jones “no” repeatedly before the then 2GB host kissed him for the first time in the lift of the broadcaster’s harbourside apartment, but the “extraordinary” power imbalance stopped him speaking out as the alleged assaults continued.

He also told the court that Jones touched him under the table on the penis over his clothing at a lunch in Sydney in front of other guests. He said one guest asked him after the lunch if he had “copped a feel”, a remark that left him “deeply embarrassed”.

The Crown alleges that Jones indecently assaulted or sexually touched six men without their consent between 2003 and 2020, and is seeking to prove 22 charges against him.

Jones’ barrister, Gabrielle Bashir, SC, said during her opening address to the court that the credibility and reliability of the complainants’ evidence would be tested.

Support is available from the National Sexual Assault, Domestic Family Violence Counselling Service at 1800RESPECT (1800 737 732) or the Men’s Referral Service on 1300 766 491.

World.title: Hit team captured surveilling gang boss’s house hours before attempted murder
World.content:
Breaking NationalVictoriaCrime Hit team captured surveilling gang boss’s house hours before attempted murder Isabel McMillan August 18, 2026 — 3:59pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The hit team responsible for gunning down crime boss Fadi Haddara surveilled his Altona North home for an hour before the execution attempt in his driveway on Sunday night, police say. The 48-year-old remains in a critical condition in hospital with several bullets still lodged in his body. He has not regained consciousness. Loading With the investigation into the brazen murder attempt in its second day, police are calling on the public to help identify a vehicle of interest in the shooting. A white Holden Commodore with a rear spoiler was captured on CCTV repeatedly driving past Haddara’s family home on Marigold Avenue, in Melbourne’s west, hours before a gunman opened fire.



Police say whoever was in the car had been keeping a close eye on the home, driving past it several times between 4.48pm and 5.45pm on Sunday afternoon. They also said it was “at times parked in the vicinity for an extended period”. Less than three hours later, Haddara was found lying in a pool of his own blood on the ground next to his black BMW. Residents reported hearing loud bangs before emergency services descended on the property. “Police are keen to speak to anyone who can identity the vehicle and its owner or occupants,” police said in a statement on Tuesday afternoon. “Detectives are also urging anyone with dashcam footage who was travelling through the Marigold Avenue area on Sunday afternoon and evening to contact police.” Fadi Haddara outside court two years ago. Jason South



Haddara remains in Royal Melbourne Hospital with life-threatening injuries, according to a friend of the family, who said the crime boss had recently undergone an MRI. The friend told this masthead that Haddara had been shot in the neck – not the face, as originally believed – and the bullet had “ricocheted through to his cheek”. Haddara was ambushed in his driveway on Sunday evening. PENNY STEPHENS Surrounded by family in hospital, the crime boss will soon undergo surgery to remove three bullets still lodged in his body, including two in his shoulders. Although he is breathing normally and is in a stable condition, the friend said Haddara’s life would probably be permanently altered by the attack.



“There is still a big feeling of surprise,” he said. “He hasn’t done anything in the last couple of years. His family is clearly distressed, including his children. Related Article Exclusive

Crime When the head of a crime family found trackers on his car, he knew the game was up “He’s been living a low-key life, looking after his kids.” Haddara was accused of holding a commanding position over the illicit tobacco trade in Melbourne – which he has always denied – but was allegedly squeezed out by a new gangland boss, Kazem “Kaz” Hamad, in early 2024. Despite his reputation, neighbours said Haddara was friendly, often waving as he drove along the street.



Detective Inspector Adam Tilley, from the Victoria Police armed crime squad, on Monday said police would remain on alert for retaliatory attacks after the failed execution. “We hope this isn’t the start of any ongoing feud,” he said. “The difference between someone receiving a non-fatal injury [and] a homicide is only a matter of centimetres.” Anyone with information or dash-cam footage is urged to contact Crime Stoppers on 1800 333 000 or online at www.crimestoppersvic.com.au Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Is being frugal really such a bad thing?
World.content:
August 18, 2026 — 3:55pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Your recent column stopped me in my tracks. You suggest that an “attachment to frugality” can limit your financial growth, and propose gradually increasing your capacity to spend, with the goal of “find[ing] yourself more inspired to want to create more wealth”. Huh? Might I ask you to have another think about your proposition? The experience of Warren Buffett suggests the nexus between frugality and limited financial growth is not fixed. If someone is content with their frugal lifestyle, why upend this? First, a correction: I suggested increasing one’s capacity to enjoy spending money. I’m not saying to spend more – I’m saying to enjoy spending more. You can spend $100, happily or unhappily. For those attached to frugality, every expense hurts. This is what I was addressing. The key difference isn’t in the amount you’re spending – it’s the mindset with which you’re spending it. Simon Letch Second, you are correct. If someone is content with their frugal lifestyle, and has no desire to change this, there’s no need to upend anything. I was not writing for that person. I was writing for the person who wants to continue to pursue more financial growth. Now, I don’t know Warren Buffett, but I have coached multimillionaires who are wealthy on paper and still feel constrained, anxious, scared to spend, or unable to experience the level of enjoyment and freedom you truly desire.



They’re not frugal because they enjoy it or want to be – they’re frugal because it’s become a habit they can’t break. So, while Warren Buffett is celebrated for being a frugal billionaire, is that admirable, in and of itself? But presumably your point was that you can be frugal and pursue financial growth. You can do both. Technically, it is possible. However, frugality can also be a constraint. Do you really not enjoy spending money? Or are you just scared of spending it? I want you to imagine you have “enough”. Maybe you have a fully paid-off home, you have enough in investments to cover a comfortable lifestyle. Now, would you choose to do the work to keep pursuing financial growth – even if you didn’t “need” more? For many people, the answer is “no”. Why keep going, if you don’t need more? You wouldn’t. Unless – there is a level beyond need. After you are financially secure, the next level isn’t defined by need. No one needs to be rich. No one needs first-class flights or an extra bedroom. Those aren’t needs. They’re desires.



But if you’ve spent the past few decades being “financially responsible”, curtailing all your “wants” and only allowing yourself “needs”, then you might not have a great relationship with desire. You might be so conditioned to suppressing your desires, squashing them before they can even surface, that you might not even feel desire any more. This might even feel like contentment. Editor's pick Opinion

Ask an expert I’m making good money. So why does everything still feel like a slog? Paridhi Jain Money contributor This takes some introspection. Are you really content? Or did you just suppress all desire? Do you really not enjoy spending money? Or are you just scared of spending it? Is there really nothing you want to spend money on? Or has frugality become an identity you’re attached to? I’m not suggesting one should pursue growth beyond what they need. I’m not saying it’s wrong to live a life of frugality. It’s your life. Live it how you want. What I’m saying is – if you do want to pursue a higher level of financial growth, being overly attached to frugality might become a constraint if it robs you of any inspiration to pursue further growth. You might find it easier and more enjoyable to continue pursuing growth if you gave yourself permission to enjoy the rewards of your work along the way.



This is applicable to many areas of life. If you have a sedentary lifestyle, you might lack any real motivation to pursue higher levels of fitness. Sure, it’s “good for you” – but that’s not a compelling source of motivation. However, if there’s something you’re actually excited to do – such as climb a mountain with a friend, get in shape for your wedding, compete in a sport you enjoy – now you have a personal, compelling reason to pursue a higher level of fitness. The difference is that when it comes to money, the dominant narrative is that spending is bad, and the goal should always be to spend less. If that’s your world view, then the idea of enjoying spending will feel triggering because spending isn’t to be enjoyed – it’s to be eliminated. But the point isn’t to spend or not spend. The point is to experience life more fully. Does this require you to spend more? No. But does it mean it might be beneficial to stop grasping so tightly to money because you’re terrified to spend it? Yes. And when you do, might the natural consequence of this be that you end up spending more? Maybe, but not necessarily. The key difference isn’t in the amount you’re spending – it’s the mindset with which you’re spending it.



Paridhi Jain is a money and mindset coach who combines practical strategies with mindset transformation to help clients create more freedom and fulfilment in wealth, work and life. World.title: Men run the AFL and it is time they fixed its dark underbelly
World.content:
SportAFLAFL off-field behaviour Opinion Men run the AFL and it is time they fixed its dark underbelly Angela Pippos Contributor August 18, 2026 — 3:54pm

August 18, 2026 — 3:54pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

When Sydney Swans CEO Matthew Pavlich addressed the media on Monday about the alleged sexual assault scandal enveloping his club, he said he was “shocked and disappointed” that the players have “found themselves in this situation”. The “situation” he was referring to was that after their game against Essendon on Sunday, five Swans players had been out drinking to 3am then invited women back to their rooms at the Pullman Hotel, which were paid for by the AFL. Swans CEO Matthew Pavlich. Sitthixay Ditthavong Pavlich’s language bizarrely implies that the players somehow stumbled into a situation not of their making. At least one woman has since made an allegation of sexual assault about what unfolded in that hotel room. Eight police officers attended the hotel and are investigating. To date, none of the players have been formally interviewed or charged.



We don’t yet know what happened in that hotel room but at a bare minimum, sexual assault allegation aside, by bringing two women back after a night drinking the players involved have apparently shown no regard towards their partners, their teammates, and their AFLW team. It’s staggering professional athletes who have had so much training about acceptable behaviour in their positions as role models to young men, who have access to club welfare and support officers, thought this would be deemed acceptable. But more important than the players’ apparent selfishness is the disturbing, all-too familiar response to the latest sexual assault allegation to rock the AFL. The knee-jerk reaction from some in football has been to erase the alleged victim/s from the picture. Clockwise from left, the Swans players involved in the hotel scandal: Chad Warner, Riley Bice, Isaac Heeney and James Jordon. Michael Howard Instead, the focus has been on the five players and the inconvenient timing of the allegation at the pointy end of the season. When Pavlich addressed the media with his carefully worded comments, he should have found space to mention that all women have a right to safety, as several other public figures have. Instead his players “found” themselves in the situation, not “put” themselves in it.



Related Article Updated

AFL 2026 ‘Extremely disappointed’: Cox breaks silence as police release update on Swans investigation Language matters in cases as serious as this. Sexual assault is a grossly underreported crime in Australia and one of the reasons why people don’t go to police is they know they’re in for an avalanche of victim-blaming if they do. But it’s not only the response from the Swans that has a Groundhog Day feel about it. Just two weeks ago, former footballer and television host Sam Newman said on a podcast that the woman raped by AFL players’ agent Ralph Carr “might have had some buyer’s remorse”.



Comments like this are sadly predictable, ill-informed and dangerous in a society where gendered violence is a national crisis. For decades, women have done all the heavy lifting in shifting the culture of sport. We’ve been the ones who have spoken out about the dark underbelly, often to the detriment of our mental health and careers. We’ve been the ones who have shouldered the conversations about basic decency and respect. We’ve put ourselves in the firing line because we want the culture to change so girls and women feel safe and respected, and have properly resourced pathways, facilities, and elite competitions to be their sporting best. And my god, at times it has been ugly.



I’ve worked in both sport and politics and women in both spheres are subject to abuse, but there’s something particularly vile about the abuse women in sport cop – it’s next level, visceral, and it comes from a belief that women don’t belong in sport. Like clockwork, this latest allegation has brought with it the “boys will be boys” defence on social media and unleashed a toxic torrent of abuse towards women who dare to question the culture and show empathy towards the alleged victim or victims. And, with it, a barrage of rape jokes. It’s time for men in football – senior figures in the AFL, retired players, current players, leaders at local clubs, commentators and journalists – to take a proactive stand against the dark elements of sporting culture in a hypermasculine team sport. It’s time for them to do their bit. And by “do their bit”, I simply mean call out and educate the community about sexist and demeaning behaviour – the kind of behaviour that excuses and validates gendered violence.



It’s time for men to wrap their heads around the misogyny pyramid, which shows how sexist jokes and banter at the bottom create the social context to excuse the more egregious behaviour that sits at the top. It’s not too much to ask. Related Article Exclusive

AFL 2026 Swans players set to be punished under AFL rules as police investigation continues I’ve seen sport change over the past three decades. The introduction of the AFL Women’s competition has brought with it a sisterhood unafraid to challenge the status quo. But there’s a limit to how much can be achieved when your views aren’t equally respected and you don’t have the same decision-making clout. Unfortunately, there is no magic wand that will get rid of deeply entrenched sexism and disrespect towards women, but the reality is we cannot affect real change without men.



Men in football have the power to create a safer and fairer environment for women, if the will is there. I’d even go a step further and say men have a responsibility to fix it. It breaks my heart but here’s another opportunity. Let’s see if they take it. Angela Pippos is a veteran sports journalist, writer, filmmaker and former political adviser. World.title: Changing fortunes: Is Biotech giant CSL’s $10 billion write-down a comeback story?
World.content:
BusinessCompaniesBiotech Opinion Changing fortunes: Is Biotech giant CSL’s $10 billion write-down a comeback story? Elizabeth Knight Business columnist August 18, 2026 — 3:51pm

August 18, 2026 — 3:51pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Rarely has an Australian company booked a write-down of the magnitude of biotechnology giant CSL’s $10 billion. It is almost as extraordinary to see the share price of a company the size of CSL – $74.2 billion – leap by more than 16 per cent in an hour. Both happened on Tuesday. CSL’s share price found a strong pulse. Eamon Gallagher History tells that only BHP and Rio have had bigger write-downs than CSL – the former thanks to a disastrous foray into US shale assets, the latter thanks to its ill-conceived takeover of Canadian aluminium producer Alcan. In all three cases the companies succumbed to the folly of hubris and wildly overpaid for a business, only to feel the time-delayed sting of buyer’s remorse and shareholder anger. The achilles heel for CSL has been the 2022 acquisition of specialty pharmaceutical firm Vifor, which is responsible for the lion’s share of the write-down it reported in its 2026 financial year.



Vifor’s sales grew in 2026 but are forecast to fall by 25 per cent in the current financial year, due in part to competition from generic products, while the performance of CSL’s vaccination business Seqirus has felt the headwind of lower vaccination rates, particularly in the US. But even more significantly, CSL’s underlying sales and profit were both down slightly in 2026, having been hit by a mix of changes in its operating environment and own goals. CSL has also felt the pain of blood plasma division Behring’s struggle with an oversupply of plasma stock in the US, an issue that it is now attempting to address. So why did CSL’s share price race ahead after Tuesday’s disclosure of its mistakes and mishaps? It’s because after the recent history of earnings disappointments, management upheaval and the negative shifts in the competitive landscape, CSL offered an unexpected peek into the beginnings of a change of fortunes.



Everyone loves a comeback story. Related Article Opinion

World markets Red alert: This chart says Wall Street is ready to crash Make no mistake, the home-grown biotechnology company that for decades had allowed Australia serious boasting rights is still a long way from redemption. The rush of positive feedback from Tuesday’s earnings announcement said more about the expectation that it would be worse. Analysts were clearly caught off-guard by the better-than-expected second-half profit performance and the promise of a return to profit growth. The 2026 result came in well ahead of all expectations and sufficiently so to prompt a decent upgrade to their financial models.



For decades CSL shareholders had faith in banking double-digit gains in annual profit, and can now look forward to underlying profit growth of about 5 per cent for the 2027 financial year. The improvement will be driven by Behring, its largest business, which is expecting mid-single-digit revenue growth. The overall performance in 2027 will also feel an easing of the headwind of immunisation rates that is now stabilising in all markets but the US, where the rate of decline is slowing. Coupled with this is the axe CSL has taken to its cost line. The company called it a reset and a clear growth signal but it could more aptly be described as the first step in a tough fightback.



Its share price responded very positively to the spectre of earnings green shoots and was up more than 16 per cent to about $156.80 by lunchtime. Remember: this was a company trading above $311 only two years ago, and would have resided in most people’s superannuation funds. Those shareholders will still be disappointed. But those who picked up the stock at its June low of $90 are already in the winner’s circle. The Market Recap newsletter is a wrap of the day’s trading. Get it each weekday afternoon.

World.title: It’s old, leaking and falling apart. Yet, this humble pool could help determine who governs Victoria
World.content:
Bass Coast residents are fighting to make the Wonthaggi pool upgrade a central election issue.

Elections can be decided on hyper-local issues. In the highly marginal Bass electorate, it is not just potholes, but pools, that will help determine the outcome.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

In its day, the Wonthaggi pool was ahead of its time. When it opened in 1980, there were few indoor pools in regional Victoria. But the pool’s heyday ended long ago. The 25-metre pool, about 140 kilometres south-east of Melbourne, is primitive by modern standards. The separate children’s pool is a cramped and brutalist concrete square. Last week, the heat pump failed, forcing the cancellation of popular classes such as water aerobics. The Wonthaggi pool has long passed its use-by date. Simon Schluter Bass Coast Shire mayor, Brett Tessari said without a major upgrade the pool faced certain closure. “We’ve got bits of material falling off the walls all the time,” he said. “It’s the only pool we have. So when this does finally die, our community has no pool.” From Port Fairy in the state’s south-west, to Bendigo and Bairnsdale, regional communities have long fought to save their pools when they fall into disrepair.



Now, the Bass Coast Shire is hoping to leverage Wonthaggi’s location in one of the state’s most marginal state seats, Bass, to secure funding pledges before the November state election. Pool users Marilyn Crump and Amy Hodson. Simon Schluter In the 2022 state election, Labor won Bass by just over 200 votes on a two-party-preferred basis. Pool advocates want the upgrade to become a local election issue. “We have been advocating to all sides of the political spectrum, asking for an election promise,” Tessari said. The council has committed $15 million to the upgrade, but wants $15 million each from the state and federal governments. Tessari said the council was told about 11 years ago that the pool had a 10-year lifespan. “It’s evaporating, losing water at an incredible rate. So, it’s costing a fortune to keep the doors open.”



Despite the pool’s dilapidated state, it remains immensely popular. Figures supplied by the pool’s management show the facility had 15,000 visits a month and about 610 members. It provides lessons for about 380 students a week. Wonthaggi lies within one of Victoria’s most marginal state electorates. Simon Schluter The council wants to widen the existing 25-metre pool and build a spa, sauna, cafe and new changing rooms. It also wants a new children’s pool and another heated pool geared towards older swimmers. The council also hopes to upgrade the centre’s existing indoor sports facilities, including a gym and multipurpose rooms. The council expects demands for the aquatic centre will continue to rise. The Bass Coast Shire’s population has already surpassed 41,600, but is set to exceed 47,400 by 2036. That population growth could also influence the outcome in the Bass electorate in November. Monash University political scientist Zareh Ghazarian said winning Bass could prove crucial for whichever side wins the election.



He said Labor faced an uphill battle to form majority government without seats like Bass. Likewise, Ghazarian said, the Coalition would struggle to win without taking Bass from Labor. The dilapidated first aid room is one of the areas due for an upgrade. Simon Schluter “There’s a lot riding on Bass,” he said. “It could be one of those handful of seats that determines who wins government.” Ghazarian said candidates in Bass would have to balance the interests of diverse communities, from growth areas on Melbourne’s outskirts to more established rural areas, including Phillip Island, Inverloch and Wonthaggi. That means election promises have to be finely tuned to local communities within Bass to be successful. “They will have to be tailor-made for Bass.” Bass Labor MP Jordan Crugnale announced last year that she would not contest the November election, robbing Labor of the advantage of incumbency.
